items.descriptionOriginal: Ο τραγουδιστής Γιώργος Τσαλίκης εξέφρασε δημόσια η χαρά και την ευγνωμοσύνη του προς τον Νίκο Καρβέλα , μετά την απόφαση του γνωστού συνθέτη να του επιτρέψει να συμπεριλάβει τραγούδια του στο πρόγραμμα των ζωντανών εμφανίσεών του. Ο γνωστός τραγουδιστής θέλησε να ευχαριστήσει προσωπικά τον δημιουργό μέσα από τον λογαριασμό του στο Instagram, δημοσιεύοντας ένα story με αφορμή την άδεια που εξασφάλισε για την ερμηνεία των τραγουδιών του στην «Αυτοκίνηση». Στο συγκεκριμένο νυχτερινό κέντρο, ο Γιώργος Τσαλίκης θα εμφανίζεται τη φετινή σεζόν μαζί με τον Διονύση Σχοινά. Η κίνηση του Νίκου Καρβέλα έχει ιδιαίτερη σημασία, καθώς ο συνθέτης έχει αλλάξει τον τρόπο με τον οποίο χορηγούνται οι άδειες για τη ζωντανή εκτέλεση των μουσικών έργων του, αναλαμβάνοντας πλέον ο ίδιος τη σχετική διαδικασία. Γιατί οι τραγουδιστές χρειάζονται πλέον προσωπική άδεια από τον Καρβέλα Η ανάρτηση του Γιώργου Τσαλίκη έρχεται λίγες εβδομάδες μετά την απόφαση του Νίκου Καρβέλα να αναλάβει προσωπικά την αδειοδότηση της ζωντανής εκτέλεσης των τραγουδιών του. Στις αρχές Οκτωβρίου έγινε γνωστό ότι ο συνθέτης είχε ανακαλέσει από τον οργανισμό συλλογικής διαχείρισης «Αυτοδιαχείριση» την εξουσία να χορηγεί τις σχετικές άδειες για λογαριασμό του. Η αλλαγή τέθηκε σε ισχύ στις 30 Σεπτεμβρίου 2026, με αποτέλεσμα οι καλλιτέχνες που επιθυμούν να ερμηνεύσουν ζωντανά έργα του να χρειάζεται πλέον να απευθύνονται στον ίδιο για να λάβουν την έγκρισή του. Η εξέλιξη αυτή έγινε γνωστή μετά τη δημόσια διαμάχη του Νίκου Καρβέλα με την Άννα Βίσση. items.titleOriginal: At 64, This Retired Delhi Judge Walked 65 km to Everest Base Camp With No Special Training
items.description: Στα 64 της, η συνταξιούχος δικαστής του Ανωτάτου Δικαστηρίου του Δελχί, Πουνάμ Μπάμπα, ενώθηκε με τον σύζυγό της σε ένα ταξίδι στην κατασκήνωση βάσης του Έβερεστ. Από εξαντλητικές αναβάσεις μέχρι έναστρες νύχτες των Ιμαλαΐων, το ταξίδι της δοκίμασε τα όριά της.
items.descriptionOriginal: At 64, retired Delhi High Court judge Poonam Bamba joined her husband on a trek to Everest Base Camp. From exhausting climbs to starry Himalayan nights, her journey tested her limits.

items.title: Destination Thessaloniki: Η Θεσσαλονίκη στο επίκεντρο του Leipzig Opera Ball με 3.000 καλεσμένους
items.titleOriginal: Destination Thessaloniki: Η Θεσσαλονίκη στο επίκεντρο του Leipzig Opera Ball με 3.000 καλεσμένους
items.description: Με τίτλο «Kalispéra Thessaloniki!» , το φετινό Leipzig Opera Ball στη Γερμανία ήταν αφιερωμένο στη Θεσσαλονίκη , προβάλλοντας τον πολιτισμό, τη μουσική, τη γαστρονομία και τη μοναδική ταυτότητα της πόλης σε περίπου 3.000 καλεσμένους. Η εκδήλωση εντάχθηκε στο πλαίσιο της πρωτοβουλίας «Destination Thessaloniki», με στόχο την ενίσχυση της διεθνούς προβολής της πόλης . Σε συνεργασία με τοπικούς…
items.descriptionOriginal: Με τίτλο «Kalispéra Thessaloniki!» , το φετινό Leipzig Opera Ball στη Γερμανία ήταν αφιερωμένο στη Θεσσαλονίκη , προβάλλοντας τον πολιτισμό, τη μουσική, τη γαστρονομία και τη μοναδική ταυτότητα της πόλης σε περίπου 3.000 καλεσμένους. Η εκδήλωση εντάχθηκε στο πλαίσιο της πρωτοβουλίας «Destination Thessaloniki», με στόχο την ενίσχυση της διεθνούς προβολής της πόλης . Σε συνεργασία με τοπικούς φορείς, παρουσιάστηκαν σε επαγγελματίες της γερμανικής τουριστικής αγοράς οι δυνατότητες της Θεσσαλονίκης ως προορισμού πολιτιστικού και συνεδριακού τ ουρισμού, γαστρονομίας και σύντομων αποδράσεων ( city break) . Στόχος των επαφών που πραγματοποιήθηκαν είναι η ανάπτυξη σταθερών συνεργασιών, η προσέλκυση περισσότερων επισκεπτών καθ’ όλη τη διάρκεια του έτους και η ενίσχυση της τοπικής οικονομίας. Στο πλαίσιο της επίσκεψης, ο δήμαρχος Θεσσαλονίκης, Στέλιος Αγγελούδης , συναντήθηκε με τον δήμαρχο Λειψίας, Burkhard Jung. Στο επίκεντρο της συζήτησης βρέθηκε η περαιτέρω αξιοποίηση της μακρόχρονης σχέσης αδελφοποίησης των δύο πόλεων, μέσα από κοινές πρωτοβουλίες στους τομείς του τουρισμού, του πολιτισμού και της καινοτομίας. Η αποστολή επισκέφθηκε επίσης το SpinLab, έναν επιταχυντή νεοφυών επιχειρήσεων που στεγάζεται στην πρώην βιομηχανική περιοχή Spinnerei της Λειψίας, όπου παλιοί βιομηχανικοί χώροι έχουν αποκτήσει νέα χρήση, συνδυάζοντας την επιχειρηματικότητα, την καινοτομία και την τέχνη. Η παρουσία της Θεσσαλονίκης στη Λειψία αποτέλεσε μια ακόμη δράση εξωστρέφειας, με στόχο την ενίσχυση της αναγνωρισιμότητάς της στη γερμανική αγορά και τη δημιουργία νέων προοπτικών συνεργασίας. www.ertnews.gr

items.description: Κρίσιμες βουλευτικές εκλογές διεξάγονται σήμερα στη Σερβία , στη σκιά σχεδόν δύο ετών μαζικών φοιτητικών κινητοποιήσεων κατά της διαφθοράς. Ο πρώην πρόεδρος Αλεξάνταρ Βούτσιτς διεκδικεί την πρωθυπουργία απέναντι στη λίστα των φοιτητών , ένα κίνημα που κατεβαίνει στις εκλογές με υποψηφίους εκτός του παραδοσιακού κομματικού συστήματος. Ανταπόκριση από το Βελιγράδι Η εκλογική διαδικασία…
items.descriptionOriginal: Κρίσιμες βουλευτικές εκλογές διεξάγονται σήμερα στη Σερβία , στη σκιά σχεδόν δύο ετών μαζικών φοιτητικών κινητοποιήσεων κατά της διαφθοράς. Ο πρώην πρόεδρος Αλεξάνταρ Βούτσιτς διεκδικεί την πρωθυπουργία απέναντι στη λίστα των φοιτητών , ένα κίνημα που κατεβαίνει στις εκλογές με υποψηφίους εκτός του παραδοσιακού κομματικού συστήματος. Ανταπόκριση από το Βελιγράδι Η εκλογική διαδικασία διεξάγεται σχετικά ομαλά . Ωστόσο, οι φοιτητές κατήγγειλαν περιστατικά εξαγοράς ψήφων έξω από τα εκλογικά τμήματα . Ιδιαίτερο ενδιαφέρον παρουσιάζει η υψηλή προσέλευση : τρεις ώρες μετά το άνοιγμα των κάλπων είχε ψηφίσει το 20% των εγγεγραμμένων . Αν η τάση συνεχιστεί και η συμμετοχή ξεπεράσει το 60-65% , τότε, σύμφωνα με τους αναλυτές, θα ευνοηθούν περισσότερο οι φοιτητές . (AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic) Στην εκλογική αναμέτρηση αναμετρώνται ο Αλεξάνταρ Βούτσιτς, που κυβερνά τη χώρα εδώ και 14 χρόνια , και οι φοιτητές. Το κίνημά τους γεννήθηκε μέσα από τις κινητοποιήσεις κατά της διαφθοράς και της αδιαφάνειας, με αφορμή την κατάρρευση του στεγάστρου στον σιδηροδρομικό σταθμό του Νόβι Σαντ τον Νοέμβριο του 2024, που στοίχισε τη ζωή σε 16 ανθρώπους . Σύμφωνα με εκτιμήσεις , αν το αποτέλεσμα είναι οριακό, τα πράγματα δεν θα εξελιχθούν ήρεμα . Όπως σημειώνεται, το αποτέλεσμα θα αμφισβητηθεί και από τις δύο πλευρές , ενώ δεν αποκλείεται να υπάρξουν και αντιδράσεις με αρνητικό πρόσημο. items.descriptionOriginal: Μια συνδρομή στο γυμναστήριο ή τα εβδομαδιαία μαθήματα pilates συχνά κάνουν την άσκηση να φαίνεται ως υποχρέωση: μια δραστηριότητα που πρέπει να ενταχθεί στο πρόγραμμα, ακόμα κι αν δεν μας ευχαριστεί ιδιαίτερα. Ωστόσο, όλο και περισσότερα δεδομένα δείχνουν ότι η φυσική δραστηριότητα δεν χρειάζεται να περιορίζεται σε οργανωμένα «μαθήματα» ασκήσεων στο γυμναστήριο. Αντίθετα, οι άνθρωποι που διατηρούν καλή υγεία και φυσική κατάσταση σε μεγαλύτερη ηλικία έχουν συχνά ένα κοινό χαρακτηριστικό: ενσωματώνουν την κίνηση φυσικά στην καθημερινότητά τους , μέσα από δραστηριότητες που απολαμβάνουν. Έρευνες το επιβεβαιώνουν: όσοι ασχολούνται με ευχάριστες σωματικές δραστηριότητες εμφανίζουν χαμηλότερα επίπεδα στρες , καλύτερη διάθεση και συνολικά καλύτερη υγεία. Μάλιστα, μελέτη σε περισσότερους από 93.000 ηλικιωμένους έδειξε ότι όσοι έχουν χόμπι παρουσιάζουν μεγαλύτερη ικανοποίηση από τη ζωή και καλύτερη υγεία σε σχέση με όσους δεν έχουν. Το βασικό πρόβλημα με τις συνδρομές σε γυμναστήρια είναι ότι πολλοί τις εγκαταλείπουν μέσα σε λίγους μήνες, όχι λόγω έλλειψης θέλησης, αλλά επειδή η διαδικασία μοιάζει με αγγαρεία. Αντίθετα, δραστηριότητες όπως οι παρακάτω, που συνδυάζουν κίνηση και ευχαρίστηση μπορούν να αποτελέσουν μια πιο βιώσιμη λύση. 1. Μαγείρεμα από την αρχή Η προετοιμασία σύνθετων γευμάτων δεν είναι μόνο δημιουργική διαδικασία, αλλά και σωματική δραστηριότητα. Το ζύμωμα, το κόψιμο, η πολύωρη ορθοστασία και η μεταφορά σκευών ενεργοποιούν μυϊκές ομάδες και συμβάλλουν στην ενδυνάμωση και την αντοχή. Ακόμη και απλές εργασίες, όπως το πλύσιμο των πιάτων, ενισχύουν τη δύναμη λαβής και συμβάλλουν στην κατανάλωση ενέργειας. Mπορείτε να ξεκινήσετε από κάτι πρακτικό, όπως φτιάχνοντας φρέσκα ζυμαρικά, σπιτική ζύμη πίτσας ή ψωμί. 2. Κηπουρική Η ενασχόληση με τον κήπο ή ακόμη και με τα φυτά στο μπαλκόνι, περιλαμβάνει κινήσεις όπως σκύψιμο, τέντωμα και μεταφορά βάρους. Πρόκειται για μια ήπια αλλά ουσιαστική μορφή αερόβιας άσκησης. Μελέτες έχουν συνδέσει την τακτική κηπουρική με χαμηλότερο κίνδυνο άνοιας , καθώς και με μειωμένη πιθανότητα καρδιαγγειακών επεισοδίων. 3. Χορός Ο χορός αποτελεί μια ολοκληρωμένη μορφή άσκησης που βελτιώνει την καρδιοαναπνευστική λειτουργία, τη μυϊκή δύναμη και τον συντονισμό. Παράλληλα, συμβάλλει στη διατήρηση υγιών αρθρώσεων και οστών. Το σημαντικότερο πλεονέκτημά του είναι ότι γίνεται αντιληπτός ως ψυχαγωγία και όχι ως υποχρέωση. Εάν μάλιστα επιλέξετε μια βραδιά χορού, ο χορός ενισχύει την κοινωνικοποίηση, προσθέτοντας οφέλη και για την ψυχική υγεία. 4. Παιχνίδι και βόλτα με σκύλο Η καθημερινή φροντίδα ενός σκύλου είναι συνώνυμη με την αυξημένη σωματική δραστηριότητα, χωρίς μάλιστα να το αντιλαμβανόμαστε ως άσκηση. Οι τακτικές βόλτες, το παιχνίδι και ο χρόνος σε εξωτερικούς χώρους οδηγούν με φυσικό τρόπο σε περισσότερη κίνηση μέσα στην ημέρα. Με ένα κατοικίδιο, έχουμε περισσότερες ευκαιρίες για άσκηση, αλλά και μείωση της μοναξιάς και βελτίωση της ψυχικής ευεξίας . Ιδιαίτερα οι σκύλοι απαιτούν συνέπεια, κάτι που βοηθά στη διατήρηση μιας σταθερής καθημερινής ρουτίνας κίνησης. 5. Περπάτημα στην πόλη Δεν λένε τυχαία για το περπάτημα ότι είναι η πιο φθηνή μορφή άσκησης. Πρόκειται για μια από τις πιο απλές και υποτιμημένες μορφές σωματικής δραστηριότητας. αφού μπορεί εύκολα να ενταχθεί στην καθημερινή ρουτίνα. Η εξερεύνηση μιας γειτονιάς με τα πόδια προσφέρει όχι μόνο κίνηση αλλά και μια πιο ουσιαστική επαφή με το περιβάλλον. Παράλληλα, τα οφέλη για την υγεία είναι σημαντικά: βελτίωση της καρδιαγγειακής λειτουργίας, ενδυνάμωση των κάτω άκρων και καλύτερη κινητικότητα των αρθρώσεων. Ακόμη και μια απλή βόλτα χωρίς συγκεκριμένο προορισμό μπορεί να οδηγήσει σε σημαντικό αριθμό βημάτων μέσα στη μέρα, χωρίς την αίσθηση της «άσκησης». 6. Αναρρίχηση Η αναρρίχηση συνδυάζει ενδυνάμωση, αντοχή, ευλυγισία και πνευματική συγκέντρωση. Πρόκειται για δραστηριότητα που ενεργοποιεί ολόκληρο το σώμα, ενώ ταυτόχρονα απαιτεί στρατηγική σκέψη. Η αυξανόμενη διαθεσιμότητα χώρων αναρρίχησης σε αστικά κέντρα την καθιστά πλέον προσιτή σε περισσότερους. 7. Ξυλουργική Η κατασκευή αντικειμένων από ξύλο απαιτεί δύναμη, ακρίβεια και αντοχή. Διαδικασίες όπως το τρίψιμο, το πλάνισμα και η μεταφορά υλικών λειτουργούν ως μορφή λειτουργικής προπόνησης. Παράλληλα, η δημιουργία ενός απτού αποτελέσματος ενισχύει το αίσθημα ικανοποίησης. 8. Κολύμβηση Το κολύμπι αποτελεί μια από τις πιο ολοκληρωμένες μορφές άσκησης , καθώς ενεργοποιεί όλο το σώμα χωρίς να επιβαρύνει τις αρθρώσεις. Όταν πραγματοποιείται σε φυσικά περιβάλλοντα, όπως θάλασσα, ενισχύει και την ψυχική ευεξία. Ιδιαίτερα το κολύμπι σε κρύο νερό έχει συνδεθεί με βελτίωση της διάθεσης και πιθανή ενίσχυση του ανοσοποιητικού. Συμπέρασμα Η σωματική δραστηριότητα δεν χρειάζεται να περιορίζεται στην προγραμματισμένη άσκηση. Όταν η κίνηση ενσωματώνεται φυσικά στην καθημερινότητα μέσω ευχάριστων δραστηριοτήτων, γίνεται πιο εύκολο να διατηρηθεί μακροπρόθεσμα. Ένας ενεργός και δραστήριος τρόπος ζωής μπορεί να αποτελέσει εξίσου αποτελεσματική -και συχνά πιο βιώσιμη- εναλλακτική του γυμναστηρίου. Διαβάστε επίσης Το ηρεμιστικό χόμπι που διώχνει το άγχος και ακονίζει το μυαλό Άνοια: Οι δραστηριότητες που μειώνουν τον κίνδυνο – Ποια είναι η καλύτερη Έχετε χάσει κάθε ικανοποίηση για τη ζωή; Οι δραστηριότητες που επαναφέρουν την χαμένη ευτυχία

Πρόκειται για ρόλους που άλλοτε επιβάλλονται από την κοινωνία και άλλοτε αποτελούν προσωπικές επιλογές, διαμορφώνοντας μια σύνθετη εικόνα της γυναικείας εμπειρίας. items.descriptionOriginal: A paintbrush moves slowly across the paper. Dhriti is focused on the colours in front of her, adding one shade after another to a painting that, to someone else, may simply look like a piece of art. But to her mother, Shweta Runwal, moments like these hold a much deeper meaning. Years ago, when Dhriti was still a little girl and could speak only in single words, she came home with a diary. On one of its pages, she had drawn two stick figures. One of them was crying. Shweta was worried and asked her daughter what had happened. Dhriti tried to explain that her friend was moving away. "It was the first time I realised she was actually trying to communicate through art," Shweta recalls. For a mother who had spent years hearing questions about what her daughter would or would not be able to do, the moment offered a different possibility. Perhaps the better question was not what Dhriti could not do, but what she could express, create and become. From paintings to lifestyle products, Tickle Your Art brings original artwork by neurodiverse artists to a wider audience while preserving the individuality of their work. That question would eventually grow into Tickle Your Art, a social enterprise that works with artists with Down syndrome and intellectual disabilities, turning their original artwork into lifestyle products, books, corporate gifts and more. But the idea did not begin as a business. It began at home, with Dhriti. Before the diagnosis, there was Dhriti Dhriti was diagnosed with Down syndrome a few days after she was born. At two months, doctors also discovered a hole in her heart and advised the family to consider surgery. For Shweta, the early years came with another challenge: the assumptions surrounding her daughter's diagnosis. "People saw her diagnosis before they saw her," she says. "They had already written her off." There were questions about whether Dhriti would walk or talk, whether she would ever have a career, and what her future would look like. At the time, Shweta says, there were fewer avenues for parents to find information or connect. Dhriti was Tickle Your Art's first artist. Today, the social enterprise has worked with more than 25 neurodiverse artists. Her own parents, however, took a different approach. "They were like, 'Just treat her like any other baby," she recalls. That trust became Shweta's biggest support system. She had trained as an architect and had also worked in London, where she first discovered how powerfully art and design could be used as forms of expression. But as Dhriti grew, Shweta began volunteering with the Down Syndrome Federation of India and meeting more families. She slowly began to notice a gap. The conversation was often about what children with intellectual disabilities might not be able to do. Shweta wanted to ask a different question: What if we started with what they could? Art became a language and a possibility After Dhriti's early experience with drawing, Shweta began looking for art classes for her. She eventually started working with several children, helping them explore different forms of creative expression. For Shweta, inclusion begins by looking beyond a diagnosis and recognising the creativity, skills and possibilities each person brings. In 2018, she organised an exhibition at Kelkar Museum around World Down Syndrome Day, bringing together artwork by people with Down syndrome and creating products around it. The response stayed with her. What began as a personal experiment eventually became Tickle Your Art, which was formally registered in October 2020, during the pandemic. Dhriti became its very first artist. Within six months, more artists began joining; today, Tickle Your Art has worked with more than 25 neurodiverse artists and is onboarding six more for upcoming launches. The organisation also runs a community centre where artists receive training, mentorship and employment opportunities, alongside an experience centre where visitors can encounter their work and the stories behind it. Importantly, the artists do not have to fit into a predetermined idea of what "good" art should look like. "We try not to change the artwork as much as possible," says Shweta. "We want to see their story." Dhriti's artwork was first showcased at an exhibition organised by Shweta at Kelkar Museum in 2018. Sometimes, that means designing around an artist's original lines or colours. Sometimes, it means finding a new way to translate their work into a product. Every product carries the story of its artist. Shweta describes the idea simply: each product should be responsible for "three smiles" — that of the artist, the person giving it and the person receiving it. At home, inclusion came naturally For Ira, Shweta's younger daughter, this entire world has always been normal. "I've never felt this is very different," Ira says. "I've never thought about inclusion, because it is normal for me, and that's how it should be for everyone." That belief has grown alongside the enterprise. Today, Ira contributes to Tickle Your Art's marketing and design decisions. Shweta jokes that nothing goes into production without Ira's approval. Ira can look at a product and instinctively understand what might appeal to someone, where something should be placed, or how a design could work better. Ira Runwal contributes to Tickle Your Art's marketing and design, believing inclusion should be a natural part of everyday life. But her role goes beyond the business. She also speaks about inclusion in schools and has received recognition for doing so. For Shweta, watching her daughters grow up together has reinforced something she has long believed: inclusion does not have to be complicated. "It doesn't belong to anybody," she says. "Just give a smile, and others will smile back at you." When talent finds a place to work For Shweta, economic inclusion is not simply about giving someone a job. It is about helping them recognise that their time, talent and contribution have value. She remembers when Rohan, a 33-year-old artist with a background in animation and digital design, began working with Tickle Your Art. When Shweta started paying him, his father wondered whether the small organisation should really be giving him a salary. For Shweta, there was no question."He is giving his time. He is coming here sincerely. And I feel that needs to add value," she says. That philosophy is also reflected in the way Tickle Your Art operates. Artists can work from home or at the centre, and their work is developed into products based on its originality and the story behind it. The organisation has now worked with artists across India, with many connections coming through disability organisations and communities. At Tickle Your Art, Rohan has found an opportunity to reconnect with his passion for art and rebuild his confidence through meaningful work. For Suzanne, who brings around three decades of HR experience and works with Tickle Your Art as an HR consultant, this has also changed the way she understands inclusion. "In corporate, we talk about diversity, equity and inclusion," she says. "But very rarely do we get to live it the way Shweta is living it." Her role is largely focused on building the systems and processes that allow the organisation to function sustainably, while Shweta works closely with the artists and creative side. Suzanne says she has also noticed something else: people sometimes hesitate because they do not know how to interact with people with intellectual disabilities. "But I have found Dhriti to be extremely loving, warm, intelligent and funny," she says. "They are just like you and I. There's no difference." When confidence finds its way back Before Tickle Your Art, 33-year-old Rohan had already worked in animation and had trained in Photoshop, Illustrator and other digital tools. But after his earlier job ended during the lockdown, he became more introverted. Then came Tickle Your Art; Rohan has now been associated with the organisation for around a year. His mother, Veena, says art has always been one of his biggest interests. At Tickle Your Art, however, she has watched that interest become a source of confidence and happiness again. Tickle Your Art develops products around artists' original creations, ensuring their distinctive styles and stories remain at the heart of the process. For Veena, that happiness is perhaps the most meaningful change. She has also seen how spaces like Tickle Your Art can shift the conversation for families, giving children opportunities to learn, work and meet people outside their homes. And that, ultimately, is what Shweta wants to build. A space that feels like home Tickle Your Art has received recognition from several platforms, including Shark Tank India, where Anupam Mittal invested in the venture. It has also received grant support from Jeet Adani, been recognised as an "Industry Disruptor" by UN Women, and showcased its work internationally in Berlin at The DO and H&M exhibition. Dhriti, meanwhile, received the National Award for Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities in the Shreshth Divyang Balika category for her achievements in art and her role in promoting inclusion. For Shweta, these milestones matter, but not simply because they validate the organisation. She remembers a parent of a six-month-old child with Down syndrome reaching out after seeing Dhriti's videos. The mother told her that she had felt shattered after the diagnosis, but seeing Dhriti had given her hope. "That is what makes me feel that all of this is worth it," Shweta says. Dhriti received the National Award for her achievements in art and contribution to promoting inclusion. Her dream now is to build similar community spaces across India, places where families can come together, where artists can learn and work, and where art can become a bridge to meaningful livelihoods. Ira imagines Tickle Your Art becoming known across India and eventually the world. Shweta has an even simpler measure of success: working with many more artists and giving them a platform to begin. For her, the centre should feel like a second home. A place where a person's diagnosis does not decide their possibilities, where a painting is not treated as something made "despite" a disability, but simply as someone's art. And perhaps, most importantly, a place where inclusion stops being a lofty idea and becomes what Ira has always known it to be — normal. All images courtesy of Shweta Runwal

items.descriptionOriginal: “Good night! Sleep tight! Don’t let the bed bugs bite!” This sing-songy rhyme that has been around for centuries alludes to the fact that bed bugs were prevalent in the past. After a significant decrease post-WWII , however, the sneaky pests have been making a comeback. Since the 1990s, bed bug infestations have risen dramatically, leading people to look for ways to avoid and get rid of the blood-sucking little buggers. Unfortunately, a lot of the information about how to do that is flat-out wrong . Popular YouTube science communicator Mark Rober invites viewers to forget what we think we know and go on an educational journey with the leading bed bug researchers at Rutgers University’s urban entomology lab. Not only did Rober subject himself to bed bug bites on purpose to see what happens when they feed, but he also conducted a series of experiments in the lab to find out what is actually effective at killing them and what is not. Bed bugs have a reputation for being nearly impossible to get rid of, which isn’t really the case, according to Rober. When you know what works, it’s actually a fairly simple process to kill an infestation. And the good news is that it doesn’t entail any toxic chemicals. In fact, the pest control chemicals sold for bed bugs don’t work at all, according to Rober’s tests. The five super wild bed bug facts In the process of learning about bed bugs, Rober shared a few “super wild” facts about the infamous creatures. Fact #1: Bed bugs can live 3 to 10 months without feeding. Eek. No wonder it seems like it’s impossible to get rid of them. Starving them doesn’t work. They can live in the resting stage for 3 to 6 months, and if the environment is cold enough, they can survive around 300 days, or 10 months, without eating. Fact #2: Bed bugs don’t transmit disease Some good news here: Unlike blood-sucking mosquitoes, bed bugs don’t carry or transmit disease. The bad news on the front is that because they don’t pose a disease threat, only an annoyance, there’s not a big incentive to fund research to eradicate them. Fact #3: Bed bugs are attracted to vertical objects In one of Rober’s experiments, he placed a dish with a cylindrical vertical post inside it an a dish without a column, and nearly all of the bed bugs in the enclosure ended up in the dish with the column. “If you think about it, humans sleep at the highest elevation any given room. So their logic is just crawl up any vertical surface you see until you eventually find a warm-blooded meal at the top.” Part of how they find humans is by smell, which is why certain strong-smelling items can act as a deterrent for bed bugs. In Rober’s experiment, Bounce dryer sheets, moth balls, baking soda, and essential oils all seemed to repel bed bugs (as opposed to ultrasonic pest repellers, which appeared to have no effect). However, none of those things did anything to kill them. Bed bugs are about the size of an apple seed. Photo credit: Canva Fact #4: Before 1950, one in three homes had bed bugs Yikes. Even with the resurgence, we’re still nowhere near those numbers, thank goodness. Fact #5: The way bed bugs mate is weird The term used to describe it is called “traumatic insemination,” and really, you should just let Mark Rober explain it with his visual metaphor. Start at minute 11:30. What actually kills bed bugs In testing chemical sprays, foggers, and other items marketed for killing bed bugs, Rober found a “superstar” in a natural, non-toxic substance. Diatomaceous earth, pulverized fossilized remains of tiny aquatic organisms called diatoms, was the most effective at killing the buggers with a 90% mortality rate after 10 days as opposed to 12% with the Hot Shot bed bug spray. Diatomaceous earth is mostly silica, which absorbs moisture, and when the silica dust sticks to the bed bugs as they walk through it, it dehydrates them. A light dusting of diatomaceous earth around all the cracks and crevices of a room is one way to kill off an infestation, though that process can take days. The other way to kill bed bugs is heat. Steam kills bed bugs, as does heating up a room to over 122 degrees Fahrenheit does the trick. Temps over 122 degrees kills bed bugs instantly, and as Rober points out, there’s no way for them to build immunity to this kind of treatment. So steamers and clothes dryers set to high are the average person’s best bet for killing off bed bugs if they have them. The “nuclear option” is to have a pro come in with big heaters and cook your home for a day. Checking mattresses for signs of bed bugs at a hotel can help you avoid bringing them home. Photo credit: Canva How do you avoid getting bed bugs in the first place? An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, and that’s true for bed bugs especially. Avoiding an infestation if there’s already one in your apartment building is trickier, but a lot of people inadvertently bring bed bugs home from hotel stays. Checking the underside of a hotel mattress as soon as you come in the room is a good habit to be in. Bed bugs poop a lot, and there will be spots along the edges of the mattress if bed bugs are present. The other tip is to use the luggage rack to store your suitcase instead of leaving it on the floor or furniture and to hang clothes on the closet hangers instead of putting them into the hotel room’s dresser drawers. Some people may even put their suitcase in the bathtub, at least until they’ve checked the bed for signs of poop. Nobody wants to deal with bed bugs, but at least now we have clear evidence of what actually works to get rid of them and what doesn’t. Cook them with heat/steam and dehydrate them with diatomaceous earth, and take some simple steps when traveling to lessen your chances of getting them in the first place. Sleep tight, everyone! This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Forget what you know about bed bugs. Avoiding and getting rid of them is pretty simple. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: People are praising 96-year-old grandma’s advice to ‘separate your actions from your feelings’
items.description: Η Σιωπηλή Γενιά, που γεννήθηκε μεταξύ 1928 και 1945, αποτελείται από ανθρώπους που έζησαν τη Μεγάλη Ύφεση και τον Β' Παγκόσμιο Πόλεμο. Καθορισμένοι μέσα από αυτές τις δυσκολίες, η δύναμη και η επιμονή τους συνεχίζει να εμπνέει τις νεότερες γενιές σήμερα, συμπεριλαμβανομένων των Gen X, Millennials και Gen Alpha. Πάνω στο Reddit σε ένα υποφόρουμ που συζητάμε…
items.descriptionOriginal: The Silent Generation , those born from between 1928 and 1945, is made up of people who lived through the Great Depression and World War II. Defined by living through these hardships, their strength and perseverance continues to inspire younger generations today including Gen X , Millennials , and Gen Alpha . Over on Reddit in a subforum discussing how to become more disciplined, member Limp_Edu4797 shared an impactful piece of advice from his 96-year-old grandma on not letting feelings and emotions get in the way of remaining disciplined and working through hard things. In the post, he shared: “For a long time, I was stuck in this cycle where I’d only be productive when I felt like it. If I was in a bad mood, I’d tell myself to wait until tomorrow. When I was tired, I’d take a Netflix break. If I was stressed about something, I’d procrastinate until my headspace cleared up,” he wrote. “One day, my grandma was watching me complain about how I couldn’t get anything done because I was ‘too anxious’ about some work project.” Grandma didn’t hold back He goes on to explain that while he was expecting his grandma to have more sympathy for him, she instead offered him hard-hitting advice from her own life experience. He continued, “She just looked at me and said, ‘You know, during the war, we didn’t have the luxury of waiting until we felt good to do what needed doing.’ Then she told me something I’ll never forget: ‘You need to separate your actions from your feelings!'” He adds that his grandma notices young people these days “think their feelings and their actions are married to each other. Happy means productive, sad means lazy, scared means stop. But that’s just a story we tell ourselves.” It’s a lot different from how she experienced life. She told him, “I didn’t feel like rationing food or working on the farm. But I did it anyway. Not because I ignored my feelings, but because I did it WITH my feelings.” When he tried to explain that things these days are just different , she didn’t argue with him. “She just nodded and said, ‘You’re probably right. But here’s what I learned: don’t lie to yourself by using your feelings as an excuse. Don’t say: I’m stressed, so I can’t do it.’ She told me to change the narrative and tell myself: ‘I’m stressed, that’s fine, so I’ll do it stressed.'” Reactions were mixed, but mostly moved Her wise words are resonating with younger generations online. “I didn’t know I needed this today. Thank you. Your grammas words are hitting hard for me this morning and I appreciate it! Fell all your feelings, they’re valid, but stay disciplined with those feelings. Not in spite of them,” one commented. Another wrote, “I think this is the root of many differences between our newer generations and our older ones. We are swung far in the direction of acknowledging our feelings, validating them, etc.—so far, perhaps, that we have arrived in a place where feelings dictate our actions. That’s what you’re describing. There’s a happy medium, and it’s required for healthy functioning adults. Sometimes situations warrant being overridden by emotion. Most don’t. You get to/have to choose what kind of person to be.” Another quipped, “I Can Do it With a Broken Heart but make it depression era,” referencing the Taylor Swift hit. Others were slightly skeptical of the advice she gave. “I get the validity in this, truly. But, we’ve also acknowledged how their stiff approach harbors trauma responses that can last generations. It’s okay to have hard feelings. We can acknowledge them, but she is right to encourage you to keep moving forward. But, we should always listen to our bodies and see where that feeling is coming from,” another shared. My grandma (96) made discipline so simple by u/Limp_Edu4797 in getdisciplined Grandma was onto something Ultimately, many appreciated the focus on re-framing your mindset to accomplish goals and remain disciplined. Another commented, “So much to ‘discipline’ is what????? The mental game. There are lots of ways to attack the mental game. At the core is…re-framing….reframing our mindset, how we look at, process our thoughts, approach to things we know we should do, want to, but don’t. Grandma was on to something with her ‘separate’ feelings from actions approach.” This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post People are praising 96-year-old grandma’s advice to ‘separate your actions from your feelings’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Moving into a retirement community is a big life transition for many senior citizens. Making the choice to downsize and move into a retirement home is not an easy one that can come with many unknowns. In an Reddit forum, member @common_grounder posed the question: “Anyone who’s downsized and moved into a retirement community, what’s the adjustment been like for you?” They continued, “Has it been hard giving up your former life and belongings? Is a more simplified existence comforting to you? Has being around lots of people who are also old been a net positive or net negative?” 16 honest answers from people who know Older people who have made the transition into a retirement community shared their real and honest experiences for those considering making the move. These are 16 of their most informative and impactful responses. Three seniors playing chess together over coffee. Photo credit: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash “I’ve been in an Independent Living Community for 2 years. I was having some health issues and I needed a place that had on duty staff. I downsized twice. My wife and I downsized from a 3 bedroom house to a 2 bedroom Apartment. My wife developed Vascular Dementia the year before the Pandemic. Eventually she went into hospice and after my 3rd hip surgery in 18 months I moved into Independent Living. My 1st year here my bride of 39 years past on from complications of the Vascular Dementia. When I first got here I participated with some of the outing and events. We get 2 meals a day and I used to do dinner with the same group daily. The Presidential election changed that. I loved the people I sat with. However I was crushed that so many of my older peers voted against their interests. I just turned 70 on D-Day. On the average I’m a “youngster” here. Before the election I constantly helped residents conquer their smartphones be it iphone or Android. Now I order lunch and dinner for me to pick up and eat alone in my apartment. I only venture out now for Dr’s appointments and the occasional family outing . I guess more than any thing I miss my bride of 39 years, 44 together. I’m looking forward that my 29 year old son is getting married in August to a wonderful woman and their future looks bright. I’m grateful technology allows me to talk, text and facetime people I care about. At my age, I don’t have many long time friends still on this plane of existence. Even when I downsized to this one bedroom Apartment I still have too much stuff including Heirloom China in my living room for my son that been here 2 years. Oh I almost forgot. We have a happy hour on Wednesday afternoon. I always go and get a vodka tonic and finger food. I was told by my parents to never drink alone. Doing that one drink a week is me not drinking alone.” – @sapotts61 For many folks, it’s been great “I live in a retirement community and I like it a lot. No exterior maintenance, lots of activities and amenities. Beautifully landscaped grounds and great views from my home. Being around similarly aged people is nice too. I really can’t think of a negative. But the quality of the communities vary. Do your homework before taking the plunge.” – @Entire-Garage-1902 Three seniors blowing bubbles. Photo credit: Curated Lifestyle/Unsplash “My wife and I did it 11 years ago. We sold our 4 bedroom 3 bath 2 story house and moved into a 2 bedroom 2 bath single level house in a 55 and better community. It’s been terrific! We have a resort like pool next to the clubhouse and gym. There are tennis and pickle ball courts, gas grills, a big charcoal grill, sauna and spa. It’s a quiet, safe, well kept neighborhood with friendly neighbors.” – @8amteetime “One month into assisted living. I think it’s going to be fine. Just another life transition like college, being on my own, getting married, having kids, building a career, moving into a bigger showplace house, etc. Just in reverse – everything getting smaller and simpler. Downsizing has been very challenging, getting rid of so many objects that still mean something to us, but won’t mean anything to our kids, and there’s not enough space in our 950 sq ft apartment. Having the staff do all the cooking – food has been quite good! – cleaning, and managing my medications, has certainly simplified our lives. And freed up time for my wife to do things she chooses, not just things she must. Moved to a different state where we knew no one, except our sons and their families, so we’re meeting a lot of new people. Haven’t really clicked with anyone yet, but have a half dozen people we can join for meals in the dining room. Yeah, adjustment is going fine.” – @dnhs47 Some people are going bigger, not smaller “We are UPSIZING when move to a retirement community.” – @FootHikerUtah “We upsized into a 55+ community. Sometimes I miss the age diversity with neighbors but my husband and I are 64, pretty active with previously established friendships, part time jobs, and our family. We like that there is a clubhouse with book clubs, game nights, community dinners and a lovely swimming pool. I feel like it’s a home where we can age in place for as long as possible.” – @Competitive-Ice2956 “I upsized when I moved to a retirement community – my Manhattan apartment was 440 square feet, and my car was in a garage two miles away. Here in Connecticut, I’ve got 1500 square feet plus a basement and garage. I’ve got more stuff than ever.” – @vinyl1earthlink “We’ve been in an over 55 community 8 yrs. I love my little house, all on one floor, lots of storage. It’s a bit lonely when our snow bird neighbors go home for the summer, but the grocery store is less crowded. We’ve had several neighbors die recently, but that’s why they call this Gods waiting room. It’s also worrisome to see neighbors having physical or dementia like issues. We aren’t into the pool scene or golf, but we love the indoor walking track. The entertainment shows are a hassle, gotta get those tickets months in advance. We tried a few day long bus trips but their prices are way too high now. Our community is over 40 yrs old and pre 2020 we had thriving crafts, cards, wood, metal, auto, photo clubs….people in charge of those kind of drifted away during the lockdown and a lot of knowledge and organizational skills to run those programs were lost. It’s very quiet here, most neighbors keep their homes very tidy. I’m in a single family home, I have yearly membership dues but no HOA…those are running around $300 a month. We have a great Facebook page that helps us all stay connected and compare notes. All in all I have zero qualms about leaving my old life.” – @Adrift715 “2/2 1400 sq ft villa. It was hard deciding what to keep and what to get rid of at first, but in the end, it was liberating. I love the fact that we can just lock the door and leave without having to worry about outside maintenance.” – @RowdyRumRunner “I’m in a 55 and over community. It’s a very active community, dances at least 2 per month, bingo on Sunday, movies on Thursday, exercise classes at least 3 per day including yoga, karaoke, cards, swimming…I could go on but you get the drift. No obligation to attend any of the activities but they are available. No meals, this is independent living. I’m really happy here, best choice I made after selling my house. Downside for some is living with rules, some people don’t like picking up after their dogs or speed limits or whatever, my place isn’t super controlling but any rules are too much for some people.” – @Kitchen-Fee-5114 “I like it, being on my own I didn’t want a house with all the maintenance. I have a small apartment so I had to get rid of a lot of stuff, that can be hard but I did it. Where I live there is a lot of activities if you are interested, but it’s independent living and some people like that and some don’t. I have made friends, play cards and always have something to do if I’m bored. One of the things you don’t think of is that you meet people and then they die. That is something that can be hard to deal with.” – @Birdy304 “We downsized from our home we lived in for 35 years to a tiny home (399 sq ft) three years ago. While the community is not age restricted, 95% of the people are retired and at least 65. We live on a lake so I get to fish as much as I want. Wife enjoys a bunch of activities such as water aerobics, arts and crafts and dancing. We travel the park in a golf cart. It’s takes minutes to get from one activity to the next. Overall we love it.” – @Dicedlr711vegas Others found it a lot tougher “I am almost 70. I have downsized hugely. I lived in a retirement community for 4 years from 61 to 65 I hated it!” – @Direct_Ad2289 “It’s a very difficult thing. It sounds simple, correct. But it’s what you make of it in your new life. I used to do warranty work for brand new modular homes. Many are doing just that…downsizing. While working, you wind up chatting with many. The stories would run the whole gamut, from ecstatic to downright miserable. My takeaway if you can afford it was maybe try a couple of years’ lease/rent before committing. Sit on any s to get a feel for it first. It was quite heart-wrenching at times. Should have, could have. There’s mental factors to think of. Your circle of friends may change. Someone other than you could be in charge of your property. Suddenly, there’s not a whole lot you can use those tools on anymore, etc. It’s a tough thing to do.” – @xgrader “I (64M) wasn’t ready for it and my wife and I are moving out. I miss seeing kids and families.” – @MacDaddy654321 Anyone who's downsized and moved into a retirement community, what's the adjustment been like for you? by u/common_grounder in AskOldPeople There’s no one right way to do this Reading through all 16 of these, there’s no single right answer here, some people thrived the moment they unpacked their last box, others are still working through the grief of what they left behind. But a theme runs through nearly every response: the hardest part isn’t the square footage you give up. It’s figuring out who you are, and what you actually want your days to look like, once all that extra space and stuff is gone. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Older people get real about what it’s like to move into a retirement community appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: In July of 2021, Simone Biles withdrew from the team final in the Tokyo Olympics and subsequently withdrew from the individual all-around finals after getting a case of the “twisties” that had the world talking. She received overwhelming support as well as overwhelming criticism for the move, with some praising her for recognizing her limits and others blasting her for not persevering through whatever she’s dealing with. Some people pointed to Kerri Strug, who landed on one foot after vaulting on a severely injured ankle in the 1996 Olympics to help the U.S. win gold, as an example of the kind of sacrifice an athlete should be willing to make for their country. One dad’s post flipped the script But was it really? A dad named Byron Heath shared some thoughts about that fateful day in a viral Facebook post that was shared more than 370,000 times in less than a day. Heath wrote: “This realization I had about Simone Biles is gonna make some people mad, but oh well. Yesterday I was excited to show my daughters Kerri Strug’s famous one-leg vault. It was a defining Olympic moment that I watched live as a kid, and my girls watched raptly as Strug fell, and then limped back to leap again. But for some reason I wasn’t as inspired watching it this time. In fact, I felt a little sick. Maybe being a father and teacher has made me soft, but all I could see was how Kerri Strug looked at her coach, Bela Karolyi, with pleading, terrified eyes, while he shouted back ‘You can do it!’ over and over again. My daughters didn’t cheer when Strug landed her second vault. Instead they frowned in concern as she collapsed in agony and frantic tears. ‘Why did she jump again if she was hurt?’ one of my girls asked. I made some inane reply about the heart of a champion or Olympic spirit, but in the back of my mind a thought was festering: She shouldn’t have jumped again. The more the thought echoed, the stronger my realization became. Coach Karolyi should have gotten his visibly injured athlete medical help immediately! Now that I have two young daughters in gymnastics, I expect their safety to be the coach’s number one priority. Instead, Bela Karolyi told Strug to vault again. And he got what he wanted; a gold medal that was more important to him than his athlete’s health. I’m sure people will say ‘Kerri Strug was a competitor–she WANTED to push through the injury.’ That’s probably true. But since the last Olympics we’ve also learned these athletes were put into positions where they could be systematically abused both emotionally and physically, all while being inundated with ‘win at all costs’ messaging. A teenager under those conditions should have been protected, and told ‘No medal is worth the risk of permanent injury.’ In fact, we now know that Strug’s vault wasn’t even necessary to clinch the gold; the U.S. already had an insurmountable lead. Kerri Strug only did that vault because Bela couldn't do math and realize that they had already clinched it. Also as everyone else said she was literally carried off the podium and handed to Larry Nassar. https://t.co/rp3itKPcK2 — Christine Rousselle (@crousselle) July 27, 2021 Nevertheless, Bela Karolyi told her to vault again according to his own recounting of their conversation: ‘I can’t feel my leg,’ Strug told Karolyi. ‘We got to go one more time,’ Karolyi said. ‘Shake it out.’ ‘Do I have to do this again?’ Strug asked. ‘Can you, can you?’ Karolyi wanted to know. ‘I don’t know yet,’ said Strug. ‘I will do it. I will, I will.’ The injury forced Strug’s retirement at 18 years old. Dominique Moceanu, a generational talent, also retired from injuries shortly after. They were top gymnasts literally pushed to the breaking point, and then put out to pasture. Coach Karolyi and Larry Nassar (the serial sexual abuser) continued their long careers, while the athletes were treated as a disposable resource. Today Simone Biles–the greatest gymnast of all time–chose to step back from the competition, citing concerns for mental and physical health. I’ve already seen comments and posts about how Biles ‘failed her country’, ‘quit on us’, or ‘can’t be the greatest if she can’t handle the pressure.’ Those statements are no different than Coach Karolyi telling an injured teen with wide, frightened eyes: ‘We got to go one more time. Shake it out.’ The subtext here is: ‘Our gold medal is more important than your well-being.’ Our athletes shouldn’t have to destroy themselves to meet our standards. If giving empathetic, authentic support to our Olympians means we’ll earn less gold medals, I’m happy to make that trade. Here’s the message I hope we can send to Simone Biles: You are an outstanding athlete, a true role model, and a powerful woman. Nothing will change that. Please don’t sacrifice your emotional or physical well-being for our entertainment or national pride. We are proud of you for being brave enough to compete, and proud of you for having the wisdom to know when to step back. Your choice makes you an even better example to our daughters than you were before. WE’RE STILL ROOTING FOR YOU!” Sending love to you @Simone_Biles -Team UNITED States of America — Kerri Strug (@kerristrug96) July 27, 2021 Plenty of people felt the same way Many people shared Heath’s sentiment, with comments pouring in thanking him for putting words to what they were feeling. We’re in a new era where our lens of what’s admirable, what’s strong, and what’s right has shifted. We understand more about the lifelong impact of too many concussions. We have trainers and medics checking on football players after big hits. We are finding a better balance between competitiveness and well-being. We are acknowledging the importance of mental health and physical health. We are also more aware of how both physical and mental trauma impacts young bodies. Though Kerri Strug pushing through the pain has long been seen as an iconic moment in sports, the adults in the room should have been protecting her, not pushing her through an obvious injury. And the way this fall of Dominique Moceanu at age 14 was handled is downright shocking by today’s standards. She said she never received an exam for it, even after the competition was over. So wrong. In our sport, we essentially dive into a pool w/ no water. When you lose your ability to find the ground—which appears to be part of @Simone_Biles decision—-the consequences can be catastrophic. She made the right decision for the team & herself. @bisping — Dominique Moceanu (@Dmoceanu) July 28, 2021 Nope — Dominique Moceanu (@Dmoceanu) July 28, 2021 Athletes are people, not machines Athletes are not cogs in a wheel, and the desire to win a competition should not trump someone’s well-being. Elite gymnasts already put themselves through grueling physical and mental feats; they wouldn’t be at the top of their sport if they didn’t. But there are limits, and too often in our yearning for a gold medal, or even for a triumphant Olympic story, we push athletes too far. Now we see some of them pushing back, and knowing what we know now, that’s 100% a good thing. Plenty has changed since then. Bela Karolyi, the coach at the center of Heath’s post, died in November 2024 at age 82. And Biles’s story didn’t end in Tokyo. After sitting out four individual finals, she returned to win bronze on balance beam. Three years later in Paris, she won gold in the team, all-around and vault finals, plus silver on floor, bringing her career total to 11 Olympic medals. She has said she is still undecided about competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Games, but that she’ll be at the Games either way, on the floor or in the stands. items.descriptionOriginal: A new study examined bacteria that live in tiny worms that kill insects, and it could help develop new antibiotics. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology and the University of Marburg studied how these bacteria produce different versions of GameXPeptides, which kill insects. The study, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, investigated how these bacterial compounds evolved, as changes in the bacteria’s DNA over time altered the GameXPeptides. This diversity could lead to new medicines, as these peptides belong to a broader class called nonribosomal peptides. How bacteria develop different chemical weapons According to the study, researchers examined GameXPeptides in Xenorhabdus and Photorhabdus bacteria that live with tiny worms called nematodes. When nematodes enter an insect host, the bacteria are released and produce these compounds that kill it. The team reconstructed the evolutionary history of GxpS, the enzyme that produces GameXPeptides, to investigate how different peptide structures evolved. The study identified 49 compounds, including side products. “It felt like playing five-dimensional chess,” said Georg Hochberg, a researcher at the University of Marburg, in Phys. “Frequent recombination obscures the evolutionary history of these enzymes—each recombination event overwrites a piece of their past. But it is precisely this complexity that makes the system so fascinating.” The study continued that natural selection, genetic drift, and recombination biases shape the evolution of nonribosomal peptides, a class of compounds used in antibiotics such as penicillin, as well as toxins. “If we better understand the mechanisms underlying bacterial natural product diversity, it may become possible to discover new antibiotics that overcome existing resistances,” as stated in the study. Scientists found three forces that help to explain why different versions of GameXPeptide exist. Understanding these processes could help scientists discover other versions of other nonribosomal peptides. But natural selection alone does not account for the diversity of these compounds. Random mutations and genetic exchange also shape which variants emerge. When DNA is exchanged or rearranged, it creates new genetic combinations, a process called recombination. The researchers identified 27 synonymous recombination events that did not alter peptide structures and 26 nonsynonymous events that could change them. The team also found that recombination was more likely between enzyme domains with similar DNA sequences, particularly within the same gene. This bias limited which peptide variants could emerge through recombination. Findings could inform future antibiotic research The study examined one family of peptide -producing enzymes. The researchers said further work would be needed to determine whether the same evolutionary principles apply to peptides that humans use in medicine. However, that being said, many antibiotics are nonribosomal peptides . These researchers might have opened up an avenue to explore that might allow scientists to investigate new antibiotics. “Our results show that the conceptual framework we developed for the GameXPeptides can serve as a guide to decipher the evolutionary forces acting on other natural product families, such as the polyketide synthases, which like NRPS, produce many clinically relevant natural products,” Helge Bode of the Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology said in Phys . By understanding how these products evolve and diversify in bacteria , scientists might be able to tackle current resistance that humans have developed to some of the antibiotics that exist.

items.descriptionOriginal: Saul Levmore and Ward Farnsworth are college professors, so it’s fitting that the title of their new book is a question rather than an answer (beyond that being a fair way to pique interest). Like all good teachers, the authors don’t just want us to learn — they want us to learn how to think . In Should You Tip for Takeout? , they mine the fields of law, economics, philosophy, sports, and rhetoric to present a “tool kit for a more rational life.” Far from being an etiquette guide, it’s instead an invitation to expand the way we look at the world, so we can better understand not only our own behavior but others’ as well. Each chapter uses a common quandary — like whether you should recline your airplane seat or get a second opinion before surgery — as a jumping-off point to introduce heuristics and critical thinking techniques that can be applied to countless other scenarios. The resulting pages offer up food for thought and fodder for lighthearted debates. “One way to think about it is we’re trying to write a book that helps people have more fun having conversations at the dinner table,” Farnsworth explained in an interview with Nice News, noting that discussions these days seem to so easily devolve into political arguments or fear-based speculations about the future. “We thought, ‘You know, there’s a lot of things just in everyday life that are actually pretty interesting to think about if you look more closely at them than most people usually do,’” he said, adding: “What would it mean to really take this one apart rationally? What can you learn about the problem that makes everyday life a little more interesting, and maybe what can you learn about rationality that makes other things easier to understand?” Again, anyone hoping for simple “yes” or “no” solutions to life’s dilemmas would be opening the wrong book. In a chapter called “Should You Keep Looking for a Better Price?,” for example, the authors encourage readers to acquaint themselves with distribution patterns and standard deviations. In another, they demonstrate how one might use the mathematical theory of optimal stopping to choose a romantic partner. (Essentially: View the first 37% of your dates or relationships as a comparison pool, and then pick the first subsequent person who’s better than the best one in the sample cohort.) Photo by Lloyd DeGrane from UChicago Saul Levmore That’s not to say there are no straightforward answers. The title chapter delves into the power we have with our wallets to vote for or against a custom when it hasn’t yet become a norm. If something has become entrenched, it’s likely in our best interest to go along with it, whether or not we agree. In the case of tipping for takeout, the authors say that the verdict is in: It’s the norm, so you should tip what you deem a reasonable amount. And doing so may not matter as much to your pocket as you might imagine. “Think of it as a hidden price hike,” Farnsworth said. “But the good news is that you have something to say about it. You have some discretion on how much you’re going to let that price go up. And that should be considered a welcome thing rather than a bad thing, because the alternative is the price goes up for everybody.” The authors said that simply musing through these kinds of common scenarios can reveal possibilities one may never have considered for why things are the way they are and what alternatives exist. Courtesy of Godine Ward Farnsworth “One broad takeaway to me is that people should experiment more in their own lives,” Levmore said, adding, “I think the book tries to encourage people to imagine how the world could be a little bit different from the way it is.” It may also help expand our empathy, Farnsworth pointed out. “Sometimes looking at life and looking for the rationality in it is a way to be more generous-minded toward other people who appear to just be annoying you at random and may be doing just what you would do if you were in their shoes.” When our conversation turned to the most favorable order in which to be interviewed for a job, the pair demonstrated — perhaps unintentionally — just how the aforementioned dinner table discourse may go. “I think it’s a disadvantage to be the last person,” Levmore said, prompting Farnsworth to disagree: “I generally think you want to go last. You want to go as late as you can.” “They get tired,” Levmore rejoined after Farnsworth elaborated, to which Farnsworth replied, “Maybe,” then added: “There’s no right answer to these questions. We just think these problems that most of us sort of wander through unconsciously, they’re just more interesting when you slow down and really ask, ‘What is the best way to handle this?’”

items.descriptionOriginal: Chinese construction equipment manufacturer Zoomlion has supplied two heavy-duty tower cranes for the construction of the Lugu Lake Grand Bridge in southwestern China, helping crews complete a 283-meter main tower on the Shangri-La side of the crossing. The tower reached its topping-out milestone on September 29, according to Zoomlion. The bridge is part of the Xichang–Shangri-La Expressway, where construction across mountainous terrain requires precise lifting and positioning of large structural components. The project used two of Zoomlion’s R4300-200 tower cranes, one serving each of the bridge’s main towers. The equipment is designed for heavy lifting at height, combining high load capacity with automated safety systems and remote operation capabilities. Cranes lift 200-ton loads at mountain bridge site The R4300-200 has a maximum lifting capacity of 200 metric tons (220 US tons) and an 80-meter jib (262 feet). Zoomlion says the crane incorporates more than 20 intelligent safety and control functions, including collision prevention, automatic operating-speed adjustments based on load, and mechanisms designed to prevent suspended loads from slipping downward. These capabilities were particularly relevant during the final 103 meters (338 feet) of construction on the Shangri-La side tower. Crews had to position the final steel and concrete sections above the central crossbeam, where changing wind conditions added to the challenges of maintaining load stability and alignment. Live camera feeds allowed operators to monitor lifting operations and control the cranes remotely from ground level. This arrangement provided visibility of component positioning while allowing operators to make precise adjustments during installation. Zoomlion said the segment-lifting work on the tower was completed safely. The announcement did not specify the bridge’s full length or when the entire crossing is expected to open. Customized cranes support Istanbul skyscraper The bridge project follows Zoomlion’s work on the 380-meter (1,247 feet) tower housing the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye at the Istanbul International Financial Center. Unlike the bridge tower, the Istanbul project involved a high-rise building that combined steel framing and precast concrete on a constrained urban construction site. According to Zoomlion , the project required 1,260 heavy lifts, including steel columns weighing up to 48.2 metric tons (53.1 US tons). To meet those requirements, the company customized its L760-50 luffing-jib tower crane , which has a maximum lifting capacity of 50 metric tons (55 US tons) and a maximum jib length of 60 meters (197 feet). Its modular mast sections measure 2.3 meters (7.5 feet) on each side, allowing them to be transported in standard shipping containers. Each crane also required 10 custom connections to the building, engineered to meet local seismic requirements. Variable-frequency drives regulate lifting, rotation, and jib movement, enabling smoother starts and stops and finer adjustments when positioning heavy components. Wind-speed monitoring provides warnings and reduces operating speeds when preset thresholds are exceeded. Remote monitoring helps manage maintenance Zoomlion also used remote monitoring technology to track equipment performance during the Istanbul project. The system transmitted 28 operating parameters, including load data, component temperatures, operating hours, and fault codes. These measurements helped teams assess equipment wear and plan preventive maintenance. Zoomlion’s research and development team in China worked remotely with engineers in Türkiye to diagnose issues and support maintenance, aiming to limit downtime. The company says its equipment selection and technical support helped sustain a construction pace of one floor every five days for the main structure. Support also covered crane placement, installation feasibility studies and dismantling simulations. Applying heavy-lifting experience to new projects Zoomlion says experience from the bridge and Istanbul projects is informing its work on other high-rise developments, including the 377-meter (1,237 feet) Ciel Dubai Marina hotel, Dubai’s 400-meter (1,312 feet) Al Habtoor Tower and Indonesia’s 331-meter (1,086 feet) Oasis Central Towers. The projects show different demands on tower-crane engineering. Bridge construction requires accurate placement of structural sections across exposed sites, while skyscraper construction can demand compact equipment configurations, custom building connections, and continuous coordination as structures rise. In both cases, crane capacity is only one part of the challenge. Control systems, wind monitoring, installation planning and maintenance support also affect how safely and efficiently heavy components can be positioned at height.

From boys learning household responsibilities to women participating in markets and community life, the idea goes beyond individual empowerment. It challenges traditional gender roles and highlights how equality can begin at home, through the habits children learn and the responsibilities families share. What can the rest of India learn from Mizoram about women’s safety, gender equality and women’s freedom? This story explores why building a more equal society requires more than asking women to be careful. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.

items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία είναι μέρος της σειράς "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's υπό την ηγεσία των ανθρώπων της σειράς γονέων που ξεπερνά τις συμβατικές συμβουλές για να τεκμηριώσει πώς οι πραγματικές οικογένειες μεγαλώνουν πραγματικά τα παιδιά τους. Μέσω πραγματικών γονέων, προπονητών γονέων, επιρροών και ειδικών, η σειρά φέρνει ειλικρινείς, διαφορετικές και σχετικές προοπτικές για το q…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can't always answer. When Aayansh Singh first visited a farm near Mumbai, the horses, pigs and hens he had seen in picture books suddenly had a life of their own. Two years later, he returned with one wish: to ride a horse. For his father, Bhanu Singh, a software engineer based in Mumbai, watching that wish come true was a reminder of how much a child can take away from an experience that seems simple to an adult. "When we first took him, I honestly thought he would forget everything because he was only two years old," Bhanu recalls. "But for the next year, he kept talking about the horses and remembering the farm." It began with a small observation at home. Aayansh, then two, could identify horses, pigs, cows and goats from his picture books. He knew what they looked like, but he had never encountered them outside the pages. What began as a day of discovery became a memory Aayansh continued to talk about long after returning home. "We wanted him to go beyond books and experience them firsthand, to see them up close, touch them, and understand how they feel and behave," Bhanu says. That thought led the family to Japalouppe, a farm they discovered while searching online for a place near Mumbai where their toddler could meet animals. When the pictures came alive The family kept their first outing simple. Japalouppe was about a 1.5-hour drive away, making it manageable for a day trip with a young child . There was no packed itinerary or long list of attractions to tick off. For Bhanu Singh, the experience was a reminder that simple outings can leave lasting impressions on young children. Bhanu was drawn to the farm's open spaces, animals and horses. They also carried some food, unsure whether they would find suitable, non-spicy options for Aayansh. To their pleasant surprise, the farm had a child-friendly menu. Once they arrived, the family let the day unfold at Aayansh's pace. "He didn't run around shouting or get overwhelmed. He was quiet, curious, and busy taking everything in," Bhanu remembers. One moment that stayed with him was watching his son run around the hens. Until then, hens had been pictures in a book. Now, they were moving around him, clucking and going about their business. The horses and pigs offered another kind of discovery. "He looked at the horse like he was thinking, 'This is the horse from my book.' He did the same with the pig. In his book, it was just a picture, but here it had a smell and made a sound. For him, it was a big thing." The family's two visits showed how hands-on experiences can help children build on what they learn from books. For the adults, these might have been ordinary sights and sounds. For Aayansh, they were details that no picture could quite capture. The family stayed close, letting him decide how near he wanted to get to each animal. A dedicated guide showed them how to approach and handle the animals safely, explaining which feed to offer and how to do it. There was no need to hurry him along. If something caught his attention, he could stay and watch. From watching horses to riding one The first visit was about getting acquainted with the animals. Aayansh was too young to ride a horse, but the experience left him with memories he continued to talk about long after the family returned home. Then, at three and a half, he asked to visit the farm again; this time, he had a plan of his own. "He clearly told us he wanted to visit again and ride a horse," Bhanu says. At three and a half, Aayansh returned to the farm with a wish of his own: to ride a horse. The family returned, and Aayansh got his wish. He was the youngest child on the farm to ride a horse that day, making the moment especially memorable for his parents. Bhanu noticed how much had changed. On the first visit, his son had watched the animals with wide-eyed curiosity. Now, he knew what he wanted to do. He approached the experience with greater confidence , going around to meet the animals again, almost as if he were reconnecting with old friends. "For us, the most special part was watching him sit on the horse with so much pride," Bhanu says. "The first trip was about discovery, while the second was about building on those memories and trying something new on his own." A holiday doesn't need a packed itinerary The two visits changed the way Bhanu thinks about family holidays. Earlier, he associated a good holiday with travelling to a new destination and having plenty of activities planned. Now, he finds himself asking a different question before choosing a place: "What will my child actually experience here? What will he see, feel, and remember?" His advice to parents who want to introduce young children to nature is to start small. Choose a place close to home, perhaps somewhere connected to an animal or activity the child already loves, and leave room for curiosity to lead the way. "Don't try to fit too many activities into one day. Let your child explore at their own pace, follow their curiosity, and enjoy the little moments," he says. After all, Aayansh's first farm visit wasn't filled with elaborate attractions or a faraway holiday backdrop. It was a day of watching hens, meeting pigs and standing close to horses he had previously known only from books. For parents, Aayansh's story is a reminder that meaningful family holidays need not involve packed itineraries or faraway destinations. Yet those encounters stayed with him. They even gave him something to look forward to when the family returned. And perhaps that's one of the loveliest things about travelling with children: you may plan the outing, pack the snacks and choose the destination, but you never quite know which small moment will find a permanent place in their hearts. And sometimes, the best souvenirs from a family holiday are the memories a child carries home, and the little adventures they can't wait to have next. All images courtesy of Bhanu Singh

items.descriptionOriginal: Cut open a ripe jackfruit, and you are greeted by its golden-yellow flesh, sweet aroma and sticky, fibrous peel. While the juicy fruit often finds its way into curries, chips and desserts, its thick outer covering usually ends up in the bin. Researchers at the National Institute of Technology (NIT) Rourkela , however, have found another use for this often-discarded part of the fruit. They have turned jackfruit peel into a material that removed more than 90% of fluoride from contaminated water in laboratory tests, in about 10 minutes. The idea brings together two things that rarely make it into the same conversation: fruit waste and safer drinking water. For families whose groundwater contains too much fluoride, which can damage teeth and bones over time, this innovation could eventually offer a more affordable way to make drinking water safer. How does jackfruit peel help clean water? The secret lies in what researchers have made from the peel. The team converted discarded jackfruit peel into activated carbon and modified it with zirconium, a metal that helps the material capture fluoride from water. Modified with zirconium, jackfruit-peel-based activated carbon helps capture excess fluoride from contaminated water. Photograph: ( Nature ) Prof. Susmita Mishra, Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering at NIT Rourkela, explains the thinking behind the innovation. "The key idea behind this technology is to use an agricultural waste material as a resource for water purification. We prepared activated carbon from discarded jackfruit peel and modified it with zirconium to improve its ability to capture fluoride from water," she adds. The material showed promising results in laboratory tests, removing over 90% of fluoride within approximately 10 minutes under the tested conditions. Fluoride occurs naturally in water, but drinking water containing too much of it over a long period can damage teeth and bones. This condition, known as fluorosis, can affect both children and adults. Removing excess fluoride, however, is not always straightforward. Reverse osmosis, a widely used water treatment method, can waste considerable amounts of water and remove minerals such as calcium and magnesium. Other methods, including ion exchange and activated alumina, also come with limitations, including the use of chemicals that can raise environmental concerns. The NIT Rourkela team's approach explores whether an agricultural by-product can help make fluoride removal more accessible. What did the researchers find? In laboratory experiments, the jackfruit-peel-based material removed more than 90% of fluoride from water containing around 1–5 milligrams per litre. Under the tested conditions, the team recorded removal efficiencies of over 90–97% within 10–20 minutes. The patented innovation by NIT Rourkela researchers offers a new approach to tackling fluoride contamination using agricultural waste. Photograph: ( Gujarat Samachar ) The researchers have also secured a patent for the technology. The team comprises Prof. Mishra and Dr. Pratima Minz, Research Graduate at NIT Rourkela. They estimate that preparing the material costs approximately Rs 37 per gram, based on the electricity and chemicals used in its synthesis. These are promising early findings, but there is still some way to go before the material can be used to treat drinking water outside the laboratory. The research has reached Technology Readiness Level 4 (TRL 4), meaning the material and its underlying concept have been validated in a laboratory environment. What happens next? For families in rural and semi-urban areas where groundwater contains excess fluoride, an affordable treatment option could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their material could eventually be used in decentralised water treatment systems, bringing purification closer to the communities that need it. Prof. Mishra says, "The potential of this technology lies in its use of an easily available agricultural by-product to develop a cost-effective material for fluoride removal. In the long term, the technology could contribute to water treatment solutions for communities in fluoride-affected regions, subject to further testing and validation." The team is now working towards a prototype to test the material's potential beyond the laboratory. Photograph: ( The Printlines ) The next step is to develop a physical prototype and test how the material performs in practical conditions. The team will also study its long-term performance and operating costs to understand whether it can be deployed on a larger scale. A discarded jackfruit peel is not yet ready to make drinking water safer on its own. But this research offers an interesting possibility: something routinely thrown away could, with further development, become part of a solution to a problem that affects communities across India.

items.descriptionOriginal: A 50-year-old Japanese planting method is quietly reshaping vacant lots, schoolyards, and parking strips across the United States -- not through large-scale industrial effort, but through the hands of neighbors who show up on a Saturday to tuck seedlings into carefully prepared soil. Developed by botanist Akira Miyawaki, the method skips the slow prologue of natural forest succession, mixing climax species and their supporting plants to create self-sustaining ecosystems within decades rather than centuries. What makes it remarkable is not just the science but the ritual embedded in it: "He would take each plant, and the community had to say its name," recalls one organizer -- "it was about restoring relationships between humans and non-humans." The miniforest movement asks something modest of each participant and returns something harder to name: a sense of belonging to a place, and a stake in its future.
