items.descriptionOriginal: At Bengaluru's Racecourse Junction, people crossing the road had to spend longer than necessary among moving vehicles. One turn gave cars a generous sweep of the road, leaving pedestrians to find their way through traffic. When urban designers Nishita Parmar and Vedanti Agarwal studied the junction, they discovered something surprising. Relatively few vehicles were using one left turn, while far more people needed to cross that stretch. Why, then, was so much space being given to cars? Working with principal designer Monik Shah and the team at Compartment S4 , they helped redesign the junction to include a pedestrian refuge island, giving people somewhere to pause while crossing. The work was part of the Orbital project, commissioned by the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) and supported by the Sustainable Mobility Network. It was one example of a question guiding their work across Bengaluru: how can streets and the spaces around them better serve people on foot? Why did one left turn have so much space? The team began at Racecourse by observing how people and vehicles actually moved. They counted traffic, followed pedestrian routes and noted where the two came into conflict. "When we actually went and mapped that entire junction, we understood that the volume of vehicles coming from [the road] and going towards the left was much lower compared to the volume of pedestrians," Parmar says. That meant pedestrians were crossing a wider stretch of moving traffic than necessary. "We call it pedestrian exposure time. To cross from A to B, it took a longer time, and that means you're getting exposed to the moving vehicle for longer," she explains. The designers proposed a more compact turn, changes to traffic movement and a refuge island to break up the crossing. For someone walking to college, work or another destination, spending less time among vehicles could make the journey easier. This matters at a junction serving the Race Course, educational institutions and other destinations. Students and other pedestrians pass through daily, while events bring larger groups into the area. At Racecourse Junction, vehicles had a generous sweep of the carriageway to negotiate one of the turns. By December 2023, BBMP had begun redevelopment work at Race Course Road junction, including plans for pedestrian crossings, seating and waiting areas. In February 2025, local reporting described the redevelopment as completed, with benches installed for pedestrians and officegoers . Compartment S4 also lists its Race Course Junction project as completed. A road can appear to need more space for vehicles because of the way it has been designed. But once actual movement is measured, the hierarchy can look different. The physical intervention is documented, although published before-and-after figures showing reduced crossing times or traffic conflicts were not available for this story. Why test a design on the street first? Parmar trained as an architect at CEPT Ahmedabad. Her experience in urban design and strategy, including work with Jaipur's Domestic Workers' Union, exposed her to the ways public infrastructure affects everyday lives. Agarwal, who has a Master's in Urban Design from UC Berkeley, has worked on urban mapping, landscape-led planning, transit-oriented development and environmentally sensitive design in India and the United States, including at WRT's San Francisco studio and Studio POD in India. Their approach begins with observing rather than assuming. Before committing to permanent changes, the team tested how a redesign worked on the street. That matters because people rarely move exactly as a drawing predicts. Someone may take a shortcut across the road; a driver may turn differently when traffic builds up. Watching these movements allows designers to identify problems and adjust plans before construction becomes permanent. "The issues never come under one sort of bucket. There is a transport issue, there is a utility issue, there is a space-constraint issue, there is a traffic issue, and everything comes together to form an urban issue," Parmar says. They began looking for locations where one intervention could address several concerns, including awkward road edges and spaces left beneath flyovers. "We started mapping these areas or these locations where there is some kind of demonstration possible to make that a lighthouse project and show how you can think of spaces, otherwise negative spaces or deformed spaces in the city, as something different," she says. Turning such ideas into actual spaces also means working within government approvals, budgets and construction constraints. "If we aim for something really high in the first go, it might not get passed or it might not have the budgets to get implemented," Parmar explains. "Whatever intervention we do, it is not only solving one particular thing, but it is looking at all the aspects of issues in an urban context," she adds. That thinking led the team to Shivananda Flyover. Turning unused flyover space into a public park At Shivananda, a large area beneath the flyover was going unused, while people passing through had barely 1.5 feet of footpath to walk on. The team's surveys showed that pedestrians were already using this route between residential neighbourhoods, universities and the Race Course. The designers wondered whether some of the underused land could become a more welcoming place for them. "The flyover was taking up a lot of space which was unused," Parmar says. "So we thought, let's take this and integrate it with the junction." Their response was Pause Park, designed with seating, platforms, steps, swings, greenery and art. The aim was to give people a place to sit and spend time in an area they previously had little reason to stop in. The area connects residential neighbourhoods with universities and the Racecourse, meaning people were already using it as part of their daily routes. Work to make the area useful was under way by June 2023, when BBMP was constructing benches and public toilets after residents objected to an earlier proposal for a basketball court and skating rink, citing safety concerns around nearby traffic . In February 2025, civic officials described Shivananda Circle among junctions they had developed. However, a report on 31 May 2025 said finishing work on the mini park's swings and greenery was still in its final stages. An exact public opening date, and whether all facilities are currently accessible, could not be independently confirmed. The idea nevertheless poses a valuable question for a city full of flyovers: could the land beneath them offer something useful to the people who walk past every day? Will people actually use these spaces? For road junctions, the team can examine crossing times, traffic flow and potential conflicts between pedestrians and vehicles. "For junctions, it is about seeing how smooth the traffic flow has become. These things are more objective," Agarwal says. The team is also examining how urban design might lessen the effects of heat. After a space is built, they consider post-occupancy studies , returning to see how people actually use it. "For open spaces, it is about going during the most active hour and seeing whether the community has adopted it," Agarwal says. The resulting Pause Park introduces seating, platforms, steps, swings, greenery and art into the space beneath the flyover. Are children playing there? Are older people sitting comfortably? Can different groups share the space? Such observations help show whether a public place is working as intended, and what may need to change. What it takes to get a better street built For the designers, a challenge lies in making the work behind the final design visible. Surveys, conversations with communities and coordination across departments all take time, even if the public usually sees only a finished image. "Research is an intangible component, but it eventually drives the project," Shah says. "The government wants to see the 3D renders." Parmar says many government agencies are more familiar with architecture and structural consultancy than with the process urban design requires. "They don't always understand that arriving at an urban-design proposal needs a different kind of process," she says. The team is therefore working on how projects are commissioned and carried out, including surveys, community engagement, procurement and implementation. "We are helping governments redesign the SOPs for how designers should engage with such projects," Parmar says. At Racecourse, their work began by noticing how much road space was devoted to a little-used turn. At Shivananda, they looked at the people squeezing along a narrow footpath beside a large, underused area. In both places, the first step was the same: pay attention to how people live with the city that has already been built, and use that understanding to make it work better for them. All Pictures: Compartment S4

items.title: Άτομα από τη Generation Jones εξηγούν τις κύριες πολιτισμικές διαφορές τους με τους Boomers
items.titleOriginal: People from Generation Jones explain their major cultural differences with Boomers
items.description: Η Generation Jones, άτομα που γεννήθηκαν από το 1954-1965, θεωρείται μια «μικρο-γενιά» μεταξύ των Boomers και της Generation X. Αν και συνήθως συγκεντρώνονται με τα Boomers, υπάρχουν μερικές αρκετά ευδιάκριτες διαφορές μεταξύ τους. Σε μια διαδικτυακή κοινότητα των Generation Jones-ers, ένα μέλος με το όνομα @WalkingHorse, παρότρυνε όσους στη Generation Jones να συζητήσουν πώς…
items.descriptionOriginal: Generation Jones , people born from 1954-1965, is considered a ‘micro-generation’ between Boomers and Generation X . Though typically lumped in with Boomers, there are some pretty distinct differences between them. In an online community of Generation Jones-ers, a member named @WalkingHorse, prompted those in Generation Jones to discuss how their upbringing differed from Boomers in a post titled “What is and who are Generation Jones. Step inside…”. “We’re often described as pragmatic idealists, raised on big dreams but tempered by economic recessions and a sense of lowered expectations compared to the Boomers’ post-war prosperity,” they wrote. “Think of us a generation that got the tail end of the party but had to clean up the mess.” So, what makes them different? It inspired many Generation Jones members to share their thoughts and opinions. These are some of the major cultural differences those in Generation Jones have with Boomers: “We were too young to fully participate in the counterculture of the ’60s but old enough to feel its aftershocks.” – @WalkingHorse Gen Jones men also signed up for the selective service, but were not drafted as the Vietnam war had ended.” – @tedshreddon “Boomers had Elvis and The Beatles. We had Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd.” – @Scr33ble “First teenage generation to experience the Space Shuttle launch. First teen generation to watch music videos in between movies on cable TV then the birth of MTV. We laughed when hearing that golf obsessed President Gerald Ford would routinely slice or hook a ball into a crowd of spectators. Then laugh at Chevy Chase for mimicking our clumsy commander in Chief. We watched our parents go through the fuel rationing days where you could only buy gas for you car if the last digit on the plate was an odd or even number. We counted days along with the media on how long the Iran hostages were being held. We lost John Lennon while not in that sweet spot age to have experienced the musical British Invasion of the 60’s. Instead, MTV opened to floodgates to the Brit-pop invasion of Duran Duran followed closely by big hair, neon clothing and wondering why saying ‘too hip’ was all that and a bag of chips. Best part was that college tuition was sorta affordable.” – @contrivancedevice There for the start of major social change “Not mentioned yet, but we were present for the rise of gay rights. Went to my first gay bar at 19. Music, especially Disco, was infused with pride and acceptance and coming out. ‘We are Family’, ‘I’m Coming Out’. Queen and the Village People, etc. The rise of ‘women’s music’ like Holly Near and Chris Williamson. Activists like Harvey Milk and later ACT UP. We were young adults when AIDS hit and the fight for treatment led to a huge wave of coming out. We lost a whole generation of gay men to that plague. ” – @BldrJanet “Boomers remember where they were when President Kennedy died. We remember where we were when John Lennon died.” – @KJPratt “Musically speaking, I think we were blessed. Our musical heyday had everything. Our moms played Elvis the king on the radio, and we had Elvis Costello. The Stones and The Who transverse generations. We are old enough to remember Joan Baez and Bob Dylan pre-Chalamet, not to mention Freddie and Elton before their bio-pics. And Johnny Cash too. And shout out to the poster girl of the 80’s Cyndi Lauper (I got special love for her as a race tracker cause she walked hots at Belmont Park.)” – @Binky-Answer896 “We gave a hoot, and didn’t pollute!” – @Awkwardimplemet698 “We are the generation that got to see the war every evening at dinner ‘live via satellite’. – @blurtlebaby “Think: 45s—albums—-8 tracks—cassettes—-CDs—-Streaming! I’ve had the Rolling Stones on all!” – @NOLALaura “I always said that I experienced it all…born in 1957. I listened to my older siblings music. I stole my sisters Woodstock album when she went off to college. I still have it. I recall all the assassinations from JFK and MLK.I saw RFK being killed on live tv.(at least I think I did), I remember the chaos of the Vietnam war, the Chicago riots, the Nixon mess. I recall the beginning of the environmental fight, Sesame Street and the moon launch. Computers, and floppy discs, cell phones that came in small cases that would plug into the car. So much good stuff. So much chaos.” – @mammaV55 “There’s a sure way to know if you’re Gen J. Were you deadly afraid of quicksand?!” – @NOLALaura What is and who are Generation Jones. Step inside… by u/WalkingHorse in GenerationJones A generation still finding its name That’s really the throughline of every response here: a generation that grew up in the gap between two much louder cultural identities, and had to piece together its own story out of half-remembered assassinations, borrowed older siblings’ records, and a war that ended just in time to spare them but not their nerves. Boomers got Woodstock. Gen X got grunge. Generation Jones got the hangover in between, and somehow turned it into its own kind of resilience. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post People from Generation Jones explain their major cultural differences with Boomers appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το κοριτσάκι μπήκε σε ένα talent show χωρίς να το πει στη μαμά του και το πλήθος ήταν εδώ για αυτό
items.titleOriginal: Little girl entered a talent show without telling her mom, and the crowd was here for it
items.description: Ένα κοριτσάκι μπαίνει μέσα στις καρδιές των ανθρώπων και υπενθυμίζει σε όλους μας πόσο σημαντικό είναι να βάζεις τον εαυτό σου έξω κάθε τόσο. Σε ένα πλέον viral κλιπ TikTok που δημοσιεύτηκε από τον @ashleydkennedy14, μαθαίνουμε ότι η ανιψιά της στο νηπιαγωγείο είχε προφανώς συμμετάσχει σε ένα talent show χωρίς να το πει στη μαμά της, κάτι που περιελάμβανε…
items.descriptionOriginal: One little girl is somersaulting her way into people’s hearts , and reminding us all of how important it is to put yourself out there every once in a while. In a now-viral TikTok clip posted by @ashleydkennedy14, we learn that her kindergarten-aged niece had apparently entered herself into a talent show without telling her mom, a feat that involved forging mom’s signature onto a permission slip, no less. And just what did this “act” consist of? Somersaults. Lots of ‘em. Six, to be exact. Also one cartwheel, for good measure. She’d basically deliver one roll, wait for uproarious applause, then do another one. Solid routine, if you ask us. Honestly, it’s hard to tell which aspect of this moment is more endearing: watching this little girl valiantly overcome a wee bit of shyness, and in the process tapping into some pretty captivating stage presence, or seeing how enthusiastic the audience was to support her. Just good, wholesome stuff all around. Watch: Even online viewers were taken aback by this girl’s fearlessness. Or rather, her determination to keep going, in spite of her fear. People couldn’t stop talking about it “I need to know what her parents did because this is CEO level confidence and I am here for it.” “She was like oh u like that ” “Im honestly impressed by her independence. She signed herself up and was confident that she had it. Good job mama.” “She will go far in life. Courage is everything.” Others noted how kind the crowd was to cheer her on. “For the people who clapped, as a mother : THANK YOU. it means a lottt.” “The cheers from the crowd are the best.” “Ok. because the crowd passed the vibe check. We cheer over here, be brave!” Funnily enough, plenty of other folks chimed in with similar stories of kiddos sneaking into talent shows…with talents they may or may not have actually possessed. “My son tried to sign himself up to do karate at his school talent show…he’s never been to a karate class in his life…” “My daughter entered herself into the talent show in 1st grade and didn’t say anything. She played the piano… she had never played piano in her life til that day lol I need that confidence.” “My brother did this! He played harmonica for the whole school. He doesn’t know how to play the harmonica.” The real lesson here is bigger While this girl might receive a stern talking to about the importance of not forging signatures, her story is nonetheless a prime example of how kids can really shine when left on their own to take risks, try new things, and opt for exploration over perfection. It can be hard for parents to not want to protect their little ones from failure (whatever that means), but life often provides moments just like this to remind them that taking a step back is a precious opportunity to help instill some self advocacy. It’s just like the old saying goes, “Leap, and the net will appear.” Or in this case…somersault, and the cheers will follow. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Little girl entered a talent show without telling her mom, and the crowd was here for it appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Άτομα που γεννήθηκαν μεταξύ 1970 και ’85 ανταλλάσσουν ταμπέλες Gen X και Millennial για το «Gen Goonie»
items.titleOriginal: People born between 1970 and ’85 are trading Gen X and Millennial labels for ‘Gen Goonie’
items.description: Η Gen X (γεννημένη από το 1965 έως το 1980) αναφέρεται συχνά ως η «ξεχασμένη γενιά», επειδή βρίσκεται ανάμεσα στις πολύ μεγαλύτερες γενιές Baby Boomer και Millennial. Ωστόσο, η ετικέτα "ξεχασμένη" έχει μια ιδιαίτερη σημασία για τους νεότερους Gen Xers, καθώς ήταν πιθανότατα η λιγότερο γονεϊκή ομάδα παιδιών στην αμερικανική ιστορία. Όσοι γεννήθηκαν τη δεκαετία του 1970 ήταν…
items.descriptionOriginal: Gen X ( born 1965 to 1980 ) is often referred to as the “ forgotten generation ” because it is sandwiched between the much larger Baby Boomer and Millennial generations. However, the “forgotten” label carries a special meaning for younger Gen Xers, as they were likely the least parented group of kids in American history. Those born in the 1970s were raised in a time when more households were dual-income and the number of divorced parents was increasing. Many wore keys around their necks and took care of themselves after school. Younger Gen Xers also grew up when parents were more permissive, allowing them to stay out all day on their bikes. They only knew it was time to come home when the street lights came on. They also grew up in the last analog era without cellphones, and parents had to call around various houses to find out where their kids were. Sure, being a kid in those days was a little risky, but it also fostered a fantastic sense of independence. Where the “Gen Goonie” name comes from This experience isn’t completely limited to Gen Xers; some older millennials also experienced this type of freedom. Because kids born between 1970 and 1985 had a very specific experience, some born in this era have taken to calling themselves Generation Goonie, after the 1985 film, “ The Goonies ” starring Sean Astin, Josh Brolin, Ke Huy Quan, and Corey Feldman. “The Goonies” was a children’s movie based on a story by Steven Spielberg, with a screenplay by Chris Columbus (who would go on to direct “Home Alone”), that was directed by Richard Donner (“Superman: The Movie,” “Lethal Weapon,” “Scrooged”), who passed away in 2021. “Having been fortunate enough to speak to a lot of audiences, I have found that younger generations consider Gen X lucky to have grown up without social media and cellphones,” Chris Clews, a keynote speaker and author of ‘The Ultimate Essential Work & Life Lessons from ’80s Pop Culture,’ told Newsweek . “They often come up to me and express a desire to have grown up in an era where we knew where everyone was based on the bikes in a front yard, rather than location sharing on Snapchat.” What is Gen Goonie? “The Goonies” is a great example of the kids from this era because they lived a feral existence, traveling long distances on their bikes, had a thirst for adventure, a crude sense of humor, and an independent spirit that meant “never say die.” When their parents were on the verge of losing their homes, they didn’t wait for them to act; they went on a dangerous mission to find pirates’ treasure to prevent the developers from destroying their homes. The Goonies’ antics serve as a sharp contrast to today’s kids, who seem wrapped in bubble wrap and closely monitored by their parents. It also shows the fun kids can have when they spend time outdoors instead of on screens. The Generation Goonie trend is taking off on TikTok, where many younger Gen Xers and older millennials proudly embrace the title. For many, the moniker is more than just ‘Good Enough’ “1981, we had the best childhood out of any generation ever,” Bugface wrote. “Now this is something I’m proud to be a part of!!!!!” Rob wrote. “Hey you guys..” 77 genx here, Yorkshire, England. We definitely are the only generation of true play outside, tree climbing, bike riding, respectful, no mobile phone, VHS watching kids,” 2Dogs wrote. A ‘Goonies’ sequel is in the works The fun discussion around the term “Gen Goonie” shows that the 41-year-old film has staying power. So much that Warner Bros. greenlit a sequel to the film, with Steven Spielberg attached as producer , though no director has been announced. In August, the sequel’s writer, Potsy Ponciroli, said the screenplay was nearly done. “I have turned in a first draft, which was very well received, and I’m on a second draft, and I’m about 95% done with that, so we’re moving in the right direction,” Ponciroli said, according to Deadline . There’s nothing wrong with people who want to embrace the term Gen X. But, 41 years after “The Goonies” came out in theaters, the attitudes and the independence of the kids in the movie can be seen as a great example of a time that, sadly, we can never go back to. Humanity has crossed the digital divide and taken some of the adventure out of childhood. “The Goonies” is an excellent example of what we’ve lost, and those who understand the spirit of that era should be proud to embrace the title of “Goonie.” This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post People born between 1970 and ’85 are trading Gen X and Millennial labels for ‘Gen Goonie’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι Αμερικανοί μοιράζονται 15 από τα πιο ωραία πράγματα που έχουν δει στο εξωτερικό που θέλουν εδώ. Όπως τώρα.
items.titleOriginal: Americans share 15 of the coolest things they’ve seen overseas that they want here. Like, now.
items.description: Η Αμερική είναι η πλουσιότερη χώρα στον κόσμο, αλλά εξακολουθεί να της λείπουν μερικά πράγματα σε σύγκριση με άλλες χώρες. Γιατί η Αμερική δεν μπορεί να έχει σιδηρόδρομο υψηλής ταχύτητας, σύστημα υγειονομικής περίθαλψης που δεν θα σας χρεοκοπήσει ή σούπερ όμορφες τουαλέτες όπως σε άλλα μέρη του κόσμου; Γιατί δίνουμε φιλοδωρήματα σε κάθε γεύμα και γιατί δεν μπορείτε να βρείτε πουθενά μια αξιοπρεπή κρεατόπιτα;…
items.descriptionOriginal: America is the wealthiest country in the world, but it still lacks a few things compared to other countries. Why can’t America have a high-speed rail, a healthcare system that won’t bankrupt you, or super cool toilets like they do in other parts of the world? Why are we still tipping on every meal, and why can’t you find a decent meat pie anywhere? The great American experiment has done pretty well for the past 248 years, but we still have some blind spots. It would be cool if a brave politician could one day make America truly great by poaching all the best ideas from around the world and creating the perfect country. A Redditor recently asked people on the AskReddit subforum, “What’s one interesting thing you saw in another country that made you think, ‘How does my country not have this?” The responses are a great starting point for this hypothetical leader to begin making the improvements we’ve all been dying for. Bidets? Yes, we can! French fries with gravy? Yes, we can! Beer at Burger King? Yes, we can! We compiled a list of the 15 most interesting things they have in countries that should be implemented in America, like yesterday. 15 cool things they have in other countries that we need in America 1. Cashiers can sit down “I was an exchange student in Germany during my Junior year in high school. Right before I left, I had a job as a cashier at a grocery store. When I first went shopping in Germany, I thought, ‘THEY GET TO SIT?! WHY COULDN’T I DO THAT?!’ The only place that does this in the U.S. now is Aldi, which of course is a German company.” “Corporations: ‘It’s a slippery slope. If we let cashiers sit, what’s next? The federal government will make a law that says that pregnant women get time off, and we have to give them money? Fathers get paid time off, too? We let people stay home if they’re sick, without a doctor’s note? Employees get more than 2 weeks of vacation per year? We have to pay people enough to afford both food AND housing? Where does it end?!'” 2. On-time public transport “I travelled everywhere in Japan by public transport. My Japanese was terrible, but I could get everywhere with Google Maps because of the utter reliability of the services. I turned up at the station or bus stop and caught the transport that presented itself. The train, which was 5 minutes early, was not my train. The one that was on time on the right platform was the one I needed to catch.” 3. Foot-pedal toilets “I saw something similar in Mexico City, only it was a foot pedal to activate/flush a public toilet. This operation seems so much more sanitary than using a handle to flush a toilet.” “You want two peddles: 1) to lower the seat (it should automatically lift back up unless it has a lid which auto-closes); 2) flush.” 4. Coupon crushers “In 1997, I was in Singapore and saw these things that looked like vending machines. It was a machine that you would take your empty pop can, and put it in this compartment, lift a handle to crush the can. It would then drop down into the machine. Then the machine printed out coupons for businesses in the area. I thought it was genius! I’ve never seen it anywhere else.” 5. Bidets “More Bidets, pls. My anus can only take so much tp.” “Honestly, every person who has tried it has understood why I love them so much. It’s uncomfortable at first because it’s different, but it really does leave you feeling much cleaner.” A bidet next to a toilet. Photo credit: Murat Ts./Unsplash 6. Private public restroom stalls “Public restroom stalls without the stupid gaps in between the doors, and smaller to zero gaps on the bottoms of the doors.” 7. Server buttons “In South Korea, there were buttons on the tables to signal you were ready to order, pay, whatever. It meant no pushy or hovering waitstaff and they were able to chill and relax a bit when no one needed their help.” “In Korea, they have a ‘bing-bong’ button on your table on a restaurant. If you need something, you press the button, your table number shows up on a screen by the server station, and they come over to your table. Usually, I just hold up my empty bottle or side dish and make eye contact from across the room, and they smile and bring me another one. Otherwise, the servers don’t come by and bother you during the meal. It’s so so so much better this way.” “We have this at Korean BBQ restaurants in Los Angeles.” 8. French fries with gravy “In Canada, you can get French fries with cheese and gravy.” “We have this in the US. If you’re in the Jersey/New York area they’re called Disco Fries.” Some delicious putin. Photo credit: Canva 9. Free healthcare “Basically, your medical bills are paid for by your taxes, so when you go into the hospital, the only thing that ends up costing money is the parking. The drawback can be that there is a waitlist for some surgery (except when it’s urgently needed to keep you alive), at this time, medical insurance can pay for it, but it’s still not as expensive as in America. Also, depending on the country, your medication is also a fraction of the actual cost. For example, in America a box of medication I have to take would cost me about US$600 a month, here in Australia that same medication only costs me about US $15” “Socialized medicine is only as good as the people implementing it. If it isn’t working properly, that isn’t really the concepts fault. It’s the people running it.” 10. Traffic light countdowns “In Germany, the traffic lights go from green to yellow to red like they do everywhere else, but after red, they light up red + yellow together before green. That way people have a head start getting ready to hit the gas and by the time it’s green you’re immediately moving forward. Bothers me more than it should when it just goes from red to green in other countries.” 11. The government does the taxes “Taxes filed FOR YOU, and the return just appearing in your bank account.” 12. Beer vending machines “Beer at Burger King” (One-upper!) A man using a vending machine. Photo credit: Canva 13. Attached caps “This one’s less exciting than a lot of others, but I bought a bottle of Coke in London, and when I opened it, I realized there was a little piece of plastic that held the lid to the neck of the bottle, so you don’t have to hold it. I can’t believe we don’t do that in the US. It’s such a tiny little thing, but it feels like a no brainer when you think about it.” “That is due to a new law (an EU law, but a lot of brands have done it for their UK products too). Bottle caps have to be attached to the bottle to prevent them from being littered and to help ensure that they are also recycled along with the bottle.” 14. Meat pies “America, they are just not as big a thing here as they are in other countries. I loved them in New Zealand, in fact, when I was there, they had a fast food joint called Georgie Pie that was absolutely fantastic, also bakeries everywhere, where you could get them too.” 15. Clean public toilets “Clean, modern public toilets. I’ve been to Japan a few times, and those public toilets are amazing. I need to go back to try the one-way glass wall ones. (On a side note, having been to some Japanese music festivals, it seems that they have no problem setting up mens bathrooms in a way that the women line up looking directly into the men’s bathroom. Very odd.) What's one interesting thing you saw in another country that made you think "how does my country not have this?"? by u/dr_doctorp in AskReddit So, what would you bring home? They say there’s no place like home, but sometimes other places have amenities that would make our home a whole lot better. From sitting cashiers to free healthcare to a toilet that doesn’t require holding the lid shut, it turns out “normal” looks pretty different depending on where you grew up. The good news is none of this is impossible, it’s just a matter of someone, somewhere, deciding we deserve it too. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Americans share 15 of the coolest things they’ve seen overseas that they want here. Like, now. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Η ανακάλυψη του γλοιοβλαστώματος αποκαλύπτει πώς τα καρκινικά κύτταρα του εγκεφάλου γίνονται πιο επιθετικά
items.titleOriginal: Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν ότι το παχύρρευστο, κολλώδες υγρό που περιβάλλει τους όγκους του γλοιοβλαστώματος μπορεί να κάνει τα καρκινικά κύτταρα του εγκεφάλου μικρότερα, πιο εύκαμπτα και καλύτερα να εισβάλλουν στον περιβάλλοντα ιστό. Ακόμα πιο ανησυχητικό, ορισμένες από αυτές τις αλλαγές επιμένουν αφού τα κύτταρα εγκαταλείψουν το παχύρρευστο υγρό, αποκαλύπτοντας έναν μηχανισμό που αγνοήθηκε προηγουμένως που θα μπορούσε να βοηθήσει αυτόν τον θανατηφόρο καρκίνο.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists discovered that the thick, sticky fluid surrounding glioblastoma tumors can make brain cancer cells smaller, more flexible, and better at invading surrounding tissue. Even more troubling, some of these changes persist after the cells leave the thick fluid, revealing a previously overlooked mechanism that could help this deadly cancer spread.

items.title: Skincubator: Επαναστατική συσκευή που επιτρέπει στους γονείς να εξασκούν την επαφή δέρμα με δέρμα με πρόωρα νεογνά
items.titleOriginal: Skincubator: Revolutionary Device Lets Parents Practice Skin-to-Skin Contact With Preterm Newborns
items.description: Η επαφή δέρμα με δέρμα, η πρακτική της τοποθέτησης ενός νεογέννητου απευθείας στο στήθος της μητέρας ή του πατέρα, θεωρείται απαραίτητη - μερικές φορές σωτήρια - φροντίδα για τα πρόωρα βρέφη. Ο Παγκόσμιος Οργανισμός Υγείας το συνιστά για τουλάχιστον οκτώ ώρες την ημέρα από τη γέννηση για όλα τα μωρά που γεννιούνται πριν από τις 37 εβδομάδες. Οι θερμοκοιτίδες μπορεί επίσης να είναι κρίσιμες για τ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Skin-to-skin contact, the practice of a newborn being placed directly onto the mother’s or father’s chest, is considered essential — sometimes lifesaving — care for preterm infants. The World Health Organization recommends it for at least eight hours a day beginning at birth for all babies born before 37 weeks. Incubators can also be critical for these newborns, however, and yet the carefully controlled environments prevent parents from performing that crucial skin-to-skin contact. A pioneering new technology has now bridged the two forms of care, allowing parents to hold their babies to their bodies without disrupting the essential treatments they require. Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital The Skincubator is a wearable medical tool designed for preterm infants weighing under 4.4 pounds that enables prolonged skin-to-skin contact beginning as early as the day of birth. A couple at Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital in Houston, Texas, recently became the first in the U.S. to experience the difference it can make. For about 10 days after their twins were born in August, Tiffany Ikwuagwu and Dorian Ojemen weren’t able to hold the babies, who arrived at just 26 weeks. “This is a great invention,” Ikwuagwu, herself an obstetrician and gynecologist, said in a video from Memorial Hermann upon using the Skincubator. “I think the fact that I can help regulate the babies’ heart[s] and help the babies relax and just have that connection to them, is very special.” Added Ojemen in an interview with CNN earlier this month: “Just the fact that you can have them on your chest, you can look in their eyes, you can hold them, feel them breathe, like, that immediately makes you feel like, wow, I’m a parent.” The tech, which was developed over four years, was granted FDA Breakthrough Device designation last December. With the Skincubator, parents can relax or rest while bonding with their baby for hours at a time, taking turns with other caregivers and family members if they so choose. Infants’ arterial, umbilical, feeding, and airway tubes all remain in place. “The baby is already in their incubator, and they’re transferred from the incubator to the Skincubator while they’re in their isolate,” explained Dr. Jaclyn Ruggiero, principal investigator for an ongoing clinical trial, adding: “The baby’s medical lines and breathing tubes or breathing support are all secured to the Skincubator base. And the way the baby gets into skin-to-skin care is there’s a retractable pad under the baby, and that pad is pulled down slowly.” Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital Skin-to-skin contact is standard practice for all babies, helping to stabilize their heart rate and breathing, stimulating digestion, regulating temperature, providing protection against infection, and fostering the bond between parent and child. “It turns on a part of the nervous system that’s really important for connection and feeling calm,” Ruggiero said. Per the website, clinicians interested in bringing Skincubators to their NICUs can book a call with the company to begin a pilot program. Learn more. items.descriptionOriginal: Most fans associate Reacher actor Alan Ritchson with kicking , punching , taking down criminals —you know, manly stuff. But the action star just revealed he also has a secret talent for singing, causing viewers to do a double take. Recently, Ritchson shared a video on his Instagram of himself singing Michael Jackson’s “Human Nature” in his hotel room (while shooting the next installment of his action-packed Amazon series). Nothing elaborate, just a backing track, a black T-shirt, and some bangin’ vocals. In his caption, he joked that the “weak attempt” was up for viewers’ pleasure or scorn. But it would quickly become clear that there would be no scorn. Fans were not prepared for Ritchson’s amazing singing voice View this post on Instagram “Calling this a weak attempt is pretty disrespectful to the rest of us who sound like injured wildlife in the shower ,” one person quipped. There were obviously more comments where that came from. On Instagram and X , people shared their shock, envy, and amazement that Ritchson had yet another special skill up his sleeve. “Bro, I’m going to call you out. You can’t be that tall, that handsome, that buff, and also have such a good voice. You need to give one up hahaha. Love your work brother,” one commenter remarked. “Remember all these buff actors used to be nerdy theatre kids. And still are lol, sing your soul dude lol,” another commenter reminisced. Actor Alan Ritchson goes viral after performing ‘Human Nature’ by Michael Jackson. pic.twitter.com/HzHPpfSjRd — Daily Loud (@DailyLoud) October 18, 2026 “Bruh had no idea this dude could sing. Was not on my bingo card this week,” commented a user. “Reacher can sing too? Some guys got handed the whole toolbox,” praised another commenter. “Reacher doing Michael Jackson is the quiet coworker who never talks in meetings and then absolutely destroys at the holiday party karaoke. Nobody looks at him the same after that,” another user noted. Newsflash: Reacher has been singing for years Of course, real ones know that Ritchson had the beginnings of a music career long before he was kicking ass onscreen. In 2004, he auditioned for American Idol in Atlanta with a flirtatious rendition of Stevie Wonder’s “You Are the Sunshine of My Life.” Earlier this year, he collaborated with artists Connor Price and Nic D on their single “Hey Heartbreaker.” And recently, he made a fan’s dream come true by filming himself singing lyrics he wrote to a piano piece they composed…all while sporting his character’s beat-up look. View this post on Instagram “Music is fun. I love music. Music makes me happy,” Ritchson wrote in the caption. It’s this enthusiasm that makes Ritchson’s abundance of gifts bearable. Do some people get an unfair amount of talent and genetic blessings? Clearly. But does it soften the blow when these people are also kind and cool to be around, and they use those blessings to share joy with others? Also yes. Now where do we sign a petition for a musical episode of Reacher ? items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, New Orleans gives thousands of discarded Christmas trees an unusual but pretty cool second life. Instead of ending up in a landfill, Louisiana National Guard helicopters fly bundled trees into the wetlands at Bayou Sauvage Urban National Wildlife Refuge. The trees support a restoration effort that helps prevent erosion, rebuild marshland, and provide habitats for local wildlife. The annual Christmas Tree Drop has been taking place for nearly three decades, bringing together New Orleans residents, local government agencies, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and the Louisiana Army National Guard. Louisiana National Guard attaches Christmas tree bundle to helicopter. Photo Credit: USFWS How Christmas trees make it from the curb to the wetlands After the holidays, New Orleans residents leave their discarded Christmas trees at the curb for collection. The trees must be bare: no lights, ornaments, tinsel, or artificial snow can be left over since they’ll eventually become part of the natural environment. Once collected, workers secure approximately 50 to 60 trees into each bundle with wire straps. Then comes the part that makes this recycling program a little different from most. Louisiana National Guard crews attach the bundles to helicopters, with each harness holding up to four bundles at a time. The helicopters then fly over the refuge and lower the trees into designated marsh areas. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service , crews carefully position the bundles in straight lines to create barriers in the marsh. Once the trees are in place, refuge workers use airboats to retrieve the harnesses. It’s a fairly elaborate system for something that was sitting in someone’s living room just a month or so earlier. Louisiana National Guard harnesses tree bundle to a helicopter. Photo Credit: Louisiana Army National Guard Discarded Christmas trees are surprisingly good for the wetlands Louisiana’s wetlands play a critical role in protecting communities from flooding and storms. But erosion and other environmental pressures damage these ecosystems. When bundles of trees are placed in shallow water, their branches help slow waves and trap sediment that would otherwise be carried away. Over time, the accumulated material supports marsh grass growth, stabilizes the shoreline, and creates new habitat for birds, shrimp, crabs, and other local wildlife. A graduate student came up with the idea after wondering whether discarded Christmas trees could help rebuild marshland. It caught on, and the project became an annual restoration effort. In 2025, the City of New Orleans reported that the program had helped restore an area of marshland roughly equivalent to 330 football fields. Bayou Sauvage Refuge using a helicopter to drop a tree bundle. Photo Credit: USFWS The National Guard gets some valuable training The Christmas tree drop also provides an unexpected benefit for the Louisiana National Guard. Originally, refuge workers transported the trees using airboats. Now, National Guard helicopters transport the bundles into the wetlands, allowing crews to practice lifting and positioning heavy loads. In a 2024 Louisiana National Guard news release, Chief Warrant Officer 4 Gabriel Ruiz explained the operation benefits to the coastal environment while “also providing valuable training hours for our pilots and crew members.” Bayou Sauvage National Wildlife Refuge staff retrieve the harnesses. Photo Credit: USFWS Christmas trees have value beyond the end of January For New Orleans residents, participating doesn’t require much beyond removing decorations and placing their tree out for collection. From there, the city and its partners handle the rest. What starts as a routine holiday cleanup becomes part of a much larger effort to protect Louisiana’s wetlands. Not a bad second act for a Christmas tree most people are done with by January. The post New Orleans drops old Christmas trees into wetlands by helicopter. They’re helping rebuild the marsh. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: “Aha!” moments are great for solving problems but less so for creative judgements, according to new research. We are all familiar with the feeling of “Aha!” that accompanies the sudden realization of our next big ideas. Notably, these insights arrive with a peculiar sense of authority—you don’t just know; you know you know. Decades of research suggest this confidence is usually merited. Across anagrams, riddles, and word problems, solutions that arrive as a sudden Aha! are more likely to be correct than through step-by-step reasoning. Researchers term this finding the Eureka Heuristic, or idea that insights act as cognitive shortcuts, telling us that a given solution is likely to be correct, against our background knowledge. Crucially, past work investigated whether insights predict solution quality in problems with one, verifiable answer. But what happens when there isn’t one? UC Santa Barbara researchers Jacqueline McGuinness, Jonathan Schooler, Shelly Gable ,and Madeleine Gross posed that question in a recent featured article in the Journal of Intelligence . Their answer: in open-ended creative work, the Aha! experience is less a signal of accuracy, and more an illusory sense of brilliance—a phenomenon they refer to as the Aha! glow. “Insights tell us that an idea is promising, but primarily when there is a correct answer to be had,” says McGuinness, manager of Schooler’s META Lab in UCSB’s psychological and brain sciences department. “When we widen the solution space in creative contexts, the feeling of insight can inflate our perception of how good our ideas really are.” Evidence for the Aha! glow first comes from re-analysis of a daily diary study that tracked professional writers and physicists over two weeks. Every night, participants logged their best idea from the day, along with how creative they thought the idea was, and whether or not it came as an “Aha!” moment. Six months later, they were asked to rate the creativity of each idea again. These professions were chosen as real-world proxies for two types of problem-solving. Physicists tend to work on problems with a single, defined solution. Creative writers, in contrast, face problems where many ideas could work, and the value of each only reveals itself once fully developed. The findings revealed a striking difference between professions: writers rated their Aha! ideas as highly creative at the time of idea generation, but much lower 6-months later. On the other hand, physicists rated their Aha! ideas as more creative over time. So when an idea arrives with a flash of insight—an Aha! moment—writers come to think less of it over time, while physicists come to think more of it. Crucially, this divergence only occurred for insights; ideas arrived at through analytical reasoning improved slightly over time for both groups. A second study had 100 participants complete two laboratory tasks: a word problem task with one answer per problem, and the alternate uses task, where participants provide unusual uses for common objects like a brick or tin can. On the alternate uses task, stronger insight experiences predicted how creative people thought their ideas were, much more than creativity judgements of independent raters. Within the same participants, the association between insight intensity and idea quality was nearly four times stronger in the word problem task, compared to the creative idea generation task. “That’s the part I find illuminating,” says Schooler, a distinguished professor of psychological and brain sciences and director of UCSB’s Center for Mindfulness and Human Potential. “For the very same person the experience of aha is well-calibrated to the quality of their ideas on the one task, but produces an Aha! glow on the other.” Yet the team suspects that the glow remains useful. Across both studies, Aha! experiences also predicted greater task enjoyment, confidence, and self-reported motivation to continue working. “In creative work where there is no singular way of assessing solution quality, it often takes months or even years to assess whether an idea will be any good,” adds Gross, a project scientist in the META Lab. “So a boost of confidence, although not always warranted, might be what you need to stick with an idea long enough to find out.” In other words, the researchers say, Aha! moments in creative contexts such as the arts may be less a verdict than a motivational impetus—one that those laboring on ideas unfinished have reason to accept, even if exaggerated. Source: UC Santa Barbara The post ‘Aha!’ moments are good for problem solving, but less helpful for creative work appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Στην αθέατη ζωή, μακριά από τα φώτα της δημοσιότητας και τον λαμπερό κόσμο με τις επιτυχίες και την διεθνή καταξίωση εμβαθύνει η μουσικοθεατρική παράσταση «Εγω ο Σερ, Γρηγόρης Μπιθικώτσης» που έκανε πρεμιέρα στο Christmas Theater και θα παρουσιαστεί στην Αθήνα για περιορισμένο αριθμό παραστάσεων από τις 30 Οκτωβρίου έως τις 28 Νοεμβρίου 2026, σε κείμενο και σκηνοθεσία Δημήτρη Μαλισσόβα παρουσιάζοντας την προσωπικότητα και τη φυσιογνωμία του Γρηγόρη Μπιθικώτση. Στόχος της παράστασης αυτής είναι να αποκαλύψει και να παρουσιάσει ταυτόχρονα ποιος ήταν ο άνθρωπος πίσω από τη φωνή που σημάδεψε την Ελλάδα, το παιδί από το Περιστέρι που μεγάλωσε μέσα στη φτώχεια, γνώρισε τον πόλεμο, τη Μακρόνησο, τον έρωτα, τις μεγάλες συνεργασίες και τελικά έγινε μία από τις σημαντικότερες μορφές του ελληνικού τραγουδιού. Μην ξεχνάμε πως και ο μεγάλος μας χρονογράφος Δημήτρης Ψαθάς αναφερόμενος στον Γρηγόρη Μπιθικώτση στο θρυλικό χρονογράφημα του στα «Νέα» με την τεράστια απήχηση, τον αποκαλούσε «Σερ του ελληνικού τραγουδιού». items.titleOriginal: Podcast Transcript October 23rd, 2026— Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law, world’s tallest wind turbine, and why fall makes you reach for reruns
items.description: Περιγραφή επεισοδίου: Η Γερμανία μόλις ολοκλήρωσε την κατασκευή της ψηλότερης ανεμογεννήτριας στον κόσμο: ύψος 1.197 πόδια και κατασκευάστηκε χωρίς γερανό. Έπρεπε να εφεύρουν μια εντελώς νέα μέθοδο κατασκευής, γιατί οι γερανοί δεν πάνε τόσο ψηλά. Επίσης αυτή την εβδομάδα: ο ουγγρικός νόμος που έπεσε με τον πιο απροσδόκητο τρόπο, ένας Ισπανός εξερευνητής διασχίζει την Ανταρκτική με χαρταετό μόνος του…
items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Germany just finished building the world’s tallest wind turbine: 1,197 feet tall, and built without a crane. They had to invent an entirely new construction method, because cranes don’t go that high. Also this week: the Hungarian law that fell in the most unexpected way, a Spanish explorer crossing Antarctica on kite power alone, and why fall makes your brain reach for the same reruns every year. Ten solutions total. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Intro Arielle: Hello everyone, I’m Arielle. Karissa: And I’m Karissa. Arielle: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. What’s new in your world, Karissa? Karissa: Well, I’m excited that this week has graced us with a little bit of rain and some cloudy weather, and it’s just really starting to make me feel pretty cozy and nostalgic, honestly. Which kind of has to do with one of our solutions later. But, uh, yeah, it’s been, it’s been good over here. What about you, Arielle? Arielle: Um, I shaved my head. Karissa: Well, that’s pretty big. Arielle: So that’s been pretty new. Yeah. I mean, obviously this is a podcast, so people don’t know what I look like regularly, but, uh, I did have hair, and now I don’t, and that’s been very liberating. Mm. But yeah, it is getting colder, so maybe not the most opportune time- I was gonna say … to have an exposed head. But, um, here we are. It’s okay. Uh, just need to get myself, like, a nice little toque, or I guess… Yeah, toque is such a Canadian word, but it’s basically just, like, a beanie. So yeah, I’ll be in the market for some cozy little beanies. But yeah, other than that, nothing really crazy to report. Karissa: Well, that’s a really big change and a very exciting one. Hmm. Um- And it kind of goes with, like, the changing of the seasons as well, so that’s, uh- Yeah. I love it. Arielle: Yeah. The, the, the trees are shedding their leaves, and so am I, in a way. Karissa: Yes. You are also shedding the season away and starting anew. I love it. Arielle: Yeah. And as you said, Karissa, some of our solutions have to do with, uh, changing seasons and nostalgia and all of that. Newsletter & Socials Arielle: But before we get into the solutions, we would love to remind everyone that they can sign up for our free daily or weekly newsletter. You can find the link to sign up for that in the show notes, and that way you’ll get all of this positive news straight to your inbox. Karissa: You can also get all of this positive news on our social media feeds. You can follow us at @optimistdaily on basically everything, except on X, where we are @OdeToOptimism. Arielle: We love it when you guys engage with us, like our stories or posts, share with friends and family, or just on your own personal stories. All of that is really, really appreciated. Your comments, questions, feedback is very welcome. Or you can reach Karissa and I directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com, so feel free to shoot us an email. Karissa: Sharing these solutions in any way possible really helps us out with our mission, and it’s a free way to help The Optimist Daily. But if you’d like to financially support The Optimist Daily, then you can become an Emissary. The link to do that is in the show notes. And Emissaries also get a really cool podcast shout-out to someone or something that makes you optimistic if you sign up. That email with the information on how to do that should automatically go to you, and we send out periodic reminders as well to- Submit your shout-outs. Emissary Shout-out & Local Changemakers Arielle: Yeah, we haven’t really mentioned the Emissary Shout-out recently, because we’ve been focusing on our Local Changemakers series. On that note, we would love to thank everyone who participated and nominated, uh, young local changemakers. This year, we were focusing on changemakers who are 30 years old and under. And it’s been really fun to read all of the submissions. And it has been a little bit difficult to choose our finalists. But we have them, and we are excited to share their stories with you in the coming weeks. Yeah, we’re gonna be starting to publish the Local Changemakers series next week on Wednesday. And we will be featuring a local changemaker every Wednesday into the run-up to Thanksgiving. Karissa: Yeah, I’m so excited to share these stories. And thank you once again to everyone who nominated a young changemaker. Arielle: Mm-hmm. We did get some comments that people were wondering why we were limiting the age. Um, and honestly, in the last two years that we’ve done the Local Changemakers series, I don’t think anyone who was nominated was under the age of 30. Most of the submissions were for people who had established charities or who were just further along, you know, in their lives and professional, uh, experiences. So, that’s why we decided to focus on the younger generation this year. If you wanted to nominate someone who was out of this age range, then there’s always next year for that. Karissa: And we always have our emails open for any suggestions on people to feature on The Optimist Daily. And we sincerely appreciate all of you sharing all the optimism in your own lives with us year-round. Arielle: But speaking of sharing optimism, should I dive into this week’s solutions? Karissa: Yeah, let’s get into all the positive news from this week. Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law Arielle: The first solution is titled “Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law, unlocking billions in EU funds”. Hungary just repealed the law that banned any mention of homosexuality or transgender identities in schools and media, a law Orbán’s government had defended for five years as, quote unquote, “child protection.” The EU had been withholding four point two billion euros over it. And the thing that finally made the law politically toxic for the government wasn’t a rights campaign. It was actually a child abuse scandal. So the political unraveling started when Orbán’s government pardoned someone who had covered up abuse at a children’s home, which turned their own child protection law into a liability rather than an asset. The repeal went further than reversing the 2021 law. It also cleared Hungary’s path to rejoin Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe. Those are major EU research programs that had been suspended along with the funding. The civil rights organization that fought this for five whole years is celebrating, but they’re clear that this isn’t full equality yet. There’s still no same-sex marriage, no adoption rights, and no legal name change process for transgender individuals. But this is a step in the right direction, and we’re here to celebrate every win. How one small device is solving the apartment solar access problem Arielle: The second solution is titled “How one small device is solving the apartment solar access problem”. Most people who live in apartments, like me, have been completely locked out of the rooftop solar boom. You can’t just install panels on a building you share with, like, 40 other households. An Australian company built a device that essentially solves that, and it just won the top design award in Australia. We actually talked about Australia’s renewable energy boom last week as well. Karissa: Yeah. Yeah, another, um, win for them is how much renewable energy they were generating on one day, and a lot of that coming from individual solar rooftops. Arielle: SolShare acts as a traffic controller for solar power, automatically reading each apartment’s real-time energy use and routing power from a single rooftop system to whomever needs it. No separate inverters, no complicated wiring per unit, or any of that. Millions of people in Australia live in apartments and have basically no access to rooftop solar benefits until now. There’s been, like, a lot of talk on how to get apartment dwellers involved in solar energy generation. I know that in Spain and I think in Germany, they have these, like, balcony solar panels that you can use. Um, but this one seems even more efficient. Karissa: Yeah. Um, balcony solar is a good approach to this too, but not a comprehensive solution. In California, I know that a bill that allows plug-in balcony solar just got passed, so that’s good because, I mean, there’s a lot of apartments here in this really big state as well. So that will help. But, um, this design could help make everything more efficient. The surprising history of pumpkins Arielle: The next solution is titled “The surprising history of pumpkins: from ancient staple to autumn icon”. So here’s a, a nice, uh, seasonal one for everyone. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: You know pumpkin as the flavor of fall, lattes, and pies, and doorstep decorations, but pumpkin isn’t actually a botanical category. It’s more of a cultural idea that’s been assigned to things for centuries, and for a while in the 1600s, it was a straight-up insult. The whole history- … is weirder and funnier than you’d expect. So the word pumpkin started with the Greeks, and then traveled through French, and landed in English as pompion in the 1500s. It first appeared in print in 1647 as a reference to how poorly early colonists were eating. Not exactly a glamorous origin. By the late 1600s, pumpkin had become an insult. Depending on who was on the receiving end, it meant either conceited and full of hot air or empty-headed. Politicians were getting called pumpkins for hundreds of years, which is funny ’cause I can think of a politician that I could call pumpkin and a lot more. Karissa: I could think of many. Arielle: Um, the reason pumpkins became a fall icon isn’t really about taste. It’s about Americans leaving rural life and then romanticizing what they left. The pumpkin became a placeholder for a simpler agrarian past that was already being lost. So I know I’ve jumped around a lot in describing this article, but you’re just gonna have to read it to, like, really get the flow of the history of the pumpkin. But- Karissa: Hmm … Arielle: you know, pumpkin spice is kind of like a mood for autumn. Um- Yeah … do you have any strong feelings about pumpkins? Karissa: Um, I am just, like, a neutralist when it comes to pumpkin spice, pumpkin-flavored stuff. Like, I think it’s good, but I don’t really, like… I’m not a huge, uh, fan and craving it all year long. When it’s here, it’s here, and I think it’s great, and I’ll grab it sometimes and maybe make something pumpkin flavored. But yeah, I’m just kind of a neutralist. What about you? Arielle: Um, I… Well, now I’m in the Netherlands, and they don’t really have this, like, big pumpkin patch culture in fall. Like, you know when, when people go pick out their pumpkins, and they bring their, like, little babies, and they have… They’re in the field, and da, da, da. I kind of miss that, so I feel like I’m- Hmm … kind of romanticizing the whole pumpkin thing- … uh, just because it’s something that I feel like I’ve lost coming to Europe. But I’m not a huge fan of pumpkin spice, if I’m being honest. I like pumpkin pie. Karissa: Yes, delicious. Arielle: Yeah. Karissa: I love the point you made about, um, you know, the pumpkin patches, being able to go to small family farms. Because those local farms, they get a real economic boost from this time of year with the pumpkin season tourism. So whether it’s just taking the family to go get your seasonal photos or going to take advantage of the cool stuff that pumpkin patches have to offer, whether it’s corn mazes or pumpkin carving. I mean, I live in an agricultural area, so I’m familiar with the pumpkin patch culture. It makes me pretty nostalgic ’cause I definitely grew up doing that. And like you said, Arielle, you have to check out the article for more. A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss Arielle: The next article is titled “A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss”. A startup in the Netherlands has developed a concrete coating that grows its own moss. No soil or irrigation. There’s no structural modifications. You just apply it to an existing wall, and the moss colonizes it on its own. They’ve already put it on warehouses, noise barriers, social housing, and bridge piers in Amsterdam, and one of those applications is specifically to deter graffiti. And I actually think I’ve passed one of these, like, in my neighborhood, um, and I just didn’t realize that that’s what it was until I read this article. Yeah. So how it works is that the moss attaches through tiny thread-like structures that grip the surface without penetrating it. So you can apply this to existing facades without any structural work. It’s a coating, not a construction project. In Amsterdam, they’re testing it out on bridge piers specifically as a graffiti deterrent, which is not a use case I saw coming. Research shows wet moss cools through evaporation the same way trees do in cities, but dry moss in direct sunlight overheats, so placement and climate really matter for how well it works. Urban greening is a major climate adaptation strategy right now, and the main barriers have always been cost and maintenance, so this solution addresses both at once. Karissa: I love that, you know, it doesn’t require, like, new construction. It can just be applied to already existing structures in cities where it gets a lot of moisture, like Amsterdam. I’m sure that this can be a really great addition. World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with everyone before I hand the reins over to Karissa is “World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany”. Germany just completed the world’s tallest wind turbine, 365 meters tall, taller than Berlin’s TV tower, which is also very tall. They couldn’t use a crane to build it because cranes don’t go that high, so they invented a new way to do it. But honestly, the most significant part isn’t the height, it’s the proposal to add thousands of these above existing wind farms without using a single square foot of new land. As I mentioned, traditional cranes couldn’t reach, so they built like a telescoping inner tower that raises itself through a surrounding lattice structure. The construction method is as novel as the turbine itself. Germany has around 30,000 existing wind turbines, and the proposal is to place taller ones above or alongside them rather than finding new land, which sidesteps one of the biggest political fights in wind energy, which is people don’t wanna give up the land. GICON, the engineering firm that built this turbine, says, uh, this design could generate roughly twice the electricity of conventional turbines with comparable rotors because winds at 300 meters are faster and more consistent. But commissioning isn’t until November, so the real world numbers aren’t in just yet. As I said, land use is one of the biggest political obstacles to wind expansion. There’s, like, a lot of not in my backyard fights that have stalled projects for years. But stacking vertically rather than spreading horizontally reframes the whole conversation Karissa: All right. Well, I’ll take it from here, Arielle. Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns Karissa: Heading back into the whole fall idea, the next article is “Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns when autumn arrives”. The urge to rewatch your comfort show every October isn’t just a personality quirk. There’s a real psychological reason your nervous system steers you toward reruns when fall arrives. Something about the season registers as a small form of loss, and your brain responds by reaching for the familiar. I mean, I’ve definitely had this feeling before. And before I go any further, Arielle, is there anything that you rewatch every fall or find yourself, uh, reaching for? Arielle: When Harry Met Sally. Karissa: Yes. That one is very, very fall indeed. Arielle: Yeah, I don’t know. I just, I love the aesthetic. And yeah, I guess I never really noticed that I always wanna watch that particular movie once, like, the leaves start to change and stuff. Karissa: Yeah. For me, I always go back to Taylor Swift’s Red album in the fall. And it’s very, like, a fall-coded album in general, but it came out in the fall when I was, like, in junior high, and it always brings me back to that time of year. And it sometimes makes me feel a little bit, like, sad too because I start missing that time in my life. In general, your body recognizes fall through a whole bunch of sensory clues. There’s wood smoke, October light, the sound of a school bus, and that’s what takes me back to Red. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Karissa: But the same memory system that holds pre-verbal experiences from early childhood is also at play here when you experience all these, these autumn, um, these autumn- Arielle: Sensations Karissa: things. Yeah, sensations is exactly the word. Psychologists say we prefer reruns in the fall because our brains favor predictability when things feel uncertain. And you already know how it ends, so that matters a lot more than you’d think. Nostalgia isn’t just about these warm, fuzzy feelings. It can also hold a lot of grief, and looking backward is a part of how we integrate the past and then move forward. So there is a psychological reason why we want to indulge in this fall nostalgia. Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Karissa: Okay, the next solution is, “Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Here’s what the sleep research says”. Apparently pistachios contain their own melatonin. They don’t just offer compounds that help your body make melatonin, they produce it themselves. A nutritional review found that one small handful covers five different sleep-related nutrients at once, which is a pretty unusual thing to find in any single food. Pistachios have more vitamin B6 than any other tree nut, and B6 is the co-factor your body needs to convert tryptophan into serotonin, into melatonin. So there’s a whole chain reaction happening from that one handful, and there’s a little bit more of the science behind it in the article. The thing is that there hasn’t been a clinical trial that has actually tested pistachios directly for sleep yet, and the review was partially funded by American Pistachio Growers, so there might be a little bit of a bias here. But in an era where sleep is kind of one of the biggest wellness obsessions right now, and there’s magnesium supplements, mouth tape, weighted blankets, people are really desperate for anything that helps with sleep. Arielle: Yeah, I really like the food as medicine angle. It’s getting way more mainstream, so people aren’t just thinking about sleep hygiene habits. They’re also starting to ask what they should be eating. And I think food is definitely underrated, especially, um, in North America as- Karissa: Mm-hmm … Arielle: as an impactful solution to some of your health issues. Um- Yeah … so even though there’s no clinical trial yet, I think it’s, it’s worth more seriously considering food as a way to help you out with whatever health or wellness issues you’re struggling with. How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration Karissa: The next solution is kind of a fun one, “How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration”. A Spanish explorer just left for Antarctica on a sled powered entirely by kites. No engine, no fuel. The last time someone made a comparable crossing, they burned through 45,000 gallons of diesel. But this sled is built on ancient Inuit design principles that this, uh, researcher has been refining for 25 years, and NASA is also along for the ride. So again, this vehicle draws from Inuit sled design and goes back to ancient indigenous knowledge. This technology is something that’s been used for thousands of years. There’s a number of onboard research projects on this kite-powered sled. One of them is a NASA study asking whether salt rocks on Antarctica’s surface could harbor microbial life. The four crew members themselves on this kite-powered sled are also research subjects. A psychologist is monitoring their isolation, sleep, and social dynamics for 85 days to generate data for future space missions. There are such harsh conditions out there, so being able to refine and use this kite technology is pretty interesting. And of course, it’s important to use sustainable science in exploration. New research identifies the exact spot where Alzheimer’s protein tangles lock in Karissa: The next solution is “New research identifies the exact spot where Alzheimer’s protein tangles lock in”. We- researchers at Northwestern and UC Santa Barbara, go Gauchos, that’s where I went, have identified the specific point on a tau protein where the misfolding that causes Alzheimer’s begins. It’s not somewhere vague in the brain, it’s the exact molecular anchor point, down to which amino acid, so really pinpointing here. And blocking that one spot in lab experiments actually stops the spread of Alzheimer’s, so this could be a very important piece of the puzzle. The mechanism that the researchers found is called dock-and-lock. The misfolded tau docks at one specific spot first, then the rest of the protein snaps into the wrong shape, and blocking just that one anchor point inhibited fiber growth in experiments. This research is part of a broader shift towards molecular level targeting in neurodegenerative disease, identifying the exact mechanism rather than trying to clear a protein broadly. There’s still a gap between, you know, pinpointing this spot and being able to create a drug that actually does something about it. But of course, the research has to come first, so we’re happy to recognize this progress. The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model Karissa: Moving on to our final solution of the week, we have “The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model”. 13 years ago, someone planted a small orchard on the corner of a shuttered school in Kansas City, and today that idea has grown into 14,000 trees across 847 orchards in 17 cities, which means that more than a million people live within walking distance of a free fruit tree. Kansas City now has more community orchards than any other city in the country. It has nearly 250 of them. The reason 80% of these orchards are still productive, which is genuinely high for grassroots urban agriculture, is that the organization didn’t just plant trees and leave them, they built a stewardship network of 1,700 trained orchard caretakers across the country. This kind of reminds me of a solution I- we just shared about, um- Some trees planted in Germany, and they have, like, a whole app in, you know- Arielle: Mm, yeah Um- So that citizens could also take care of the trees and give them water when they, when they needed it. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I love this, uh, citizen agriculture movement. So cool. These orchard caretakers operate on about a million dollars a year and only go where they’re invited. Communities have to request orchards, so the model has held up because they don’t impose the model at all. The idea is spreading across to other cities. San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York are now in discussions to join this trend of community orchards. So it’s actively scaling, and it’s a, you know, a very hyper-local solution that individual communities can focus on and implement themselves. Arielle: And it really addresses the issue of food access. Um- Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: Food access equity is a real issue right now. There’s food deserts. There’s rising produce costs. There’s diet-related chronic illnesses, and this kind of a solution that you mentioned, it’s low-tech, it’s hyper-local, um, and it’s pretty permanent. I think this can address a lot of those issues. I know that urban agriculture has been having a cultural moment, but a lot of urban agriculture is focused on, like, boutique rooftop gardens, and- Karissa: Yeah Arielle: you know, not everyone has access to that. So a community orchard serving everyday neighborhoods is a different category, and I can just imagine, like, rocking up to a tree and picking a fruit off of it- … and eating it. That… It’s also so satisfying. Karissa: Okay. Well, that’s all the positive news we had from The Optimist Daily this week. Positive Quote & Wrap-up Karissa: Before we log off for the day, we have a positive quote to share with you. Arielle: This one’s from E.B. White, the author of Charlotte’s Web, one of my childhood favorites. Okay, so the quote says, “Hang on to your hat, hang on to your hope, and wind the clock, for tomorrow is another day.” We will be back next week with more solutions, but until then, we hope you enjoy your weekend. Karissa: Yeah. Bye, everyone! Arielle: Bye!
