items.title: Θα μπορούσαν μικροσκοπικά ρομπότ να αντικαταστήσουν την επέμβαση ανοιχτής καρδιάς;
items.titleOriginal: Could tiny robots replace open-heart surgery?
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες δημιούργησαν ρομπότ στο μέγεθος μιας μύτης μολυβιού που προορίζονται να ταξιδέψουν μέσα στο σώμα για να μεταφέρουν φάρμακα σε λοιμώξεις μέσα σε μια καρδιά που χτυπά. Τα ρομπότ, που σχεδιάστηκαν για να αντικαταστήσουν την επικίνδυνη χειρουργική επέμβαση ανοιχτής καρδιάς και την αναποτελεσματική ενδοφλέβια θεραπεία με φάρμακα για τη θεραπεία απειλητικών για τη ζωή καρδιακών λοιμώξεων, θα μπορούσαν επίσης να χρησιμοποιηθούν για τη λιγότερο επεμβατική και ακριβέστερη θεραπεία άλλων…
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have created robots the size of a pencil tip intended to travel through the body to deliver medicine to infections inside a beating heart. The bots, designed to replace risky open-heart surgery and ineffective IV-drug therapy to treat life-threatening heart infections, could also be used to less invasively and more precisely treat other hard-to-reach diseases, including cancer. “With just a little pinprick, you insert a micro robot and do a procedure without infection or blood loss. And you don’t need to have a surgeon operating it to get the drugs robustly, safely, and efficiently to the right place,” says senior author Axel Krieger, a medical roboticist known for creating robots that perform surgery without human help. “There’s a lot of areas beyond heart infections where this kind of targeted drug therapy and these kinds of steerable robots could play a major role. It’s really the frontier of surgical robotics.” The work appears in Advanced Materials Technologies . Each year about 50,000 people in the United States contract endocarditis, a heart tissue infection. The typical treatment is a weeks-long course of intravenous antibiotics, which often fails because the drugs are too diluted by the time they reach the heart. Doctors are then left with two risky choices—prescribing more and higher doses of antibiotics, which can be toxic, or extremely risky open-heart surgery. To get the drugs directly to the infected heart tissue, the team developed magnetically-powered robots called “millirobots,” because of their size—they’re as wide as a pencil tip or a matchstick head, and about as long as a grain of rice. The robots work in pairs. There’s one the team calls the needle module, which gently latches onto heart tissue right at the infected site. There it serves as a docking station, waiting right on the beating heart for the drug module. The drug module carries medicine to the docking station, where it magnetically docks and slowly releases the antibiotics right where they’re most needed. Both robots are magnetic and guided wirelessly by an external electromagnetic coil system that works like an MRI machine. Having two tiny robots instead of one larger one allows the device to reach tight spots in the body. The needle can remain docked while the drug module is replaced, allowing for repeat doses of medicine if needed. “Magnetic guidance is exciting because you don’t have to power the robot itself. It doesn’t carry batteries and motors,” Krieger says. “The drugs can be delivered safely, with technology like the gradients and fields in an MRI. But instead of using it for imaging, it drives the millirobots.” The researchers successfully tested the robots on phantom heart models that closely mimic a human heart, and on real porcine heart tissue. The robots traveled smoothly and autonomously, even against simulated blood flow. “We can just inject a robot with a little pill into your vein where it travels to the site, right to where we really need to deliver the drugs, and it’s minimally invasive,” says first author Anuruddha Bhattacharjee, a former Johns Hopkins postdoctoral student who is now an assistant professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In addition to eliminating the need for open-heart surgery, drug treatment with the robots could take hours instead of weeks. “Usually if you do IV drug treatment, you need four to six weeks of therapy. But with these robots the entire procedure might take 10 minutes—maybe an hour if you want to do a couple rounds,” Bhattacharjee says. “If everything works well, you go from four to six weeks of treatment to one day or less.” The team also believes the robots would be helpful delivering targeted medications to fight cancer where it’s spreading. The researchers next plan to test the robots in more realistic phantom hearts, with muscle contraction and the beating movement of a real heart. The work was supported by the National Science Foundation’s Foundational Research in Robotics CAREER program. Additional authors are from Johns Hopkins, the University of Maryland, and Weinberg Medical Physics. Sukhma’s journey began when a joke turned into a secret learning adventure between her and a family member. Away from the rest of the family, they practised together until she finally learnt to ride. Eight years later, she’s doing much more than riding a bike. She drives a tractor and runs her own social media page, sharing reels of herself riding. She didn’t learn because she had to. items.descriptionOriginal: Search any grocery store for protein-rich food that’s good for both you and the planet, and you’re buffeted by certified labels claiming organic-grown, ocean-friendly, low-carbon, fair trade, free range, or other shining attributes. These well-meaning labels can obscure serious tradeoffs—for example healthy tree nuts that minimize greenhouse emissions while guzzling scarce water, or organic meats and cheeses that spew water pollution or planet-warming gases. A health tech scientist has proposed a new solution to this problem , in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems . The paper sketches a new rating system for high-protein foods that encompasses multiple dimensions of environmental, health, and human impacts—calculating simple overall scores that can be compared across a variety of plant- and animal-derived foods. “The goal is not necessarily to create another front-of-package label, but to foster a new literacy” that enables better-informed decision-making, writes Chris Macdonald of the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom. Maintaining sufficient dietary protein is a major concern when it comes to reconciling modern agriculture with future climate change. Scientists have spent years searching for new, non-meat protein sources , ranging from marigold flowers to fungi to alternative cropping schemes . But currently available non-meat foods are also high in protein, and Macdonald has found that misunderstandings about protein content are a major factor preventing people from choosing these In his latest research, Macdonald is trying to provide people with information that is accurate, comprehensive, and simple, so they can make good choices on dietary proteins. He mined scientific data on the environmental impacts and nutrient contents of various foods to develop two simple ratings. A Planet Score, ranging from 0 to 16, includes measures of greenhouse emissions, water pollution, water use, and land use per hundred grams of protein. A separate People Score, ranging from 0 to 24, includes measures of cholesterol, saturated fat, sodium, essential amino acids, commercial availability, and affordability. The Planet and People scores are then combined into an overall Better Proteins Institute (BPI) score. When Macdonald applied the system to 20 foods (10 animal and 10 plant) , tofu, chia seeds, beans, and quinoa had the highest scores (30 to 36), while cheddar, mozzarella, lamb chops, and beef steak had the lowest scores (13 to 16). The highest-scoring animal foods were chicken breast and tuna, ranking 7th and 8th out of 20, based largely on their affordability, low saturated fats, low land use, and moderate greenhouse emissions. Walnuts and brazil nuts were the lowest-scoring plant foods, ranking 11th and 12th out of 20, due to their high prices, saturated fats, and water use. Macdonald views this as a starting point, which he hopes to improve over time. Affordability and commercial availability, for example, were determined within the U.K. for this study—but they will vary substantially between regions. Future versions may also contain additional factors such as fair trade, ethical treatment of workers, or animal treatment. Macdonald. “ What are the best sources of protein? items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "How Does It Work?" — The Better India's series that takes the everyday things you see, use and rely on, and uncovers the clever technology, design and sustainable thinking that makes them work better. From the objects in your home to the systems around you, we break down the ideas behind them in simple, easy-to-understand language. Because innovation isn't always about futuristic machines or complicated technology. Sometimes, it's hiding in the things we use every day. Look at a satellite image of a cyclone, and you will see enormous bands of clouds spiralling over the ocean. What looks like a swirling mass of white clouds is actually a complex weather system, powered by warm seawater and shaped by winds moving thousands of metres above the Earth. Predicting where this storm will travel, how strong it will become, and whether it will make landfall is no small feat. Yet, today, satellites and artificial intelligence (AI) are helping scientists make these forecasts faster and more accurately, giving communities valuable time to prepare. In India, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) uses satellites such as INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR to monitor cyclones. In 2025, satellite imagery helped track weather systems, including Cyclone Montha, which crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast as a severe cyclonic storm. But how do machines in space and AI models on Earth work together to forecast a storm that has not yet reached the coast? Step 1: Satellites keep an eye on the ocean The first step is observation. Geostationary weather satellites orbit approximately 36,000 km above the equator, moving at the same rate as the Earth's rotation. This allows them to continuously observe the same broad region, capturing changes in cloud formations and atmospheric conditions. India's INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR satellites monitor clouds, atmospheric moisture and temperatures to track developing storms. Photograph: ( The Week ) India's INSAT satellites use specialised sensors to capture visible-light and infrared images, as well as information about water vapour in the atmosphere. Unlike ordinary cameras, infrared sensors can measure temperatures even at night, helping scientists identify the cold, high cloud tops associated with powerful thunderstorms. Scientists look for clues such as clusters of thunderstorms, curved cloud bands and the beginnings of a rotating system. Other satellite instruments measure ocean temperatures, rainfall and wind-related conditions, helping meteorologists understand whether the environment is becoming favourable for a cyclone. Think of it as watching a storm's earliest movements from above, even when it is far out at sea and beyond the view of coastal observers. Step 2: AI learns to recognise weather patterns Collecting data is only half the job. Scientists must also work out what it means for the storm's future. This is where AI comes in. AI weather models are trained using decades of historical weather observations , atmospheric measurements and records of past storms. By studying these examples, they learn relationships between variables such as wind speed, air pressure, humidity and temperature. For instance, a model may learn that certain combinations of atmospheric conditions and ocean temperatures have previously been associated with a storm strengthening or changing direction. AI models analyse historical weather data to learn patterns in wind, pressure and temperature. Photograph: ( CNET ) It is a little like learning to recognise a familiar pattern in a jigsaw puzzle. The AI compares the current conditions with patterns it has learnt, then estimates how the weather could evolve. Google DeepMind's WeatherNext Cyclones is one example. Its model combines global weather information with historical cyclone records to forecast a storm's path, intensity and wind structure. In 2025, its forecasts helped the US National Hurricane Center anticipate Hurricane Melissa's rapid intensification and landfall in Jamaica. Step 3: The AI runs multiple possible futures Here is where the technology becomes particularly useful. Weather is a constantly changing system. A small difference in wind direction or atmospheric pressure can alter a cyclone's eventual path . So, instead of treating one prediction as certain, advanced AI models can generate multiple possible scenarios. This technique is called ensemble forecasting . Imagine a cyclone moving towards the eastern coast of India. One forecast might show it turning north, another might suggest it moving towards the northwest, while others may predict different speeds or intensities. Ensemble forecasting generates multiple possible storm tracks, helping meteorologists assess uncertainty. Photograph: ( FOX Weather ) By comparing these possible tracks, meteorologists can identify areas that are more likely to be affected and understand where uncertainty remains. WeatherNext Cyclones can generate 1,000 possible scenarios in less than a minute on specialised computing hardware. Its forecasts can extend up to 15 days ahead, although uncertainty generally increases the further into the future a prediction looks. Step 4: Forecasters turn predictions into warnings AI does not replace meteorologists. Instead, its predictions complement satellite observations, conventional weather models and expert analysis. Forecasters assess the available evidence before issuing official warnings about a cyclone's likely track, strength, rainfall and landfall. These warnings help authorities plan evacuations, fishermen return to shore, and emergency teams prepare shelters and supplies. The goal is not to predict every movement perfectly. It is to reduce uncertainty early enough for people to act. Early warnings help coastal communities prepare, fishermen return to shore and authorities organise evacuations. Photograph: ( facebook/@TheMech Mind) As satellites collect more detailed observations and AI models become better at interpreting them, cyclone forecasting continues to improve. Every additional hour of reliable warning can give vulnerable communities more time to protect homes, secure essential supplies and move to safety. A cyclone may be impossible to control, but understanding its likely path is becoming easier. And that growing ability to see a storm coming is one of the most important ways technology can help save lives. Sources: 'Cyclone Track Forecasting Based on Satellite Images Using Artificial Neural Networks' by Rita Kovord nyi and Chandan Roy. 'How Satellites Track Hurricanes' by National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service 'How we're supporting better tropical cyclone prediction with AI' by Google Deep Mind.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Provincial Tree Pageant Reminds Communities to Honour Their Big Trees Reading Time: 2 minutes Ontario’s Tree Trust celebrates a rare, century-old Cucumber Tree in St. George, honoring one family’s decades of stewardship and the community’s growing love for mature trees. In recent years, the Ontario government has significantly reduced environmental protection legislation. Increased development with minimal consequences threatens the province’s biodiversity, habitat, and once-protected natural character. But people are fighting back. Despite the current lack of legislation, environmental communities continue to raise awareness and push their cause. Tree Trust , a not-for-profit, grassroots organization that focuses on mature tree protection, is one of them. Education, advocacy, and community engagement are Tree Trust’s core values. Based in Elora, Tree Trust launched in 2019 and now extends to 12 communities, with chapters run entirely by volunteers. In addition to offering educational events like tree walks and talks, Tree Trust works with ISA-board-certified arborists committed to improving the health and longevity of mature trees. Protecting mature trees is essential to urban communities. Many are older than most community members, and these legacy trees offer immediate, irreplaceable benefits to our cities. Increased health and mental well-being, stormwater reduction, climate change mitigation, and economic benefits are all reasons to invest in big trees. One way Tree Trust does this is by welcoming the province to participate in the Ontario Tree Pageant. This engaging, inviting competition reminds the province that a love of trees goes far beyond the surface. For the past three years, hundreds of nominations have been received, special stories have been shared, and majestic trees have been recognized. This year’s esteemed panel of judges chose a tree that represents togetherness, a tree that is beloved and highlights a story of community awareness and environmental stewardship. This year’s winner is a Cucumber Tree ( Magnolia acuminata ), estimated to be over 100 years old, standing tall in St. George. This year’s winning tree was nominated by St. George resident and artist, Meredyth Kutt. This endangered, Ontario-native specimen stands among many other trees and is over 75 centimeters in diameter. Photo courtesy of Tree Trust . This tree is being recognized not only for being a unique and endangered species, but also for its history. Researchers at the University of Guelph have studied this individual for its ability to thrive outside its expected range. Some even say it is the farthest west mature Cucumber Tree in Canada. Beyond its uniqueness, this tree is celebrated as the epitome of environmental and community connection. The Kutt family, the tree’s owners, have stewarded it for over 20 years. They have cultivated a second Cucumber tree and currently support six of the original’s progeny. This cucumber tree’s story is exactly the kind of stewardship Tree Trust wants to support. The Ontario Tree Pageant gives people a platform to share special stories about trees that mean the most to them. It reminds us how connected we are to nature and that, for all these big trees give us, they deserve to be celebrated. The post Provincial Tree Pageant Reminds Communities to Honour Their Big Trees appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: Don’t Throw Away Last Year’s Diyas: This Simple Trick Makes Them Diwali-Ready Again
items.description: Το Diwali είναι μια εποχή για να φωτίσουμε τα σπίτια μας με ντιγιά, αλλά το να γιορτάσουμε το φεστιβάλ βιώσιμα μπορεί να ξεκινήσει με κάτι τόσο χωρίς προβλήματα όπως η επαναχρησιμοποίηση αυτού που ήδη έχουμε. Αντί να αγοράζετε νέα χωμάτινα φωτιστικά κάθε χρόνο, λίγη δημιουργικότητα μπορεί να σας βοηθήσει να δώσετε στα παλιά diya μια νέα εμφάνιση. Η δημιουργός του lifestyle και των ταξιδιών Sharon JM Nathani, η οποία μοιράζεται ιδέες για DIY στο Instag…
items.descriptionOriginal: Diwali is a time to light up our homes with diyas , but celebrating the festival sustainably can begin with something as hassle-free as reusing what we already have. Instead of buying new earthen lamps every year, a little creativity can help give old diyas a fresh look. Lifestyle and travel creator Sharon JM Nathani, who shares DIY ideas on Instagram through her page @thatangloindiansindhi, suggests a simple way to reuse diyas from the previous year and make them ready for the festive season. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sharon JM Nathani || Lifestyle & Travel Creator (@thatangloindiansindhi) A trick to keep the wicks in place Her method involves using desi ghee and candles to prepare the diyas for lighting. She recommends heating the ghee, melting the candles into it, and pouring the mixture into the diyas before placing the wicks. This small change in the process makes a difference. Often, when the wicks are placed inside the diya before the liquid is poured, they can fall over or become crooked while filling. Sharon suggests pouring the mixture first and adding the wick afterwards, helping it stay upright and in place. Once the diyas are ready, you can add a little glitter or finely cut flower petals to decorate them. These small touches can give old lamps a festive makeover without the need to purchase new ones. Reusing diyas is an easy way to reduce waste during the festive season while making the most of items already at home. With a little effort, last year's lamps can return to your Diwali decorations, bringing the same festive warmth without adding to unnecessary consumption. This Diwali, before heading out to buy new decorations, take a look at what you already have. Sometimes, the most sustainable festive ideas begin with giving familiar things another chance.

items.title: Πώς ο «Artivism» οδηγεί την αντίσταση στο Παρίσι
items.titleOriginal: How ‘Artivism’ Is Driving the Resistance in Paris
items.description: Ξαφνικά ο Darth Vader ανεβαίνει σε μια καρέκλα μπροστά από το Hôtel de Ville στο Παρίσι. Ντυμένος στα μαύρα, κουνάει το σπαθί του σαν μαέστρος, ενώ 200 μουσικοί και εθελοντές, οι περισσότεροι γύρω στα είκοσι, ετοιμάζονται. Ξεπακετάρουν τα όργανά τους: βιολιά, τσέλο, κλαρίνα. Τότε ο πραγματικός μαέστρος, Étienne Jarrier, ανεβαίνει σε ένα πράσινο sh…
items.descriptionOriginal: S uddenly Darth Vader climbs up onto a chair in front of the Hôtel de Ville in Paris. Clad in all black, he swings his sword like a conductor’s baton while 200 musicians and volunteers, most in their early twenties, get ready. They unpack their instruments: violins, cellos, clarinets. Then the real conductor, Étienne Jarrier, steps up in a green shirt and the musicians of the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde (New World Orchestra) begin to play. Their song is a poignant one — El Pueblo Unido Jamás Será Vencido (The People United Will Never Be Defeated), a Chilean protest song written in the 1970s by the composer and pianist Sergio Ortega and folk group Quilapayún. It has since become an international hymn of resistance, and the members of the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde chant its refrain again and again to support the student protests in France this October, voicing their solidarity with the half million young people who are protesting high living costs and deteriorating conditions in their schools. “Music is a way for us to be heard,” says 25-year-old Jarrier, who co-founded the orchestra in 2022 “to find new ways forward.” A self-described “member of the climate generation,” the young man with the red-tinted black locks says he felt that climate activism had exhausted most avenues of protests and found it was time for “artivism,” art as a vehicle for political expression, “as a way of reaching people at the deepest level.” The post How ‘Artivism’ Is Driving the Resistance in Paris appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Για…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News PANORAMA Builds Replicable Conservation Solutions Database Spanning Nearly 1,900 Case Studies Worldwide Reading Time: 3 minutes A decade-old platform now hosts 1,897 conservation solutions from over 1,300 contributors, turning local environmental successes into replicable conservation solutions database entries anyone can adapt. For over ten years, PANORAMA – Solutions for a Healthy Planet has pursued a deceptively simple mission: build a global community where changemakers share, adopt, and scale up what already works. Rather than compiling passive success stories, this replicable conservation solutions database structures each entry as adaptable building blocks, distilling complex projects into stepwise blueprints practitioners elsewhere can actually apply to their own contexts. The scale is substantial. PANORAMA now hosts 1,897 documented solutions from 1,327 contributing organizations and individuals across 11 thematic communities spanning restoration, species conservation, marine and coastal ecosystems, One Health, protected areas under the 30×30 framework, and nature-culture heritage sites. This solutions database aligns explicitly with major global directives, including the Kunming-Montréal Global Biodiversity Framework, the Paris Agreement, and the UN’s 2030 Agenda, translating local action into evidence that supports international sustainability commitments. What distinguishes each entry within this replicable conservation solutions database is methodology rather than mere documentation. Every solution unpacks the how and why behind an effective environmental initiative, breaking successful projects into essential components others can adapt rather than simply admire. Solutions must be practical and tailored to specific scenarios, relevant to sustainability frameworks, proven through real-world results, and flexible enough for varied environments and sectors. Recent additions illustrate this approach in practice. In Mongolia, pastoral communities facing recurrent droughts and dzud , severe winter disasters causing catastrophic livestock losses, needed climate-resilient infrastructure. The UN Development Programme (UNDP) ADAPT Project responded by establishing 48 hay and feed storage facilities across four climate-vulnerable provinces, using risk assessments combining climate, vegetation, and livestock mortality data to identify optimal locations. The solution strengthened emergency fodder reserves while improving herders’ adaptive capacity against increasingly unpredictable seasons. Around Lake Victoria, shared by five East African nations and supporting over 45 million people through fisheries, water supply, and agriculture, declining water quality made coordinated basin management nearly impossible without shared evidence. The Lake Victoria Basin Commission, supported by GIZ, developed the first-ever State of the Basin Report, combining water quality sampling at 44 stations across three countries with consultations spanning all five partner states. This replicable conservation solutions database entry identifies wetland rehabilitation, reforestation, and catchment restoration as the most cost-effective pathways toward improved water quality, now serving as a shared baseline for planning across the entire basin. PANORAMA’s replicable conservation solutions database documents how five East African nations built a shared State of the Basin Report for Lake Victoria and how a multi-stakeholder partnership restored Ethiopia’s Lake Hawassa, both now scaled into national and regional policy frameworks. Photo by David Munyasa on Pexels. In Ethiopia’s Rift Valley, Lake Hawassa faced accelerating degradation from deforestation, pollution, erosion, and rapid urbanization, pressures no single actor could address alone. A multi-stakeholder partnership uniting public authorities, private companies, and civil society applied a Natural Resources Risk and Action Framework developed between 2015 and 2020, jointly assessing risks and implementing nature-based solutions. The partnership succeeded so thoroughly that it transitioned to full government management and scaled into federal guidelines, now restoring water bodies nationwide. This replicable conservation solutions database operates through a partnership network spanning 12 organizations, including GIZ, IUCN, UNDP, GRID-Arendal, UNEP, Rare, EcoHealth Alliance, ICCROM, the World Bank Group, OCTO Group, ICOMOS, and IFOAM. Together with over 1,000 individual solution providers representing institutions worldwide, this network forms the backbone connecting grassroots knowledge to global policy forums, ensuring diverse local perspectives genuinely influence international environmental decision-making rather than remaining isolated success stories. Peer-to-peer exchange sits at the platform’s core philosophy. Rather than treating conservation knowledge as proprietary or locked within academic journals, this replicable conservation solutions database transforms tacit, hard-won field experience into explicit, shareable wisdom. A coordinator from the Fiji Locally Managed Marine Area Network described the platform as compelling solution providers to examine their own work more critically, improving quality and scalability specifically because their solutions will be judged against a global standard for replicability. The database’s cross-cutting scope extends far beyond conservation biology alone. Communities addressing gender mainstreaming, financing mechanisms, governance structures, technology for nature conservation, and geodiversity all coexist within the same searchable platform, filterable by ecosystem type from agro-ecosystems to urban built environments, and by region spanning Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania, and the Coral Triangle. As climate and biodiversity crises intensify simultaneously, the pressure to avoid reinventing solutions grows correspondingly urgent. This replicable conservation solutions database offers exactly that efficiency: proven building blocks from Mongolian herders, East African basin commissions, and Ethiopian multi-stakeholder partnerships, structured so practitioners facing similar challenges elsewhere can adapt rather than start from zero, accelerating the pace at which local innovation becomes global practice. The post PANORAMA Builds Replicable Conservation Solutions Database Spanning Nearly 1,900 Case Studies Worldwide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Ένας νομικός γραμματέας πήγε στο μετρό για να δουλέψει για 67 χρόνια. Κανείς δεν ήξερε ότι είχε 9 εκατομμύρια δολάρια.
items.titleOriginal: A Legal Secretary Rode the Subway to Work for 67 Years. Nobody Knew She had $9M.
items.description: Για 67 χρόνια, η Sylvia Bloom οδηγούσε το μετρό για τη δουλειά, ζούσε σε ένα διαμέρισμα που ελέγχεται από το ενοίκιο και περπάτησε μέσα από χιονοθύελλες στα 96 αντί να φτιάχνει ταξί -- όλα αυτά ενώ έχτιζε αθόρυβα μια περιουσία 9 εκατομμυρίων δολαρίων αντικατοπτρίζοντας τις μετοχές των αφεντικών της με μισθό γραμματέα. «Ήταν γραμματέας σε μια εποχή που έτρεχαν τη ζωή του αφεντικού τους, συμπεριλαμβανομένης της προσωπικής τους…
items.descriptionOriginal: For 67 years, Sylvia Bloom rode the subway to work, lived in a rent-controlled apartment, and walked through blizzards at 96 rather than hail a cab -- all while quietly building a $9 million fortune by mirroring her bosses' stock trades on a secretary's salary. "She was a secretary in an era when they ran their boss' lives, including their personal investments," her niece explained, and Bloom simply applied that same attentiveness to her own future, one modest purchase at a time. She never mentioned it to anyone - not colleagues, possibly not even her husband -- because, as her niece recalled, "she didn't think it was anybody's business but her own." What she did think was her business was what happened to it after she was gone: nearly all of it went to scholarships for students who couldn't afford college, becoming the largest individual gift in Henry Street Settlement's 125-year history. There is something clarifying about a life like hers -- the discipline kept private, the wealth worn invisibly, the generosity revealed only at the end, as if the whole thing had been a very long, very patient act of faith in someone else's future.

items.description: Για δεκαετίες, οι αναπτυσσόμενες πόλεις της Ινδίας αντιμετώπιζαν τα απόβλητά τους μετακινώντας τα μακριά από το οπτικό τους πεδίο. items.descriptionOriginal: For decades, India's growing cities have dealt with their waste by moving it out of sight. Over time, municipal dumping grounds have grown into mountains of mixed garbage, often close to homes, informal settlements and roads. But what happens when a city finally clears one of these mountains? Can land occupied by garbage for years become a park, a forest or another public space? And what happens to the people who have depended on these sites for their livelihoods? The Dumpsite Remediation Accelerator Programme (DRAP), launched in November 2025, seeks to accelerate the cleanup of 214 major legacy dumpsites across 200 urban local bodies (ULBs). These sites account for 80% of the remaining legacy waste targeted under the programme, which aims to reclaim land for productive urban use while preventing the creation of new dumpsites by September 2026. The real value of a reclaimed site will depend on what replaces the dump, and how effectively the city manages the waste it generates every. day Photograph: (Needpix) The programme covers 200 ULBs and targets complete remediation of 214 of the most challenging dumpsites across states and Union territories. The scale of the task is considerable, but the experiences of cities already working on or reclaiming such sites show that the challenge extends beyond removing old waste. It involves deciding what happens to the recovered land, where the extracted material goes, and whether the people who have worked with waste for years have a place in the new system. 1. Gorakhpur: A former dumping ground becomes an eco-park In Gorakhpur , Uttar Pradesh, a 40-acre site that had served as the city's primary waste disposal ground for seven years has been transformed into the Kachre Se Kanchan Rapti Eco Park, in September 2026. The remediation involved processing around 400 tonnes of accumulated waste every day. Instead of treating the site as a dumping ground indefinitely, the project sought to recover the land and give it a public-facing purpose. The cleared site was subsequently developed into a public space with green lawns, walking and jogging tracks, a children's play area, an open gym and a yoga zone. Solar lighting and water-conservation structures were also incorporated. According to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the park also has a livelihood component. A women-led self-help group, Shakti Ki Rasoi, operates a restaurant on the premises. The park reportedly attracts around 500 visitors daily. 2. Raichur: Reclaiming a dumpsite for green cover In Raichur, Karnataka, the reclamation of the Yakalaspura dumpsite is taking a different route. Rather than developing a conventional public park across the reclaimed land, the project includes restoring green cover. The 35-acre site has undergone scientific remediation, with approximately 62,252 metric tonnes of waste processed and nearly 22 acres of land reclaimed till 2026, according to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. Part of the restored area now supports a Miyawaki forest spread across approximately five to seven acres. The Miyawaki method involves planting a dense mix of native species to encourage the development of green cover. At a former dumpsite, such an intervention offers a potential ecological use for land cleared of accumulated waste. Planting trees alone does not establish that the land is free from contamination or suitable for every ecological use. Soil quality, the survival of planted species, groundwater conditions and continued maintenance all matter. 3. Delhi: Bhalswa shows why clearing a landfill takes time Delhi's Bhalswa dumpsite offers a contrasting picture. While cities such as Gorakhpur have developed public spaces on reclaimed land, Bhalswa illustrates the scale and complexity of processing decades of accumulated waste. Dating back to 1994, the landfill occupies approximately 70 acres. In June 2022, it held around 73 lakh metric tonnes of legacy waste. Biomining operations began in July that year, involving the excavation, treatment and mechanical separation of old waste into different material streams. By 26 May 2026, approximately 43 acres had been reclaimed. However, around 23.17 lakh metric tonnes of waste, including legacy and fresh waste, remained to be processed, according to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. The figures show that reclaiming a large dumpsite is a gradual process. Biomining involves separating recoverable materials from mixed waste, with different fractions requiring different destinations. Recovered recyclables may enter recycling chains, combustible material may be processed into refuse-derived fuel, and soil-like or inert material may be used for suitable purposes, subject to its quality and applicable environmental requirements. Even after the visible mound shrinks, the land cannot automatically be considered ready for housing, parks or other public uses. Environmental safeguards, including leachate management and fire prevention, remain important, as does monitoring the quality and stability of reclaimed ground. For communities living near Bhalswa, the measure of success is therefore not just the volume of waste removed. It is whether the risks associated with the landfill actually decline, whether fresh waste is managed appropriately and whether the recovered land ultimately serves a clearly defined local purpose. 4. Pune: What happens to the people who work with waste? Pune provides an example of how waste workers can be incorporated into a city's everyday waste-management system. SWaCH, a worker-owned cooperative of waste pickers, enables its members to collect segregated waste door to door and recover recyclable materials. Workers provide a service to households while earning from user fees and the sale of recyclables. The model grew out of organising by the Kagad Kach Patra Kashtakari Panchayat, a waste-pickers' union that has advocated for workers' rights since 1993. Although Pune's cooperative model is not itself an example of a former dumpsite being turned into a park, it offers a useful way to examine the livelihood dimension of remediation. Where new processing facilities are established, cities should assess whether experienced waste pickers can be employed or organised into cooperatives to run parts of the system. Photograph: (Sajjad Hussain/AFP) A 2025 study on Delhi's waste infrastructure highlights a related concern. The closure of traditional waste collection and sorting points, known as dhalaos, and their replacement by compactors or other facilities have affected informal waste pickers, particularly women. Some have had to use their homes for sorting and storing waste, blurring the boundary between their workplace and living space. The transition to a new waste-management system therefore needs to account for the people already working within the old one. Workers need safe working spaces, protective equipment, fair and predictable earnings, access to social security and a meaningful role in decisions affecting their livelihoods. Where new processing facilities are established, cities should assess whether experienced waste pickers can be employed or organised into cooperatives to run parts of the system. The real test begins after remediation DRAP's national target is ambitious, but the scale of the remaining work is substantial. In January 2026, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs reported that 1,138 dumpsites had been fully remediated and 1,020 were under remediation, out of 2,488 identified sites containing more than 1,000 tonnes of waste each. Approximately 15.51 crore metric tonnes of legacy waste had been processed, and 8,484 acres of land reclaimed. These figures indicate the scale of the intervention, but they do not by themselves establish whether nearby residents are experiencing better air quality, whether groundwater risks have declined, or whether waste workers have secured safer livelihoods. The examples from Gorakhpur and Raichur show how reclaimed land can be put to new uses, while Bhalswa demonstrates why remediation cannot be measured only by the visible reduction of a garbage mound. So for cities, the practical priority is twofold: deal responsibly with the waste accumulated over decades and stop creating new mountains through inadequate segregation, collection and processing. A reclaimed site is only the beginning. Its real value will depend on what replaces the dump, how effectively the city manages the waste it generates every day, whether the land is safe for its intended use, and whether the people who have long handled that waste are recognised as essential workers in the process. items.title: «Το δάσος είναι το σπίτι μου»: Αντιμετώπισε τη βροχή, τις βδέλλες και τις σκοτεινές νύχτες για να ελέγξει 3000+ βατράχους για μια θανατηφόρα ασθένεια
items.titleOriginal: ‘The Forest Is My Home’: She Braved Rain, Leeches & Dark Nights To Check 3000+ Frogs for a Deadly Disease
items.description: Κάθε φορά που η μητέρα της Keerthi Krutha, T V Champakalatha, της ζητούσε να γυρίσει σπίτι για φεστιβάλ, συχνά λάμβανε μια απάντηση που έλεγε τα πάντα για την αγάπη της κόρης της για την ερημιά. "Άμμα, είμαι ήδη σπίτι. Το δάσος είναι το σπίτι μου", της έλεγε η Κερθή. Για τον 36χρονο ερευνητή άγριας ζωής που γεννήθηκε στο Τσενάι, τα δάση των Δυτικών Γκατς εκτάρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: Whenever Keerthi Krutha's mother, T V Champakalatha, asked her to come home for festivals, she often received an answer that said everything about her daughter's love for the wilderness. "Amma, I am already home. The forest is my home," Keerthi would tell her. For the 36-year-old Chennai-born wildlife researcher, the forests of the Western Ghats had become part of everyday life. After sunset, when frogs began calling from streams and insects filled the air with their sounds, she would set out with a torch, sampling kits and notebooks. Her task was to find the frogs, collect samples from their skin, record what she saw and release them unharmed. Some nights meant crossing slippery rocks and swollen streams. Others brought leeches, unpredictable rain and hours of walking. Yet these were the places Keerthi had always wanted to be. Over several years, working largely on her own, she surveyed 49 protected areas and 19 other landscapes , documenting more than 3,000 amphibians. She was searching for answers to a worrying question: was a fungus that had devastated frogs in other parts of the world spreading through India's forests too? Her research would help scientists understand where the fungus had reached in the Western Ghats and how to keep checking for it. "If frogs are dying, then it means there is a problem," Keerthi told The Hindu in 2015. "Frogs are ecological indicators." Speaking to The Better India , she traces this work back to a childhood spent learning about snakes, crocodiles and forests. It began with a childhood love for wildlife Growing up in Chennai, Keerthi looked forward to nature documentaries and filled her shelves with wildlife books. Family trips often took her to forests rather than popular tourist attractions. The more she learnt, the more time she wanted outdoors. "It wasn't something that came suddenly," her mother tells The Better India . "Nature was always where she felt happiest." Growing up in Chennai, Keerthi looked forward to nature documentaries and filled her shelves with wildlife books. In 2004, as a school student, Keerthi was selected as a Sanctuary Asia Tiger Ambassador through the Kids for Tigers programme. Visits to protected forests introduced her to people who had made wildlife conservation their life's work. Conservation began to feel like a possible future. She also volunteered at the Madras Crocodile Bank, helping clean crocodile enclosures after the 2004 tsunami. While studying for a BTech in Biotechnology at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore, she joined local snake rescues, participated in wildlife estimation exercises and volunteered with conservation organisations. "Wildlife became the direction she wanted her life to take," her mother says. By the time Keerthi graduated in 2012, she knew she wanted to work in conservation. An opportunity soon took her back into the forests, this time to study frogs. Looking for a fungus in frogs After graduating, she joined a project run by the Wildlife Information Liaison Development (WILD) Society and Zoo Outreach Organisation, affiliated with the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER), Pune. The team was investigating a fungus that infects frogs and other amphibians in the Western Ghats. It causes a disease called chytridiomycosis . Scientists call the fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis , or simply chytrid fungus. The fungus attacks their skin, which frogs rely on to absorb water and breathe. In some frogs, a serious infection can be fatal. "It has resulted in the extinction of nearly 200 species of frogs globally and threatens almost 40 percent of amphibian species," Keerthi tells The Better India . The Western Ghats, one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, are home to more than 200 frog species, many found nowhere else. Although India had not seen the mass frog deaths reported elsewhere, scientists had already detected the fungus in several species. "The incidence of this disease was recorded for the first time here in 2011," Keerthi explains. "That made long-term monitoring especially important." Researchers needed to find out which forests harboured the fungus and whether it appeared in new places over time. That meant searching for frogs in the wild, without hurting them. Keerthi was ready to do the work. What it takes to survey thousands of frogs after dark Frogs are especially active at night. Following their calls, Keerthi searched rainforests, evergreen forests, shola grasslands and streams, often working until late in the nights. Even finding these tiny animals could take hours. She carefully took a skin swab from each frog, recorded its details and released it. The swabs could then be tested for fungus without harming the animals. On one of her expeditions, her mother joined her and saw how difficult and demanding her work really was. Between surveys, she stayed in forest camps. Leeches, slippery paths, rising streams and unpredictable weather became familiar parts of the work. On one visit, her mother joined her and saw what these nights demanded. "I realised how difficult and demanding the work really was," she tells The Better India . "But I also knew she was exactly where she wanted to be." For Keerthi, each sample brought scientists closer to understanding the possible danger facing the animals she had spent so long searching for. How tiny skin samples helped track a hidden threat Collecting frogs' skin samples was only half the job. Scientists also needed a reliable way to repeat these checks in different forests and compare what they found. Keerthi helped develop clear steps for finding frogs, taking samples and recording results, so other researchers could follow the same process in the years ahead. Tests at IISER Pune found that the fungus belonged to a type already known to occur widely in Asia. The findings were published in the scientific journal PLOS ONE , adding to what researchers knew about its presence in the Western Ghats. As the work expanded, Keerthi independently secured two grants from the Mohamed bin Zayed Species Conservation Fund. This allowed the surveys to reach more places and the team to continue documenting frogs. The samples and methods gave future researchers a starting point for checking whether the disease was spreading or changing over time. An unexpected discovery in the woods The forests held another surprise. While studying a disease already known to scientists, Keerthi and her colleagues helped identify a frog species that had never been formally described. In 2017, they described Nyctibatrachus mewasinghi , or Mewa Singh's night frog, found only in Kerala's Malabar Wildlife Sanctuary. Discoveries like this help scientists understand where a species lives and which habitats may need protection. But finding a species is only the first step. Understanding the threats it faces is equally important, and frogs themselves can offer valuable clues. Tigers and elephants often draw the spotlight in wildlife conservation. Frogs are easier to overlook, but they can tell us a great deal about the health of our forests. Their skin absorbs water and helps them breathe, making them especially sensitive to pollution, habitat damage and disease. When frog populations begin to decline, it can be an early warning that something is wrong in their surroundings, potentially affecting other wildlife too. "If frogs are dying, then it means there is a problem," Keerthi says. This is what makes her research so important. By identifying where the fungus has been found, Keerthi is helping scientists keep watch for a threat that could affect frogs across the Western Ghats, including species found nowhere else on Earth. For Keerthi, the forest has always been home The child who explored tiger reserves , cleaned crocodile enclosures after the tsunami and rescued snakes grew into a researcher documenting frogs and helping scientists understand a disease threatening them worldwide. Her surveys, scientific work and role in discovering a new species have added to what we know about the Western Ghats and the wildlife that depends on them. Her mother has watched that commitment carry Keerthi through long field trips and festivals away from home. "She has always chosen the forest," she says. All Pictures: Keerthikrutha Seetharaman

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Northwestern University and UC Santa Barbara identified a specific contact point on tau proteins where the misfolding that drives Alzheimer’s disease begins. The finding , published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , suggests the site could be targeted with drugs designed to slow tau tangle growth in the brain. How tau proteins misfold In healthy brains, tau proteins stabilize the internal scaffolding of nerve cells. In tauopathies , including Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia, tau misfolds and recruits healthy proteins to adopt the same abnormal shape. The result is fibrillar aggregates: knotted threads that accumulate and spread through brain tissue. What happens the moment a newly produced tau protein first encounters an existing tangle wasn’t well understood. To find out, chemist Songi Han and colleagues at Northwestern used nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to track engineered tau as it attached to pre-existing tau fibers, watching individual regions as the process unfolded. The region around amino acid 300 stood out because it made contact with existing aggregates faster than any other site examined, acting as an initial anchor. The rest of the protein then aligned to the fiber’s structure. The team calls it “dock-and-lock”: tau docks at the contact point first, then the remaining sections fall into place. Where water comes in The anchor’s stickiness wasn’t fully explained by the protein’s structure. Molecular simulations and water dynamics experiments added a piece: the region around amino acid 300 has an unusual arrangement of water molecules that are easy to dislodge when another tau molecule gets close. That displacement lowers the energy cost of attachment and nudges the docking forward. Chemically blocking the anchor site inhibited fiber growth. Blocking other positions had much less effect. That gap in response is what gives the finding traction as a potential drug target. A possible drug target “Once you know that aggregation-prone tau proteins always have a hotspot that is first attracted to the same site of tau that is stacked to fibrils, then you know there’s always some part of the protein that you can target to neutralize,” said Han. “If you know where to block its action of misfolding, you could block it to prevent it from propagating.” The experiments used a shortened tau construct with a disease-associated mutation, not full-length tau from human tissue , so translation to disease conditions isn’t established. The anchor point’s location may also shift between tau variants and disease types. Whether the mechanism holds across different tau structures, and whether it can be safely disrupted in a living brain, are the next questions. Source study: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences- A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation Did this solution stand out? items.title: The Giving Grove: πώς οι δωρεάν κοινοτικοί οπωρώνες του Κάνσας Σίτι έγιναν εθνικό πρότυπο
items.titleOriginal: The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Είναι ώρα συγκομιδής στο Κάνσας Σίτι και στην Ακαδημία του Κάνσας Σίτι, οι μαθητές βγαίνουν έξω κατά τη διάρκεια του γεύματος για να μαζέψουν τζίτζιφι κατευθείαν από τα δέντρα. «Νιώθω σαν μια πριγκίπισσα του παραμυθιού κάθε μεσημεριανό γεύμα», είπε η Νόβα Χένρι, ηλικιωμένος, «επειδή βγαίνω έξω και απλά γεύομαι μικρές λιχουδιές». Τα δέντρα είναι δωρεάν για οποιονδήποτε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It is harvest time in Kansas City, and at Kansas City Academy, students are stepping outside during lunch to pick jujubes straight off the trees. “I feel like a fairy tale princess every lunch,” said Nova Henry, a senior, “because I get to go out and just feast on little treats.” The trees are free for anyone to take from. That is the whole premise of the Giving Grove , a Kansas City organization 14 years into planting fruit orchards on vacant land and asking nothing in return. It now has 14,000 trees in 847 orchards across 17 cities, and more than a million people live within walking distance of one. The Giving Grove’s origin story The Giving Grove began with a small stand of trees planted 13 years ago on the corner of a shuttered public school in the Waldo neighborhood. The school has since reopened and is expanding, so the original orchard is currently behind a construction fence, but it is still there. “This little orchard we’re standing in here started a national movement,” said Giving Grove Marketing Director Sarah Sikich. “I think it’s one of Kansas City’s best-kept secrets.” From that corner, the organization partnered with Kansas City Community Gardens to spread orchards across unused plots throughout the metro, from a few trees on a school parking lot to plots with over a hundred. Kansas City now has 248 free orchards with nearly 4,600 fruit, nut, and berry trees. “I joke that Kansas City should be the city of orchards, not the city of fountains,” Sikich said. “No other city in the United States has as many orchards as we do.” Built on shared knowledge More than four out of five Giving Grove orchards remain in production. The reason, according to founder Kevin Birzer, is that the organization never just plants trees and walks away. “It’s stuff people can learn, but it takes a long time, and it’s not really efficient for one group to do that,” he said. “So our thought from day one was we would provide that expertise, the knowledge of how to grow the trees , how to select the trees.” About 1,700 “orchard stewards” across the country maintain that relationship. The Giving Grove offers training, workshops, help finding grants, soil improvements, pruning support, and succession planning for when stewards move on or burn out. Janet Porter, a science teacher who tends the orchard at Kansas City Academy, has found the same to be true. “They do training. They do workshops. If I ever have any questions, they’re just a phone call away.” It is not just fruit, either. The trees attract insects , which attract songbirds, which attract predators like hawks. At least one Kansas City student turned pruning experience into a job at a tree nursery. A model spreading city by city Nine years ago, a community gardening group in St. Louis asked for help, and the Giving Grove said yes. Now the organization is in cities across the country, with conversations underway about San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York City. Different communities want different trees, and growing in Brooklyn is not the same as growing in Utah, especially without chemical pesticides or herbicides. “Some environments are more challenging,” Birzer said. “Creating something really cool for the neighborhood, that part’s universal.” The Giving Grove runs on just over $1 million a year. Most of it comes from 1% for the Planet , a network that channels one percent of member businesses’ annual revenue toward environmental causes; corporations sometimes add volunteer labor, and individual donors fill in the rest. The organization only enters communities that invite it, and right now it is working through a backlog of those invitations. “I think people have an easy time falling in love with what we’re doing,” Sikich said. “Planting fruit trees is something everyone can agree with.” Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Is it a hummingbird, a hawk, or a moth? The somewhat confusingly named hummingbird hawk-moth is (drumroll, please) a moth species that migrates to the U.K. and Ireland from southern Europe and North Africa each summer. Its moniker comes from the way it feeds — hovering over flowers like a hummingbird. Wildlife photographer Andrew Fusek-Peters captured that feeding process earlier this month in a series of stunning photos that show the 2-inch insect beating its wings at a staggering 85 times a second while drinking from a valerian bush in his garden in Shropshire, England. Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS The striking moths have been thriving in the U.K. thanks to the warm summer. James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, told the BBC that 2026 was a “record year” for sightings in the country. “They’ve had a really good year this year,” he said. “Normally they would come in small numbers. We’d normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we’ve seen loads of records of them.” Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS Though it borrows its name from the hummingbird, this hawk-moth actually has the avian species beat when it comes to hovering speed — hummingbirds average about 50 beats per second, while the insects can hit up to 85 beats per second. (Another fun fact: Hummingbirds are native only to the Americas, and hummingbird hawk-moths only to the U.K., Europe, and North Africa.) “The hummingbird hawk-moth is a summer visitor to the U.K. from southern Europe and North Africa but can be seen in most months of the year and is a favorite garden visitor,” Fusek-Peters told SWNS. “With warmer summers, it now breeds in the U.K. and will often overwinter here and can now be considered a U.K. breeding species.” He noted that the bugs “emit an audible hum” as they hover. “It means that it can maneuver easily with its long proboscis able to delve into deeper flower stems such as red valerian.” Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS As for how he captured such action-packed photos, Fusek-Peters said it took time and experimentation. “I spent much of the summer photographing them and experimented with slowing down my shutter speed to capture the incredible motion and orange flash of the wings.” This article was originally written by Ed Chatterton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment Reading Time: 2 minutes How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment Driving more safely doesn’t just benefit road users. Many of the habits associated with safer driving can also reduce a vehicle’s environmental impact by lowering fuel or energy consumption and cutting harmful emissions . While wider developments in vehicle technology and transport policy play an important role, individual driving habits remain part of the picture. How smoother driving can cut fuel use and emissions According to Energy Saving Trust, efficient driving techniques such as smooth acceleration, staying within speed limits and avoiding unnecessary braking can help reduce fuel consumption and emissions. This means anticipating traffic conditions and maintaining a steady speed wherever it’s safe and practical to do so. Frequent acceleration and harsh braking require more energy than gradual speed changes. In petrol and diesel vehicles, this typically means burning more fuel. In electric vehicles, it can increase battery consumption and reduce driving range. Why speed, braking and forward planning matter Safe driving is closely linked to awareness and anticipation. Giving yourself more time to react to changing road conditions can help reduce sudden manoeuvres that increase fuel consumption and vehicle wear. For example, noticing traffic slowing ahead allows you to ease off the accelerator gradually instead of braking heavily at the last moment. Likewise, anticipating junctions and changing speed limits is key. Drivers looking to improve their awareness may find that utilising telematics insurance to help you be more aware of your driving style encourages more consistent habits, as many telematics systems monitor factors such as braking, acceleration and cornering behaviour. Look after the vehicle as well as your driving style Environmentally responsible driving is not solely about behaviour behind the wheel. Keeping your vehicle in good mechanical condition can also support efficiency and help emissions-control systems operate as intended. Regular servicing allows potential issues to be identified before they affect vehicle performance. Maintaining correct tyre pressures can reduce rolling resistance, while replacing worn components when required can help the vehicle run more efficiently. Drivers should also address dashboard warning lights promptly and ensure emissions-related components are functioning correctly. A poorly maintained vehicle may consume more fuel or energy than necessary. Motoring experts regularly highlight the importance of maintenance as part of environmentally conscious driving, alongside habits such as reducing unnecessary vehicle weight and keeping tyres correctly inflated. Put greener driving into the UK’s bigger environmental picture The UK’s transition towards lower-emission transport involves multiple factors, including advances in vehicle technology and public policy. However, driver behaviour still plays a role. If millions of motorists adopt more efficient driving habits, the combined effect can contribute to lower fuel consumption and reduced emissions across the vehicle fleet. While no individual action can solve environmental challenges on its own, small changes across a large population can support wider sustainability goals. The post How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams Reading Time: 3 minutes How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams Retail teams work across different stores, shifts, and job roles, so training must stay accessible during busy working days. Sales associates need product knowledge, supervisors need management guidance, and every employee must complete required safety courses. A dependable training platform helps meet these demands without disrupting daily store operations. A Learning Management System (LMS) brings these needs into one trackable program. The right retail LMS software also gives leaders a clearer view of participation, assessment results, and unresolved gaps, creating a practical foundation for consistent store training. The following areas outline what to consider when choosing a system. Create One Training Hub For Every Store A retail LMS gives employees one place to access onboarding, product updates, customer service lessons, and compliance courses. A retail LMS software directory helps decision-makers compare systems built for retail requirements, including mobile access, short lessons, progress tracking, and reporting. Centralized content reduces inconsistent instructions between locations and lets training leaders update a course without distributing new files manually. Store teams also benefit from clear learning paths. A new sales associate can complete orientation, point-of-sale training, and product lessons in sequence. A department supervisor can follow a separate path covering coaching, scheduling, inventory procedures, and incident reporting. Deliver Training Around Store Schedules Retail employees rarely share the same hours, making classroom sessions difficult to coordinate. Mobile access lets employees complete assigned lessons between shifts, during scheduled training time, or at another approved location. Short lessons support this schedule. A five-minute module can explain a product feature, customer greeting standard, or safety procedure without removing an employee from the sales floor for a long session. Managers can assign content by role, location, or employment stage, so each learner receives relevant material. A Learning Management System also records completion automatically. Managers do not need separate spreadsheets for each store, which reduces manual follow-up and gives regional leaders a consistent record. Keep Product And Service Knowledge Current Retail information changes often. Product lines, prices, promotions, return rules, and service expectations require regular updates. A central course library lets training teams revise a lesson once and publish the current version across selected stores. Knowledge checks give managers more than a completion mark. Short quizzes can test whether employees understand product differences, warranty conditions, or escalation procedures. Assessment results show where a team needs a refresher before a new promotion begins. Store leaders can also use assigned learning for seasonal hiring. Temporary employees receive the same essential service and safety information as permanent staff, with a clear deadline before their first scheduled shift. Track Compliance Without Manual Chasing Retail organizations must monitor courses related to workplace safety, data protection, harassment prevention, and other internal requirements. An LMS records assignments, due dates, completions, and assessment results in one system. Automated reminders help employees address overdue courses before managers need to contact each person. Escalation reports show which store, role, or department needs attention. These records also give training leaders evidence that required instruction was assigned and completed. Access controls support accurate reporting. A district manager can review assigned stores, while a store manager sees the employees within that location. This structure keeps reports useful without giving every user access to unnecessary information. Use Reports To Improve Store Performance Completion data helps leaders measure participation, but useful reporting goes further. Scores, attempts, time spent, and course status reveal whether employees understood the material or rushed through it. Training leaders can compare results by location or role to find recurring gaps. If several stores perform poorly on a product assessment, the lesson needs clearer explanations or better examples. If one location has low completion rates, managers can review scheduling, communication, or access problems. Learning data also supports regular management routines. Regional leaders can review a monthly report, discuss overdue assignments with store managers, and adjust upcoming training according to business needs. Give Managers A Practical Coaching Tool An LMS supports daily coaching when managers connect online lessons with store activity. After an employee completes a customer service module, a supervisor can observe a customer interaction and discuss the result privately. Managers can assign refresher lessons after an observed gap. They can also recognize completed development paths during one-on-one meetings and use assessment results to plan the next coaching conversation. This approach keeps training connected to job behavior. Employees receive instruction, practice the skill, and discuss progress with a manager instead of treating courses as isolated administrative tasks. Conclusion Retail LMS software gives store teams a shared training structure without forcing every employee into the same schedule. The strongest implementation starts with role-based learning paths, mobile-friendly lessons, current product content, and compliance tracking. Training leaders should audit existing courses, group them by role and store need, then select a system that reports completion and assessment results clearly. A small pilot across several locations provides useful evidence before wider deployment. The post How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable Reading Time: 5 minutes How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable There are events across the entire school/university year for students that cover everything from orientation to graduation, conferences and cultural festivals, sports competitions. These events gather people together, but they also produce extensive waste disposable food containers, printed materials, decorations and single-use supplies for the event. Educational institutions can also lower their carbon footprint by implementing greener practices, because it also teaches students sustainable habits that they will take with them through the rest of their lives after graduation. Sustainable changes to campus events do not necessarily require a large amount of money or radical alterations. Many of the most helpful changes grow out of responsible planning, smart purchasing and greater engagement from the campus community. Think Of Events With Preventive Waste Sustainability needs to be planned in since the earliest stages of planning an event rather than being afterthought once waste is already generated. Organisers can start by estimated attendance, main supplies need to get for use and reference the environmental concern with previous events. Digital registration, electronic invitations and online event schedules are opportunities to eliminate the fabric of waste by cutting out unnecessary paper consumption. For printable materials which are necessary, organizers can print only the copies needed and use double-sided printing when they should be. Also, some schools or universities create sustainability checklists that include catering, transport, energy use and waste management. Clear responsibilities for event teams allow environmentally-sensitive matters to remain part of the planning process. Bottom line prevention from unnecessary consumption tends to work better than fully relying on recycling or disposal systems post-event. Minimize Usage of Single Use Plastics and Disposable Materials But disposable cups, plastic cutlery, food containers and water bottles are other elements of the large waste generated on an important campus meeting. A practical solution would be to offer refill water stations and promote the audience to bring reusable bottles. In places where catering facilities are present, reusable plates, cups and cutleries can take the place of disposable ones. Now when organizing the event, one should count on all the required water, energy as well as cleaning and logistics that are needed to handle reusable items properly. Easily identifiable waste stations are another effective way in which to help participants sort recyclables, general rubbish and food scraps. Such stations would need to mirror local collection and processing facilities available to residents. As there is no appropriate infrastructure, items labelled recyclable or compostable are not necessarily recycled or composted. Prevent unnecessary waste and ensure unavoidable waste is managed properly. Opt For Eco-Friendly Supplies And Materials Another consideration is your event materials. Banners, decorations, name badges, lanyards and exhibition materials are sometimes only used for a limited time before ending up in the bin, even though they can remain in good condition. By selecting durable supplies that can be stored and used again for future events, institutions can minimize this waste. With reusable signage, interchangeable name inserts and returnable badge holders, the need to buy replacements for each event can be limited. Organizers planning student orientations or academic conferences can review the reusable badge and lanyard options available through suppliers such as 4inlanyards when evaluating event identification materials. The broader environmental priority should be to select suitable products, recover them after each event, and reuse them wherever practical. Material composition also matters. Making polyester using recycled PET plastic is a way of reducing the need for virgin polyester, but there are many factors that define the environmental benefits over the whole lifecycle including how it is produced, the length of each product life and end-of-life options. Natural fibres themselves can have environmental impacts involving the cultivation of raw materials, consumption of water, post-harvest processing and transport. Instead of expecting that a single sort of material will always be the most sustainable alternative, institutions should assess durability, practicality, sourcing and end-of-life together. Environmental Initiatives for Campus Catering Food waste is a widespread problem during conferences, student parties and university-wide events. Ordering too much leads to waste, wasting not only the food but also all the resources spent to produce, deliver, and prepare it. By analyzing registration data, organizers can better prepare catering by accurately predicting expected attendance and adapting amounts to the timing of the event. Knowledge, practices and behaviour Change sProviding food that is rich in plant ingredients also can have a positive impact on the environment footprint of catering although this will vary with different components and production methods. Subject to local regulations and food safety and suitability requirements, eligible surplus food may be donated to community groups. Inappropriate collection systems may make even unavoidable food scraps unrecyclable, although these might otherwise be compostable. Institutions can record quantities of food leftovers after an event, which can potentially improve catering estimates for future events and identify sources of recurring waste. Promote Sustainable Transport and EnergyUse Individual travel by car to events over long distances can be a major aspect of the carbon footprint for campus events. Where practical and feasible, universities can promote the use of public transport, walking, cycling and carpooling. Depressingly, taking venues closer to public transport links might also reduce the emissions from travel as well. Energy consumption deserves similar attention. Organizers can have efficient lighting, switch off obsolete equipment, choose rooms according to attendance that are not unnecessarily large and so avoid heating large, empty spaces. Hybrid participation may be appropriate for certain conferences where the reduction in long-distance travel is not outweighed by a disproportionate extra energy use, nor does it exclude people who benefit from attending in person. Such decisions illustrate that event sustainability goes well beyond the materials used on the day. Get Students, Teacher, and the Campus Community Sharing responsibility for being environmentally responsible is what helps sustainable events succeed. Societies on campus, environmental groups, teams from facilities and event volunteers can all help with planning and implementation. They can assist attendees in finding out where they can refill, return reusable items , and sort the waste properly. Student groups can also hold environmental awareness sessions where it explains the reason that such practices are important. Feedback is equally valuable. Holding short post-event surveys can help determine if recycling stations were accessible, if digital materials were available and convenient, and what restatement attendees would support in the future. Participation should remain inclusive. Sustainability programmes must also take account of disabled people, financial inequalities and different access to transport or reusable products. Students engage more in these developments and are likely to continue these routines when practiced. Metrics for Better Future Events Institutions require measurable knowledge to comprehend if their sustainability endeavors are effective. Useful indicators comprise waste generation, food surplus and left over contrary to advice by the industry (i.e.feedback) as well as recovered reusable items and low-impact transportation mode-share. This allows organizers to compare the results of similar events and record which actions made a real difference. It can be something as simple as showing a post-event review that identifies the opportunity to reduce excess orders or enhance waste collection. Environmental reporting should remain transparent. Do not claim that an event is entirely sustainable based on a singular action particularly, as we have seen above where other impacts remain unmeasured or poorly-evaluated. Having a history over time for tracking progress against these targets makes it more likely that schools will set realistic targets and use them to guide decision-making. Final Thoughts Pragmatic choices to reduce waste encouraging printing less, reusing what can be reused again, the selective planning of catering and reducing travel unnecessarily are fundamental ways in making campus buildings and events environmentally sustainable while involving a wider audience on campus. The place to begin can be small steps, monitor outcomes and continuously enhance later on. These initiatives not only lessen environmental impacts but they also create an opportunity to implement practical experience relative to sustainability. Exposure to responsible resource use in everyday campus operations can shape student behavior as they move into their careers and communities. The post How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: At 5 AM, while Kolkata sleeps, a 74-year-old woman is busy spreading happiness, one doorstep at a time. Meet Ratnabali Ghosh, lovingly known as Kolkata’s Alpona Didi. Every year, just before Diwali, she steps out early in the morning to paint beautiful traditional alponas outside strangers’ homes, turning ordinary doorsteps into heartwarming surprises. For elderly residents living away from their children, these intricate patterns mean much more than art. They bring a sense of connection, care, and the comforting feeling that someone is thinking of them. Through this simple yet beautiful gesture, Ratnabali is keeping Bengal’s traditional alpona art alive while bringing smiles to people across Kolkata. Her story reminds us that making a difference doesn’t always require grand gestures. Sometimes, a little kindness can brighten someone’s entire day. ❤️ What is one small act of kindness that has stayed with you? Watch Ratnabali Ghosh’s full story on YouTube ➡️ https://youtu.be/O87taxrk_aM ⁠￼ 🎥 @ratnabali.ghosh #RatnabaliGhosh #AlponaDidi #AlponaArt #Kolkata #BengaliCulture #BengaliTradition #TraditionalIndianArt #Diwali #IndianCulture #ActsOfKindness #InspiringStories #WomenWhoInspire #CulturalHeritage #PositiveIndia #thebetterindia
