items.descriptionOriginal: "It was given to me in Rs 100 notes, and I remember feeling them in my pocket as I rode my bike back home." That is how Nani described his first salary as an assistant director in an interview Koimoi later revisited, and the sum was Rs 4,000. He has said he felt rich enough that evening to imagine buying half of Hyderabad. Today, the man who counted those notes is Telugu cinema's Natural Star, an actor whom audiences describe as one of the industry's most relatable, and his road there began far from any spotlight. Learning cinema from behind the camera Born Ghanta Naveen Babu in Hyderabad, Nani did not set out to act. Inspired by filmmaker Mani Ratnam , he wanted to direct, and producer Anil Kumar Koneru let him join the sets of Radha Gopalam (2005) as a clap assistant. He then worked as an assistant director on Allari Bullodu, Dhee and Asthram , learning how a film comes together one shot at a time. Nani spent about a year as a radio jockey, hosting Non-Stop Nani before an advertisement led to his acting debut in Ashta Chamma in 2008. Photograph: ( India Today ) But before the camera found him, a microphone did. A friend working at WorldSpace Satellite Radio offered him a job as a radio jockey , and he spent about a year hosting a programme called Non-Stop Nani. According to The Times of India, the show made his voice familiar to listeners, although acting remained his greater ambition. The films that put Nani on the map In 2008, director Mohana Krishna Indraganti noticed Nani in an advertisement and cast him in Ashta Chamma , which gave him his lead-acting debut. The romantic comedy, a free adaptation of Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest , was released on 5 September 2008 and earned Rs 6 crore as the distributors' share, so the newcomer arrived with a success behind him. Ride (2009) and Bheemili Kabaddi Jattu (2010), a remake of the Tamil film Vennila Kabadi Kuzhu, kept the momentum going, with the latter becoming a surprise hit. Snehituda (2009) did not succeed, yet Nani kept getting lead roles, and in 2012 he won the Nandi Award for Best Actor for Yeto Vellipoyindhi Manasu , directed by Gautham Vasudev Menon. Ala Modalaindi , a 2011 romantic comedy directed by Nandini Reddy, became his breakthrough. In 2012, S S Rajamouli cast him in Eega , where Nani's character returns as a fly to take revenge on the man who wronged him. The film earned over Rs 125 crore and won two National Film Awards, which showed how willingly Nani backed ambitious ideas. How he became the 'Natural Star' The nickname arrived with Bhale Bhale Magadivoy in 2015. It was one of the few small-budget Telugu films to cross US$1 million at the box office, and it became the first blockbuster of his career. Nani won the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor in Telugu for it, and audiences began calling him the Natural Star because his performances felt so unforced. In S S Rajamouli's Eega (2012), Nani played a man who returns as a fly to seek revenge, taking on an unconventional role early in his career. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) What kept the title alive was the kind of person he chose to play. His characters are flawed people working through love, ambition, family and the uncertainties of ordinary life, so viewers tend to see themselves in them. In Jersey (2019), he played a former cricketer who returns to the game for the sake of his young son, a performance that Film Companion placed on its list of the 100 greatest performances of the decade. In Hi Nanna (2023), he played a fashion photographer raising his daughter alone, and the film became a commercial success. He also took risks with the image he had built. V (2020), his 25th film and first OTT release, cast him as a serial killer, his first negative role, and it became the most-watched Telugu film on streaming, according to Wikipedia's account of his career. The honours followed. Nani won the Filmfare Critics Award again for Shyam Singha Roy , which made him the only Telugu actor to win it twice. In 2024, he took home his first Filmfare Award for Best Actor in Telugu for Dasara at the 69th Filmfare Awards South, where he was also nominated for Hi Nanna. His next project, The Paradise , reunites him with Dasara director Srikanth Odela. For an actor who once measured success in a pocketful of Rs 100 notes, the journey suggests a career can be built one opportunity at a time, through patience, a willingness to try unusual roles, and a gift for looking like someone the audience already knows. items.descriptionOriginal: With fuel prices sky-high, the need for fuels from non-petroleum sources has taken on a new urgency. And researchers at Worchester Polytechnic Institute say they might have just the alternative source we need for low-carbon and low-cost fuel: bamboo. Bamboo could power trains, planes, and automobiles for as little as $2.75 per gasoline-gallon equivalent at mature commercial scale, the researchers calculate. The fuel would emit greenhouse gas emissions 26 times lower than conventional diesel fuel. What’s more, bamboo promises to be a more sustainable biofuel feedstock than conventional ones like corn and sugarcane. Bamboo is a grass, and one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Some species growing several dozen inches in a day. Because of this fast growth rate, the US could make as much fuel from bamboo as it makes ethanol from corn while using about 13% as much land . The WPI researchers published their results in the journal Sustainable Energy & Fuels . “I think this research is especially timely and important because fuel prices are high and the transportation sector produces more greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. than any other,” said chemical engineering professor Michael Timko in a press release . “Bamboo would use different land than we are using for food production, so there is no food versus fuel trade-off. Farmers win, consumers win.” .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , .IRPP_ruby:visited , .IRPP_ruby:active {border:0!important;}.IRPP_ruby .clearfix:after {content: "";display: table;clear: both;}.IRPP_ruby {display: block;transition: background-color 250ms;webkit-transition: background-color 250ms;width: 100%;opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: #eaeaea;}.IRPP_ruby:active , .IRPP_ruby:hover {opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: inherit;}.IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl {background-position: center;background-size: cover;float: left;margin: 0;padding: 0;width: 31.59%;position: absolute;top: 0;bottom: 0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {float: right;width: 65.65%;padding:0;margin:0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text {display: table;height: 130px;left: 0;top: 0;padding:0;margin:0;padding-top: 20px;padding-bottom: 20px;}.IRPP_ruby .IRPP_ruby-content {display: table-cell;margin: 0;padding: 0 74px 0 0px;position: relative;vertical-align: middle;width: 100%;}.IRPP_ruby .ctaText {border-bottom: 0 solid #fff;color: #0099cc;font-size: 14px;font-weight: bold;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .postTitle {color: #000000;font-size: 16px;font-weight: 600;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .ctaButton {background: url(https://www.anthropocenemagazine.org/wp-content/plugins/intelly-related-posts-pro/assets/images/next-arrow.png)no-repeat;background-color: #afb4b6;background-position: center;display: inline-block;height: 100%;width: 54px;margin-left: 10px;position: absolute;bottom:0;right: 0;top: 0;}.IRPP_ruby:after {content: "";display: block;clear: both;} Recommended Reading: How sustainable are aviation biofuels really? Timko and colleagues evaluated bamboo for biofuel production using a process called hydrothermal liquefaction. In the process, wet biomass or organic wastes are subjected to high heat and pressure. Polymer chains in the mass breaks down to form a biocrude oil. The oil can then be converted to other liquid fuel products. The researchers heated wet bamboo pulp to 300°C for 10 minutes. The process converted about 36% of its mass into biocrude. Unlike corn or sugarcane, which are the main plants used to make biofuels today , bamboo wouldn’t compete with agricultural land and doesn’t need much water or energy to grow. And compared with other perennial grasses that are also being considered for biofuel, it has very low ash content—less than 1% by weight—so the fuel-making process generates minimal waste. ”Bamboo may eventually offer industry a way to generate low-carbon liquid fuels at scale,” Timko said. Source : Timothy M. Woodard et al. Bamboo as a cost-effective feedstock for production of low carbon transportation fuels. Sustainable Energy & Fuels , 2026. items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with S M Sehgal Foundation. For 26-year-old Anchal of Hussaini village, leaving home for a meeting was once difficult to imagine. Her days revolved around household chores, livestock, farm work and caring for her children. In her community, women had few opportunities to attend meetings outside their homes or speak to people from the village. So when she decided to join the Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise in Chhata block of Mathura in 2023, the first hurdle was at home. "They felt that the women of the house should not go out and work," she recalls. It was not an easy argument to make. Anchal had a household to run and three children to care for, two of whom have disabilities and need regular treatment. But staying at home had begun to weigh on her. "I was confined at home, and getting stressed. I wanted to do something of my own," she says. Nearly three years later, Anchal is part of the team running the mustard oil unit in her village. She earns around Rs 5,000-6,000 a month and contributes towards her children's treatment. But to get there, she first had to find a way to step outside a life that had largely been defined for her. The first hurdle was at home Anchal had completed her bachelor of arts after studying up to Class 12 in her village. Yet her education had not translated into work outside the home. "I didn't want to be confined to the house. I was waiting for a chance to step out and work," she says. Her family did not agree immediately. She had to convince them that she could work while continuing to care for her children and manage the household. She began waking early to finish her chores before leaving for the unit. The Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise was set up in 2023 with a total investment of Rs 14 lakh. Anchal joined the enterprise in November 2023. Her mother-in-law takes care of the children while she is away, and Anchal returns early whenever they need her. Joining the enterprise changed more than her daily routine. She had also been uncomfortable speaking to anyone outside her immediate circle. "Earlier, we couldn't speak freely with anyone outside our community. We hardly had any contact with outsiders," she says. That changed once she began working at the unit, alongside women she had never had any reason to speak with before. 'I was just looking for a chance to work' Preeti, now 32, arrived at the enterprise from a different starting point. Originally from Haryana, she moved to Hussaini after marriage. She had completed her bachelor of arts and taught children at schools in her village for around three years. Her father had also taught her tailoring and encouraged her to become self-reliant. After marriage, however, her days became centred on the household, cattle and fields. "I was always looking for a chance to work somewhere," she says. The opportunity came through the Shri Ji self-help group, which is linked to the National Rural Livelihoods Mission. When S M Sehgal Foundation began discussing a mustard oil unit in Hussaini around January-February 2023, Preeti became involved. But like Anchal, she first had to convince her family. Her in-laws worried about women working outside the home, what people might say and whether they could be exploited. Preeti asked her husband to come and see the work for himself before deciding. "I wanted him to understand what I was doing before I stepped out to work. If he was comfortable, I would take the chance," she says. He eventually supported her and helped convince his parents. Preeti also helped prepare the space for the enterprise , including arranging money for the electrical connection through contributions from home and their milkman. The women were ready to work. The next challenge was getting the enterprise itself off the ground. Before production, they had to win trust The Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise was set up in 2023 with a total investment of Rs 14 lakh. Of this, Rs 8 lakh came through the S M Sehgal Foundation's project supported by HDFC Bank Parivartan, while Rs 6 lakh was mobilised as community contribution, largely in kind. The idea emerged after a survey found that families in the area widely used mustard oil. Given the Foundation's existing work with local women, the team felt the women could run the enterprise on their own. Not everyone agreed. Chhaya Singh, 36, a field specialist in data and documentation at S M Sehgal Foundation, has worked closely with the enterprise for the past three years. She remembers village elders suggesting that the project be handed to men instead. "They believed women could not do it. That only made us more determined to prove them wrong," she says. For Chhaya, the goal was always for the women to take charge of the enterprise themselves. "We wanted women to be part of an enterprise, but more importantly, we wanted them to run it themselves," she says. "We also wanted them to see what is possible and help other women get the same opportunities." The machine at the centre of it all — an expeller that crushes mustard seeds to extract oil — was initially unfamiliar to all of them. For five to six months, the team met regularly with the women's family members, explaining what the enterprise involved and making the case for why the women were capable of running it. Once that groundwork was done, the team trained the women in financial literacy, stock management, and technical skills to prepare them for the work ahead. Five women now run the whole unit For Anchal, even approaching the mustard oil machine initially felt intimidating. "At first, I was afraid to even touch the mustard oil machine. I had never worked with anything like it before. But slowly, I learnt, and today I can run it on my own," she tells The Better India. With training from a technical expert, she learnt to operate the machine, understand the demand, track prices, and work through different stages of production. Preeti learnt the technical side too. "I learnt all the work in just 10 to 15 days because the team was always there to guide and support me," she says. The machine at the centre of it all — an expeller that crushes mustard seeds to extract oil — was initially unfamiliar to all of them. Eight women received technical training from an expert who supplied the expeller unit. The five women who run the enterprise today were among them. They learnt every step of the process, from handling mustard seeds to filtering the oil, filling and capping bottles, and even resolving voltage issues on their own. S M Sehgal Foundation supported the unit during its initial years and gradually stepped back as the women took on greater responsibility. How the women run the business today The unit is run by the Shri Ji self-help group, and decisions are taken collectively. Five women associated with this unit since its inception run the enterprise today. Kavita, the president, coordinates the group, reviews accounts, leads meetings and works on market linkages. Preeti, the treasurer, handles accounts, expenditure and cash flow. Anchal, the secretary, oversees operations, maintains registers and tracks stock, receives visitors and participates in decisions. Bati cleans mustard seeds and extracts oil , while Ritu handles filtration, filling, sealing, labelling and packaging. Between January and August 2026, the women sold 2,995.5 litres of mustard oil and 3,841.5 kg of oil cake. Their market now extends beyond Hussaini and neighbouring villages to Kosi Kalan town in Chhata block of Mathura district, as well as Mathura, Aligarh and Bulandshahr in Uttar Pradesh; Gurugram, Faridabad, Palwal and Hodal in Haryana; and parts of Rajasthan. According to the Foundation's latest figures, the enterprise generated Rs 6,53,980 in sales between January and August 2026. Since beginning commercial operations in November 2023, its cumulative sales have crossed Rs 24 lakh. Five percent is set aside for maintenance, and the remaining amount is divided equally among the five members. If someone does not need her share immediately, it can remain with the group and be lent to another member at one percent interest. 'Money has given me stability' For Preeti, the biggest changes can be seen outside the unit too. She has travelled for meetings in Uttarakhand, Mathura and Chhata. She contributes towards her children's school fees and household expenses and is able to save some money herself. Her family now sees her work differently. Her mother-in-law, who was initially unsure about her stepping outside the home, now cooks with the oil the enterprise produces and has come to rely on Preeti's earnings too. Even with that growing support, Preeti still seeks her in-laws' permission before visiting other people's homes. She hopes this will change with time. S M Sehgal Foundation supported the unit during its initial years and gradually stepped back as the women took on greater responsibility. For Anchal, earning has changed how she can contribute at home. Before she began working, she had to depend on her husband's income for purchases. Today, she can share those expenses, including the ongoing care her two children with disabilities need. "Earlier, my husband had to manage every expense on his own. Now, I can share that responsibility. If my children need medicines, I don't have to wait or depend on him to buy them," she says. "My biggest wish is to see my children get better. I am ready to work as hard as I have to if it can help make that happen," she says. What the work looks like beyond Hussaini The Hussaini enterprise sits within a wider network of women involved in S M Sehgal Foundation's work. The organisation has worked with rural communities for 28 years, focusing on skills, market connections and helping communities manage enterprises themselves. In Maharashtra, women in Nanda Agade's self-help group, who previously worked as farm labourers, now run a Custom Hiring Centre with its own tractor. The initiative has reduced annual rental costs by Rs 4 to 5 lakh. In Kolar, Karnataka, 389 women are shareholders in the Laxmisagara Horticulture Farmer Producer Company. 'I have a lot of hope for this enterprise' Anchal hopes to see another enterprise come up in Hussaini one day, giving other women the same chance to work and earn that she had. But her children remain at the centre of what she wants for the future. For Preeti, earning more is tied to the opportunities she hopes to give her children. She wants them to receive the best education possible and dreams of seeing them become teachers, following a path she once envisioned for herself. This is also part of why she has begun thinking about the future of her enterprise, as its growth will shape the opportunities she can provide for her children. "I have a lot of hope for this enterprise. I want to see it grow stronger so that all of us women can run it confidently on our own," she says. Both women came to the unit with fairly simple wishes. Anchal wanted space beyond a home life. Preeti wanted work that felt like her own. Both also needed an income of their own: Anchal for her children's treatment, and Preeti for school fees and household expenses. The unit is run by the Shri Ji self-help group, and decisions are taken collectively. Since then, both women have challenged what their families once thought possible for them. They have learnt to operate unfamiliar machinery, taken on responsibilities they once had little opportunity to pursue, and grown more confident in making decisions for themselves. Today, when mustard arrives at the unit , the women collectively know how much to buy, how to run the machine, how to keep the accounts, how to fill and seal the bottles and how to speak with customers. And when a decision has to be made, the women sit together and make it. All pictures courtesy S M Sehgal Foundation.

items.descriptionOriginal: For Kalpana, a woman artisan in Andhra Pradesh's Chinnapuram village, something that once clogged local waterways has become a source of income. She works with water hyacinth, an invasive plant that spreads rapidly across canals and ponds. Once removed, it was usually thrown away. Today, women like Kalpana are turning it into handbags, baskets, lampshades and other products people can use at home. "This work needs skill and dedication. Every product we make carries our effort and creativity," Kalpana told The New Indian Express . She reported earning around Rs 500 to Rs 700 a day from the craft. And she is part of a growing effort that has trained around 150 women across Andhra Pradesh's Krishna district to earn from a plant long considered a nuisance. How did a troublesome weed become a livelihood? For years, water hyacinth has troubled Krishna district's canals and water bodies. The fast-growing plant forms thick mats across the water, blocking movement and making it difficult to keep canals clear. Irrigation workers would remove it, only for the weed to grow back. But what if the material being discarded could be put to use? In October 2024, the Krishna district administration launched a training programme in Chinnapuram village, Machilipatnam mandal, to help women from self-help groups learn the craft of making products from water hyacinth. The initiative began with 50 women and involved experienced artisans from Assam, including national award-winning craftsperson Rita Das and her team. During the initial training phase, approximately 100–120 tonnes of water hyacinth were removed each month. Photograph: (newsmeter) The women learnt how to collect, dry, weave and finish the plant into products suitable for sale. The process requires patience. Once collected, the water hyacinth is dried in the sun for nearly 15 days. Its dried stalks are then woven by hand into different shapes, followed by gumming and polishing to give the finished products strength and a smooth appearance. During training, participants received an allowance of Rs 300 a day. Today, the Chinnapuram artisans produce around 50 to 60 varieties of handicrafts, including storage containers, mats, trays, handbags and decorative items. The women have also formed a society called Hyaloom to manage orders, production and income sharing. According to a February 2026 report by The New Indian Express , artisans in the group were earning an average of Rs 10,000 to Rs 15,000 a month, with earnings varying according to demand. From one village to 150 trained women What began in Chinnapuram has since expanded to other villages across Krishna district, including Chevendra, Leelagudem and Tamirisa. By September 2026, around 150 women had received training under the initiative. And the results extend beyond the products they make. During the initial training phase, approximately 100 to 120 tonnes of water hyacinth were being removed every month. With growing orders, the programme now has the capacity to handle around 150 tonnes monthly in the areas covered. According to The Times of India , the initiative has generated approximately Rs 20 lakh in combined sales and earnings, with an estimated margin of 20% after expenses, including labour charges. The products are reaching buyers through Lepakshi, which has been supporting their marketing. The district administration is also exploring opportunities with major temples, including those at Srikalahasti, Srisailam and Kanaka Durga. Women in Andhra Pradesh are converting water hyacinth into eco-friendly products, creating steady incomes while restoring local water bodies. A powerful blend of sustainability, innovation and women-led growth. 🌿✨ #AndhraPradesh #SustainableLivelihoods #EcoInnovation #WomenEmpowerment — Andhra Community (@AndhraCommunity) February 1, 2026 Even the organic manure produced through the process is finding buyers among local farmers. The next challenge is ensuring that women continue receiving orders. "The next priority is to provide regular orders and sustainable market opportunities to the trained women," Y Hari Hara Nath, project director of the District Rural Development Agency, told The Times of India . The administration hopes to expand the programme to the district's remaining 20 mandals. For women like Kalpana, the change is already meaningful. A weed that once had to be cleared and discarded is now something they can shape with their own hands and sell. And with each new order, the skills they have learnt offer another opportunity to earn. Sources: 'Women in Krishna district turn water hyacinth into source of livelihood' : By Vidya Dusi, Published on 26 September 2026 'Women turn water hyacinth into livelihood' : By Y Brahmaji, Published on 1 February 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Battery-Like Technology Offers a New Path for Capturing Carbon Dioxide Reading Time: 3 minutes A new battery-like technology developed by University of Illinois and Toyota engineers pulls carbon dioxide straight out of open air using electricity instead of heat. A new battery-like device can now pull carbon dioxide straight out of the air. Engineers built it by borrowing tricks from rechargeable battery technology. The approach could make direct air capture cheaper and easier to scale. Researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign built the device with Toyota. Their findings appear in the journal Environmental Science & Technology. The team says its method could outperform existing direct air capture (DAC) systems. Mechanical engineering professor Kyle Smith led the Illinois side of the project. Graduate students Paul Rozzi and JeongA Lee also contributed to the design and testing. Toyota researchers Chip Roberts and Tim Arthur rounded out the collaborative team. Cutting emissions alone likely will not meet global climate targets. Scientists say some carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere must also be removed. Doing it directly from open air, though, remains technically difficult and costly. Fossil fuel use keeps climbing worldwide, even as renewable energy expands rapidly. That trend makes atmospheric carbon removal an increasingly urgent complement to emissions cuts. A cheaper battery-like device could help close that gap faster. Most carbon capture technology targets concentrated sources like factory smokestacks. Open air contains far less carbon dioxide per breath than smokestack exhaust. Current DAC systems rely on giant fans and costly materials to make up the difference. Smith and his colleagues describe this diluted atmospheric carbon as a legacy problem. Decades of past emissions remain mixed into the air at very low concentrations. Addressing that backlog requires tools built specifically for open-air conditions, not smokestacks. Battery-like technology designed for open-air conditions rather than factory smokestacks addresses what researchers call a legacy problem, targeting the decades of past emissions now diluted across the atmosphere at concentrations too low for conventional direct air capture systems to handle cost-effectively. Photo by Nikita Belokhonov on Pexels. Those materials also need heating once they have soaked up enough carbon dioxide. That step releases the gas for storage or reuse elsewhere. Heating adds significant energy costs to the whole process. The new battery-like technology skips heat altogether. It relies on an electrochemical cell built from specialized manganese dioxide electrodes. A saltwater solution flows through the cell during operation. Running current in one direction makes the solution more alkaline. That alkaline solution readily absorbs carbon dioxide from the surrounding air. Reversing the current makes the solution less alkaline, releasing pure carbon dioxide for capture. This alkaline shift allows carbon dioxide to dissolve far more readily than in neutral water. Researchers describe the setup as a cation-compensated cell built around proton-intercalation electrodes. That design keeps the whole cycle reversible, much like charging and discharging a battery. Similar electrode materials already appear in some rechargeable battery designs. Applying that same chemistry to carbon capture is part of what makes this approach unusual. It also helps explain why the team compares the device’s operation to a battery. Early lab results already look encouraging for the new method. Researchers still need to prevent the device’s two liquid streams from mixing. Solving that problem should improve both energy use and overall capture efficiency. Toyota Motor North America helped fund the research alongside university grants. The University of Illinois has filed patent applications, with Toyota holding joint rights. Toyota describes the work as part of its broader push toward long-term decarbonization. Additional support came from the university’s Campus Research Board and Grainger College of Engineering. That mix of industry and academic funding is common for early-stage climate technology. Researchers say continued support will be needed to move the device beyond the lab. Full details of the study appear in a University of Illinois news release describing the project. Battery-like technology like this one add a new option to a still-young field. Some direct air capture methods use heat, while others use chemical filters instead. Electricity-driven designs like this one could offer a cheaper path toward pulling old carbon back out of the sky. Wider testing outside the lab will show whether that promise holds up at scale. For now, the results mark a hopeful early step for a technology the world will likely need. The post Battery-Like Technology Offers a New Path for Capturing Carbon Dioxide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: O ne weekend, a canvasser — let’s call her Cindy — was out door-knocking and found a gentleman at home. After establishing that he’d heard of gender transition surgeries for minors, a topic that’s become a major focal point across the U.S. in the run-up to the midterm elections, Cindy asked him where on a scale of zero to 10 his views were, where zero meant he was against banning procedures for minors and 10 meant he was in favor of the ban. “I’d be about an eight,” said the man. Let’s call him Ethan. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “About an Eight” Then ensued an open-hearted conversation during which Ethan admitted he thinks minors don’t always know what’s best and Cindy divulged that she is transgender. She went on to share her experience of how she had come to recognize she was trans — how she had felt like she was wearing a costume that didn’t fit. “I actually like clothes now, which is crazy,” she said. “Now I get to just pick something that’s me.” “Good!” Ethan replied. “That’s good.” Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “A Costume That Didn’t Fit” Only towards the end of their conversation did they get back to the ballot measure. Cindy explained that gender-affirming care for minors typically follows a multi-stage, developmentally-paced model, starting with visits to doctors and counselors with family in tow, and then “social transition,” where individuals change their name and pronouns. Personal storytelling and active listening, rather than debate, are at the heart of deep canvassing. Credit: JJ Lane / Be Lovely Photography Only then can they start taking puberty pausing medication, which is reversible, and after a couple years of that, usually from the age of 18, they can begin taking hormones to go through the puberty that aligns with how they want to live their life. “I wish that I had been able to access this kind of care when I was younger,” Cindy said. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “I Only Have One Go-Around” At this point, she asked Ethan where he would now put himself on the scale they’d discussed at the start. “I’d probably be more like a three,” Ethan said. “Boy, you gonna have me thinking the rest of the day. I probably won’t sleep tonight!” Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “About a Three” Cindy and Ethan, canvasser and voter, are engaged in what’s known as deep canvassing, a technique of going door-to-door where the canvasser does more listening than talking. The idea is to have an open-minded, non-judgmental conversation about a hot-button issue, be it abortion, trans rights or mass deportations, and have the canvasser share their own vulnerabilities while asking questions about the voter’s life. The hope is to connect on an emotional level and find out what’s really going on for folks. The post The Door-to-Door Technique That Actually Changes Minds appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Come winter, a typical Bengali turns romantic about nolen gur. This fresh jaggery is made from the sap of the wild date palm (Phoenix sylvestris) and is usually available from mid-November to February. The love comes in many versions. There is liquid jaggery, warm and fragrant . There are chhanagolla (cottage cheese balls) shaped in the freshest gur. If we are feeling indulgent, there is a thin, flaky paratha to go with a bowl of jhola (nolen) gur. For all that, I would still choose a crisp slice of toast with nolen gur. Literature romanticised it too. In Bhalo Rey Bhalo, the pioneering Bengali writer and poet Sukumar Ray celebrates life's many pleasures, from the fragrance of flowers to the cottony blooms of the shimul tree. Few of them, he suggests, can rival eating nolen gur with bread. It belongs as much to memory as to the kitchen. But it has a constraint that sugar and many other sweeteners do not. It can only be made when the weather, the tree and the sap align. That gives Bengal a short winter window to make the most of it. Why the window is so short The window is set by temperature, the chemistry of the sap, and how quickly it can be harvested and processed before it ferments. Fermentation is the clock. Fresh palm sap contains fermentable sugars, which microorganisms can begin converting into alcohol and organic acids. As fermentation progresses, the sap's acidity, sweetness and other properties change, and so does its suitability for jaggery-making . A 1988 study by T R Shamala and K R Sreekantiah, published in Food Microbiology, identified yeasts, including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and several types of bacteria in freshly tapped wild date-palm sap. The researchers documented changes in microbial growth and in the production of ethanol, acids and esters during fermentation. Their findings help explain why freshly collected sap cannot be left standing for long before processing. Cooler winter conditions help slow fermentation, giving tappers a better chance of collecting usable sap. Photograph: (Indrajit Lahiri/moha-mushkil) Cold buys time. Cooler winter conditions slow fermentation and give tappers a better chance of collecting usable sap. Once the weather warms, that window becomes harder to manage. The sap must be brought down early and processed promptly to preserve the qualities nolen gur needs. Even within winter, the sap keeps changing. A 2015 study in the Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences looked at this in Bengal itself. Dipak Girhepuje, S Mondal and P K Bandopadhyay of Bidhan Chandra Krishi Viswavidyalaya examined sap from 15-to-20-year-old trees in Haringhata block, Nadia district. They took separate samples between December and February across two seasons, 2012–13 and 2013–14. Their findings: Total soluble solids, which indicate the concentration of dissolved substances, reached 14.33% in February. Total sugar rose from 11.37% in December to 12.50% in February. The sugar-to-acid ratio fell sharply, from 325.47 in January to 42.93 in February. Vitamin C declined from 18.75 mg per 100 ml in December to 13.75 mg in February. Alcohol content was highest in February. So the sap does not stay chemically identical through winter. Its properties shift even within the traditional harvesting period. How nolen gur is made Before Kolkata's sweet shops fill their trays with nolen gur sandesh, and before we get the first taste, a lot happens in villages across Bankura, Birbhum, Jhargram and Khejuri (Purba Medinipur). The night a tree fills a pot. The process begins with the khejur gaach, or date palm. Traditional tappers, known as shiuli or siuli, make a controlled incision in the tree and fit a small bamboo channel to guide the sap into an earthen pot. The pot hangs overnight and collects the liquid that flows from the cut. In the hours before dawn, the tapper returns to the tree he climbed the previous evening and lowers the pot. The timing is essential, for the reasons above. When the sap meets the fire. Freshly collected sap is not yet jaggery. It is filtered and heated in large pans so that water evaporates and the sugars concentrate. As the liquid thickens, its colour, viscosity and flavour change. The result may be jhola gur, a pourable jaggery, or patali gur, the solid variety used in sweets. For sweet-makers, the quality of the finished jaggery depends on both the sap they receive and how carefully it is processed. Photograph: (Sabyasachi/foodaholix) A 2009 study in the Journal of Food Engineering examined this transformation. P V K Jagannadha Rao, Madhusweta Das and S K Das studied how boiling changes the physical properties of sugarcane, palmyra-palm and date-palm juices. As dissolved solids increased, the juices became more viscous and their boiling temperatures rose. For date-palm juice, the changes were particularly pronounced in the final stage of concentration. For sweet-makers, this means the quality of the finished jaggery depends on both the sap they receive and how carefully it is processed. More than a seasonal sweet Nolen gur connects Bengal's winter landscape to its food traditions and rural livelihoods. It gives pithe, payesh and sandesh their seasonal character. It also supports the people whose knowledge of trees, tapping and boiling makes it possible. That dependence on winter has consequences. As warmer weather threatens to shorten the tapping season, producers face declining yields, and sweet-makers face uncertain supplies of an ingredient central to the winter table. A shorter winter can mean fewer litres of sap, less jaggery to sell and a smaller income from months of specialised work. Preserving nolen gur therefore means looking beyond the sweet shops. It means understanding how changing temperatures affect the date palm's harvesting cycle, documenting changes in sap yields over time, and supporting the tappers whose livelihoods rest on a narrow winter window. As climate change reshapes seasonal patterns, the challenge is to safeguard the ecological conditions and traditional knowledge that make nolen gur possible. Sources: 'Microbiological and biochemical studies on traditional Indian palm wine fermentation' : By T.R Shamala, K.R Sreekantiah, Published on 20 October 2004 'Changes in physico-chemical properties of wild date palm (Phoenix sylvestris) sap over its peak production period' : Dipak Girhepuje, S Mondal and P K Bandopadhyay, Published on 8 July 2015 'Bhalo re Bhalo' : Sukumar Ray

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Soil Literacy Education Gets a Hands-On Makeover in Europe Reading Time: 3 minutes A European Union-funded initiative is expanding soil literacy education across 10 countries, helping students and citizens reconnect with the ground beneath their feet. Soil literacy education is taking root across Europe through a project called CURIOSOIL. The initiative teaches students, teachers, and everyday citizens why healthy soil matters. It launched in February 2024 and runs for four years, making it a long-term priority rather than a one-time campaign. CURIOSOIL is funded by the European Union and led by the University of Aveiro in Portugal. Fourteen partner organizations from 10 countries work together on the project. Their combined expertise spans natural science, education, and social science, giving the literacy education effort a wide research base to draw from. The project responds to a real gap. Many people never learn how soil supports food, water, and climate systems. CURIOSOIL calls this gap soil illiteracy and treats it as a barrier to protecting land for the future, which is exactly why soil literacy sits at the center of its mission. To close that gap, the team builds education tools for different age groups. These include curriculum materials for primary and secondary schools. Teachers also receive dedicated training programs so they can bring soil science into their own classrooms. The project also produces Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) for both higher education and primary and secondary teachers. It offers online challenges and micro-credential modules for university students. Guidelines for blended and remote learning round out the soil literacy education toolkit for educators who teach outside a traditional classroom. One tool is the Soil Curiosity Kit, a hands-on activity set for classrooms, gardens, and community spaces. Another is the World Soil Museum, an app that lets users explore soil types from their phone. A guiding character named Petra leads younger students through these lessons. CURIOSOIL also runs hackathons and art competitions called Artathons. These events invite students to reimagine soil health through design and technology. Winning ideas get shared across the project’s full partner network, extending the reach of soil literacy education beyond the schools that first tested it. This approach turns soil science into something creative rather than abstract. A student who builds an app about soil health understands the topic differently than one who only reads about it. That hands-on shift is central to how the project measures its success. CURIOSOIL extends soil literacy education beyond the textbook through hackathons and Artathons that challenge students to reimagine soil health through design and technology, with winning ideas shared across the project’s full 10-country network. Photo by Anna Shvets on Pexels. Beyond classrooms, CURIOSOIL works to influence policy. The team has already published a report analyzing soil education policies across Europe. It plans 15 additional national policy briefs, along with a final EU-wide brief containing recommendations for lawmakers on how to fund and scale the campaign. The project also built a Community of Practice, a network of educators and specialists who share soil teaching methods. Anyone working in soil education can join, whether they teach at a university or run a school garden program. The network exists so good ideas in soil literacy education spread, rather than staying isolated in one classroom or country. CURIOSOIL sits within the EU Mission Soil, a larger initiative to protect European soils by 2030. It coordinates with several sister projects tackling related soil health goals. Together, these efforts aim to reach farmers, students, and policymakers with consistent, science-based messaging. The scale of the challenge is worth noting. Europe has millions of students who could benefit from stronger soil literacy education, yet few schools currently teach the subject in depth. Closing even part of that gap could shift how an entire generation treats farmland, gardens, and green spaces. CURIOSOIL marked its latest milestone at the Soils for Europe Conference, held in Coimbra, Portugal, from September 7 to 11, 2026. The event brought together dozens of EU-funded soil projects to share results and plan next steps under the banner “Healthy Soils for a Sustainable Future,” with sessions spanning soil degradation, organic carbon stocks, biodiversity, and citizen engagement. The gathering reflected the project’s broader goal of connecting research with real classrooms, not just policy papers. Soil rarely gets the attention it deserves, despite holding the nutrients that grow the world’s food . Projects like CURIOSOIL are working to change that one lesson at a time. As more schools and communities invest in soil literacy education, that quiet resource under our feet may finally get the recognition it has always needed. The post Soil Literacy Education Gets a Hands-On Makeover in Europe appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When Liam Heneghan became a grandfather, he made a quiet promise: to be fully present in his granddaughter's life. Unlike his years as a busy father, when work and responsibilities often had pulled him away, he now devotes two full days each week to caring for his granddaughter, sharing in the ordinary rhythms of childhood. A Dublin-born ecologist, Heneghan finds himself rediscovering the natural world through her eyes -- from the wonder of a passing bird to the simple delight of exploring outdoors. Along the way, he's discovered that grandparenting offers something unexpected: a chance not only to give love, patience, and attention, but to receive the gift of seeing life anew. His story is a tender reminder that the most meaningful thing we can offer another person may be our time, freely and wholeheartedly given.

items.descriptionOriginal: By day, Vimal Kishore runs a small coffee stall in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. By night, he puts his earnings into something he has pursued for years: building machines that solve everyday problems. His latest creation is Lailo, a car he built for Rs 90,000 using parts from a scooter. Equipped with solar power, GPS and a rear-view camera, the vehicle grew out of his own need to travel independently. By running a coffee stall in Prayagraj, Vimal funds his experiments and turns everyday challenges into inventions. For Vimal, who lives with a disability affecting his legs, building a car was not just about creating a machine. It was about finding a way to drive despite the physical limitations that prevented him from using a conventional vehicle. When he decided to build his own car Vimal's journey began much earlier. When he was just eight months old, a severe fever affected his legs. Growing up, he watched other children walk, run and play, activities he could not participate in the same way. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) He eventually turned to understanding how things worked. Taking objects apart and putting them back together became a way to explore his curiosity and find better ways of doing things. In 2011, Vimal bought an Alto, hoping it would give him greater independence. However, his disability made it impossible for him to drive the car. Instead of giving up on the idea of travelling independently, he decided to build a vehicle of his own. Building a car without an engineering team Vimal began by drawing his design on paper and sourcing parts from discarded Ambassador cars. Working without a laboratory or a team of engineers, he put his ideas into practice with the resources available to him. The result was Lailo, a vehicle assembled using scooter parts and built at a cost of Rs 90,000. Its solar-powered system, GPS and rear-view camera add practical features to the design. Equipped with solar power, GPS and a rear-view camera, Lailo is Vimal's answer to a problem he faced himself. His coffee stall continues to fund his experiments. Every morning, he opens the counter to earn a living, while the money he saves goes towards researching and building new inventions. From scrap materials to miniature machines Lailo is only one part of Vimal's work. He has also made a power bank from scrap materials and a cooler using a discarded drum. Among his other creations is a working charkha measuring just 2.5 cm, which received recognition as a world record. His inventions have earned him wider recognition over the years, including an award from former President Dr APJ Abdul Kalam. Vimal's inventive spirit has earned him several accolades, including an award from former President Dr APJ Abdul Kalam. Despite these achievements, Vimal continues to run his coffee stall while pursuing his experiments. His work begins with problems he encounters in everyday life and the materials he can afford to access. Whether it is a vehicle that helps him travel independently or a machine assembled from discarded objects, he continues to find ways to turn limited resources into working solutions.

items.titleOriginal: How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Την τελευταία φορά που μια ομάδα ολοκλήρωσε μια παρόμοια διέλευση του εσωτερικού της Ανταρκτικής, έκαψε περίπου 170.000 λίτρα (περίπου 45.000 γαλόνια) καυσίμου για να το κάνει. Η αποστολή Wind Sled που έφυγε από την Ισπανία στις 18 Οκτωβρίου σχεδιάζει να μην χρησιμοποιήσει κανένα. Ο Ισπανός πολικός εξερευνητής Ramón Larramendi οδηγεί τέσσερα άτομα σε 3.400…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The last time a team completed a comparable crossing of Antarctica’s interior, they burned through roughly 170,000 liters (about 45,000 gallons) of fuel to do it. The Wind Sled expedition that left Spain on October 18 plans to use none. Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi is leading four people across 3,400 kilometers (about 2,100 miles) of Antarctic interior on a kite-powered platform he has been designing for 25 years, with 16 research projects running the entire way. The vehicle runs on wind and solar energy , meaning no combustion engine at all. Twenty-five years of design, rooted in Inuit tradition Larramendi has spent 25 years developing the Wind Sled and has logged more than 28,000 kilometers (about 17,400 miles) across ice on earlier expeditions while refining it. The platform is built on Inuit sled-building techniques, which is an unusual starting point for a cutting-edge scientific research vehicle, and Larramendi doesn’t try to make it sound otherwise. “The wind sled is something completely unique in the world,” he says. “This sled combines Inuit techniques, which can look like old-fashioned and slightly strange bits of technology. That makes it a very, very unusual mix, but hugely efficient.” The sled is 15 meters (about 49 feet) long across four modules, capable of carrying up to 2,100 kilograms (about 4,600 pounds). This expedition is running lighter, around 250 kilograms (about 550 pounds) of instruments. The crew has 20 kites ranging from five to 150 square meters (about 54 to 1,615 square feet) in sail area, swapped out as conditions change. The sled can hit 80 kilometers per hour (about 50 miles per hour) in a strong wind; average cruising speed is around 25 (about 15 miles per hour). Sixteen research projects in terrain that rarely gets visited The route goes from Russia’s Novolazarevskaya base in Queen Maud Land, through the Pole of Inaccessibility and near the Pole of Cold, finishing at the Concordia research station at Dome C. Five scientific stations will be established along the way. The 16 projects were selected by Spain’s polar research committee, with collaborators including NASA’s Ames Research Center , six Spanish universities, and several national research bodies. One of the NASA projects is asking whether salt rocks sitting on Antarctica’s surface could harbor microbial life. Sensors embedded in the rocks will measure temperature, humidity, and electrical conductivity to determine whether liquid water could form inside them despite conditions that make that seem impossible. It’s the kind of question that sounds like astrobiology because it basically is. The Dinglac project will use ground-penetrating radar to map the top 10 meters (about 33 feet) of snow to track how ice layers accumulate and shift. The campaign will also sample for microplastics and chemical pollutants, test for microorganisms and viruses, and run assessments of the European Galileo navigation system . The location makes all of it harder to get any other way. Satellites and permanent stations have limited reach into this interior. “It is taking place in an area for which there are practically no data,” Larramendi says. The crew are their own experiment All four team members are Antarctic veterans: Larramendi; Hilo Moreno , a polar guide and mountain technician; Mariusz Potocki , a researcher at the University of Maine; and Javier Selva , a documentary filmmaker who crossed Antarctica with Larramendi in 2011-2012. They’re also research subjects. The WindSled Mind project, led by Gabriel G. de la Torre of the University of Cádiz, will monitor the team’s psychological responses, sleep, and social dynamics across the 85 days. The data is meant to inform planning for long-duration space missions, where small crews face confinement and extreme isolation from Earth, conditions the interior of Antarctica replicates about as well as anywhere. “We are the experiment ourselves,” Larramendi says. “Four people isolated for 85 days in the interior of the Antarctic continent.” A route designed to be repeated The point isn’t just to complete this crossing. Each return trip lets researchers compare data across seasons to track real changes in ice, climate, and polar ecosystems over time. “Repeated data collection is absolutely key to tracking variations,” Larramendi says. When the team arrives at Concordia, they’ll fly out and leave the sled dismantled at the station, ready for the return journey. The fuel comparison says most of what needs saying: the last comparable crossing burned through about 45,000 gallons. This one runs on kites and a design that’s been in development since the 1990s, and when it’s done, the plan is to come back. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Κάνετε τα πάντα σωστά την ώρα του ύπνου: μένετε μακριά από τις οθόνες μετά τις εννιά, κάνετε ένα χαλαρωτικό σκοτεινό ντους, πίνετε ένα δροσερό τσάι από βότανα στο κομοδίνο και διατηρείτε ένα αρκετά σταθερό πρόγραμμα ύπνου. Ωστόσο, μερικές νύχτες το ταβάνι εξακολουθεί να έχει την πλήρη προσοχή σας μετά τα μεσάνυχτα και δεν μπορείτε να το καταλάβετε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You’re doing everything right at bedtime: you stay away from screens after nine, take a soothing dark shower , sip on that herbal tea cooling on the nightstand, and maintain a reasonably consistent sleep schedule. Yet some nights the ceiling still has your full attention past midnight, and you can’t quite figure out why. If you’ve been treating sleep as mostly a habits problem, a recent nutritional review suggests there’s a variable you might be overlooking: what you eat in the evening. The review, published in the journal Nutrients , made the case for pistachios as a bedtime snack, and the reasoning holds up better than most food-and-sleep claims do. There’s no single magic compound, but what’s unusual is that one ounce of pistachios stacks five separate sleep-relevant nutrients at once, each arriving via a different route. That’s a rare combination to find in a single snack. Why diet is an underused sleep lever Most sleep advice focuses on behavior such as consistent wake times, a cool and dark room, or no caffeine past the early afternoon. Diet gets surprisingly little attention, even though a lot of research connects eating patterns to how well people sleep. People who follow the Mediterranean or DASH diets tend to sleep better, and both lean on nuts and legumes. That link pushed researchers to look more closely at which nutrients might be responsible. With pistachios, there turned out to be several working at the same time. Vitamin B6, tryptophan, and the sleep hormone chain One ounce of pistachios provides close to 40 percent of your daily vitamin B6, more than any other tree nut. This is noteworthy because B6 is what your body uses to turn tryptophan into serotonin, and serotonin is the raw material for melatonin. B6 also helps produce GABA, the neurotransmitter that tells your nervous system to settle down at night. The same one-ounce serving contains about 71 milligrams of tryptophan. In a survey of more than 11,000 Spanish university students, higher tryptophan intake was tied to longer sleep and a lower likelihood of insomnia. In a separate trial , adults between 55 and 75 who ate tryptophan-enriched cereal for a week fell asleep faster, slept longer, and produced more melatonin than those eating standard cereal. Plant-made melatonin, found in the nut itself Plants make their own melatonin, called phytomelatonin, and it has nothing to do with the melatonin your body makes from tryptophan. One analysis of American pistachios found roughly 18.7 micrograms per serving, which puts them in the same range as tart cherry and tomato, two foods with a reasonable body of sleep research behind them. Other analyses have found lower amounts, so the exact number varies, but phytomelatonin shows up in pistachios consistently. Magnesium, fiber, and the gut Magnesium supports melatonin production and plays a role in deep sleep through GABA activity. Pistachios have about 31 milligrams per ounce, around 10 percent of the recommended daily amount. Almonds have more (76 milligrams in the same serving), but every bit adds up. The CARDIA study , which tracked a large group of young adults over many years, found that those with the highest magnesium intake slept better and were less likely to get fewer than seven hours a night. A one-ounce serving of pistachios also covers about 11 percent of your daily fiber. Gut bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids like butyrate, which have been linked to sleep quality. In a lab comparison of common nuts, pistachios produced the most of these compounds. They also rank second among tree nuts in polyphenols, and a recent meta-analysis found polyphenol supplements helped people with sleep disorders fall asleep faster and sleep longer, though most of those trials used extracts rather than whole foods. The clinical trials that haven’t happened yet No study has directly tested whether eating pistachios helps people sleep better. The review draws a reasonable line through a lot of supporting research, but connecting individual nutrient mechanisms to actual sleep outcomes still requires human trials that don’t exist yet. It’s also important to note that the review was partially funded by American Pistachio Growers . If you already snack in the evening, a small handful of pistachios, around 28 grams, is an easy substitution to run for a week. The usual sleep hygiene advice still stands, and matters more than any snack. But if you’ve already worked through that list and you’re still not sleeping well, what you eat before bed is a reasonable next thing to look at. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Here’s what the sleep research says first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Creating a More Sustainable Workplace Reading Time: 3 minutes Sustainability has moved from being a nice extra to something many businesses are expected to think about as part of everyday operations. Sustainability has moved from being a nice extra to something many businesses are expected to think about as part of everyday operations. Customers, employees and clients are increasingly interested in how organisations manage energy, waste and travel, but creating a greener workplace doesn’t necessarily require a dramatic redesign or a huge environmental budget. The good news is that creating a greener workplace does not always require major investment. Often, the most effective changes are simple adjustments that reduce environmental impact while improving day-to-day operations. The workspace itself can play a big part. For some businesses, this could mean looking at how they use their office space, while others are reducing unnecessary travel and allowing their staff to work from home and only meeting face-to-face for genuine reasons. Those trying to reduce travel emissions find that some cities offer flexible office space, like Leeds . These coworking and flexible office options can reduce the need for employees to travel into a permanent office every day when face-to-face collaboration is only required occasionally. Businesses that require regular in-person collaboration are increasingly choosing locations with strong public transport connections. This can help reduce reliance on car travel and make lower-carbon commuting a practical choice for more employees. Make Energy Efficiency an Everyday Habit Energy efficiency sounds like a major infrastructure project, but plenty of improvements begin with ordinary workplace habits. Lights left on in empty meeting rooms, computers running overnight and heating operating when nobody is in the building all represent avoidable energy use. Reducing energy use can lower operating costs while also helping organisations cut the emissions associated with powering their workplace. Motion-sensitive lighting, sensible heating controls and making sure equipment is switched off when it isn’t required can make an immediate difference. Businesses can also look at practical ways to reduce workplace energy consumption , including reviewing heating schedules, monitoring usage and considering smarter controls. Make Greener Commuting Easier Supporting cycling, walking and public transport can be as simple as providing secure bike storage, showers or clearer information about nearby transport connections. Flexible and hybrid working can help too. Fewer commuting journeys can also help lower transport-related carbon emissions, making hybrid working beneficial for both employees and the environment. If employees don’t need to be physically present every day, reducing unnecessary journeys may be more practical than expecting everyone to commute simply because that’s how the working week has traditionally been structured. The key is making greener choices convenient. People are far more likely to change their habits when the alternative actually works for their lives. Reduce Waste Without Making Work More Complicated Sustainability initiatives tend to lose momentum when they create additional hassle. Waste reduction works best when the greener option is also the easiest one. Moving routine documents online can reduce unnecessary printing, while clearly labelled recycling points make it easier for employees to dispose of things correctly. Reviewing purchasing habits can help as well. Ordering fewer disposable supplies, reusing equipment where possible and resisting the temptation to replace perfectly serviceable office furniture all add up. Get the Team Involved Finally, no workplace sustainability plan will get very far if it exists only in a policy document nobody reads. Employees need to understand what the organisation is trying to achieve and, ideally, feel that they have some ownership of it. That might mean creating small team targets, inviting staff to suggest improvements or simply making recycling, energy saving and sustainable travel part of everyday workplace conversations. Progress doesn’t need to be turned into a competition, but sharing the results can help people see that individual actions genuinely add up. Over time, small changes to energy use, commuting habits and waste management can reduce a workplace’s environmental impact while supporting wider sustainability goals. The post Creating a More Sustainable Workplace appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Cloud Technology Can Support Business Sustainability Goals Reading Time: 2 minutes Businesses across the UK are facing more and more pressure to reduce their environmental impact while maintaining operational efficiency. Both customers and investors are paying closer attention to sustainability commitments, and many organisations are being encouraged to look for practical ways to make a real impact with long-term environmental goals. While most initiatives often focus on transport , energy use and supply chains, technology decisions also play an important role. Many organisations are now reviewing how their IT infrastructure contributes to their wider sustainability strategy. By adopting scalable digital solutions and working with providers that offer Managed Cloud services for improved efficiency and resource management , businesses can reduce unnecessary energy consumption while maintaining the performance and flexibility needed to support growth. Reducing reliance on energy-intensive on-site infrastructure Traditional on-site IT infrastructure can require significant resources to operate and maintain. Physical servers consume electricity around the clock and often require dedicated cooling systems to prevent overheating. As equipment ages, performance can decline, leading to increased maintenance demands and higher operating costs. Moving workloads into efficiently managed cloud environments can help reduce the energy demands associated with maintaining multiple on-site servers. For example, your business may replace ageing server equipment with cloud-hosted applications and storage solutions rather than investing in additional physical infrastructure. Supporting flexible and remote working Cloud technology has transformed the way employees access business systems and collaborate with colleagues. Staff can securely access files and data from different locations, whether they are working from home or visiting client sites. This flexibility can support your objectives by reducing the need for daily commuting and frequent business travel. For example, team members can collaborate on projects remotely using cloud-based platforms. Alongside environmental benefits, flexible access can improve employee satisfaction and help organisations attract and retain talent. Businesses that support remote working and secure access to business systems can often create a more agile, environmentally friendly operating model. Making better use of business resources Another advantage of cloud technology is scalability. Unlike traditional infrastructure , businesses do not need to purchase large amounts of hardware in anticipation of future demand. Instead, you can increase or decrease capacity as requirements change. For example, a retailer may temporarily increase storage or computing resources during a busy trading period without investing in additional physical equipment that may sit unused for much of the year. This approach helps reduce waste and prevents overinvestment. Improving monitoring and reporting Accurate data is essential for sustainability targets. Cloud-based platforms often provide advanced reporting and monitoring capabilities that can help you gain better visibility into your operations. You could use cloud-based dashboards to analyse performance metrics and identify inefficiencies across different departments or locations. This information can support more informed decision-making and help businesses prioritise areas for improvement. Better access to data can also assist with reporting, making it easier to measure progress against environmental goals and demonstrate accountability to stakeholders. To summarise… While sustainability requires a broad business commitment, being fully sustainable for many businesses is not something that can be achieved quickly. Cloud adoption can be an important step towards reducing resource consumption, improving operational efficiency and supporting long-term environmental goals. The post How Cloud Technology Can Support Business Sustainability Goals appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim Reading Time: 3 minutes Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim According to a study published in Patient Safety and highlighted by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), diagnostic errors accounted for 26.6% of closed medical malpractice claims reviewed over a 20-year period. Among all claims related to the diagnoses, 39% were fatal. Misdiagnosis and delay in diagnoses were the most often made claims. Medical malpractices have severe implications for patients, which may range from delays in treatment to deterioration of medical conditions or even disability and death. In the USA, one is entitled to filing medical malpractice if a healthcare professional fails to adhere to the acceptable level of care, resulting in preventable harm. There are actually more malpractice cases that happen in the healthcare industry than people realize. But it’s also important to understand that not all unfavorable medical outcomes qualify as malpractice. A claim will require evidence of negligence and resulting injury. But what is an example of malpractice ? Let’s take a closer look at the common medical errors and what steps you need to take to seek a possible claim. Diagnosis Is Where Most of It Happens In the AHRQ systematic review of ED care, the rate of diagnostic errors was found to be 5.7% with an extrapolated estimate of 7.4 million diagnostic errors and 371,000 severe harms per year associated with diagnostic errors. These overall rates were based on results from three prospective studies conducted outside of the U.S. in Canada, Spain, and Switzerland. AHRQ commissioned an independent review after its publication because of the high numbers that were cited. This is an order of magnitude, not a number count. Rates of disease-specific errors have higher validity. On average, physicians fail to diagnose stroke in about 17% of patients. The list is completed by myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, spinal cord compression, and venous thromboembolism. These conditions share a profile. They present atypically often enough that a physician working quickly can reach the wrong conclusion. The Procedure Itself Surgical and anesthesia errors sit at the opposite end of the evidentiary range. Wrong-site surgery. A retained sponge. An anesthesia dosing failure during a routine case. Proof of breach in wrong-site and retained object surgeries is seldom disputed since there is evidence of negligence in the records. Firms handling this work tend to sort it by mechanism rather than by specialty. Medical malpractice lawyers in Marietta, GA , separate birth injuries such as cerebral palsy, brachial plexus injury, and hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy from anesthesia errors, emergency room errors, and surgical errors. Medication Errors More defendants get implicated in medication cases than any other type. A prescriber orders a prescription, a pharmacist dispenses the prescription, a nurse delivers the prescription, and the electronic health record alerts for a possible drug interaction or not. Wrong dosage, lack of allergy information, and drugs with similar appearances on the screen cause claims. Each individual has his own employer and his own insurance. Birth Injuries Obstetric negligence claims hinge more on timing than anything else. Whether or not someone interpreted the fetal monitoring properly. How quickly the decision was made to utilize the C-section procedure. Whether or not the procedures used were appropriate for shoulder dystocia. These cases require more time than adult claims. In fact, some states also set a separate limitations period for minors in malpractice cases that ends well before adulthood. What Turns an Error Into a Claim Expert testimony does most of the work. A plaintiff cannot establish the standard of care without a qualified physician stating what it was. A number of states, including Georgia, require a sworn expert affidavit filed alongside the complaint. That single requirement can end a case before anyone takes a deposition. Damage caps are the other structural variable. It’s important to understand, though, that these caps could shift. The non-economic damage cap in California remained unchanged at $250,000 for decades before AB 35 changed it to $350,000 for cases other than death. It is at $500,000 for wrongful death starting from 2023, increasing by $40,000 and $50,000, respectively, each year for ten years. The distance between a medical error and a malpractice claim is mostly documentary. Whether the chart recorded the symptom the patient actually reported. Whether the monitoring strip survived. Whether anybody wrote down a time. Errors are common and claims are not, and most of what fills the space between those two facts is records that either exist or do not. items.descriptionOriginal: First, the good news: The world might be a lot closer than we think to an international goal of protecting 30% of land by 2030. The bad news: It’s probably not all the right land. The nations of the world have placed protections on roughly 27% of the planet’s land masses, far more than the 19% previously thought, according to research recently published in Nature . There has been much hand wringing among conservation-minded folks that countries were woefully behind on land protection pledges made in 2022 to shield 30% of Earth’s land and 30% of the ocean from development as part of an update to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the main international agreement aimed at the current extinction crisis. But “our analysis suggests that much more of the land is in some type of conservation area than currently recognized,” said lead author Helen O’Neill, a postdoctoral researcher at the United Kingdom’s Institute of Zoology, London. The official tally tracking protected lands is a database at the Protected Planet website , a collaboration between the United Nations and the International Union for Conservation of Nature. While this is the authoritative source, it’s incomplete. Some protected land hasn’t been registered there by countries. And it doesn’t include significant acreage that falls into a kind of gray area – land that isn’t formally protected chiefly for wildlife, but where regulations provide many of the same benefits. Known as “other effective area-based conservation measures” or OECMs, this might include land protected as sacred by Indigenous groups or managed to improve water quality. O’Neill and 35 other scientists from across the globe set out to tally this overlooked land to create a more complete picture. To reduce the massive effort required to scrutinize the status of every piece of land on the planet, the researcher selected pieces totaling 10% of all the world’s land masses. That included terrain scattered across the world and covering major types of ecosystems, from the Rocky Mountains in Montana to the Amazonian jungle to the desert of the Arabian Peninsula. .IRPP_ruby cropland in protected areas than we might think For each piece of land, they added up how much was listed as protected under the global database, as well as national records and conservation areas where regulations and management practices made them good candidates for being OECMs. The scientists used the results to create a computer model that estimated how this pattern would apply to the entire world. The result was the encouraging estimate that 26.8% of all land is protected, at least on paper. But that doesn’t mean conservationists can cruise across the 2030 finish line with their arms raised. Because the research also revealed troubling holes in where these lands are being conserved. Of the 173 different ecological regions scientists have mapped around the world, fewer than 100 have greater than 17% of their land protected, the scientists estimated. Regions that are primarily ice and rock – polar and alpine landscapes – are significantly overrepresented in the catalog of protected areas. That’s not a big surprise, since those regions are often less attractive for human settlement or exploitation by farming or other activities. By contrast, deserts, woodlands, grasslands and temperate forests all fall below the 30% target. Then there is the question of whether land that’s conserved on paper is really being protected . The new research points to the potential gains that can be made, particularly with the recognition of the conservation potential of these OECMs. But “conserving 30% of land and seas is not sufficient on its own,” said Heather Bingham, a co-author who heads the Protected Planet Initiative. “The target also calls for these areas to be managed effectively for positive biodiversity outcomes, and to be placed where they will have the greatest impact on biodiversity.” O’Neill, et. al. “ Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates .” Nature.
