items.title: Η καινοτόμος προσέγγιση του Ocean Cleanup
items.titleOriginal: The innovative approach of Ocean Cleanup
items.description: Happy Eco News Η καινοτόμος προσέγγιση του Ocean Cleanup Χρόνος ανάγνωσης: 4 λεπτά Από την ερώτηση ενός Ολλανδού εφήβου το 2013 έως την αφαίρεση 50 εκατομμυρίων κιλών συντριμμιών, το Ocean Cleanup αποδεικνύει ότι η εφευρετικότητα μπορεί ακόμα να αντιμετωπίσει ένα από τα πιο συντριπτικά προβλήματα του ωκεανού. Οι ωκεανοί μας καλύπτουν το 71% της επιφάνειας του πλανήτη, βυθίζοντας σχεδόν 11.000 μέτρα…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The innovative approach of Ocean Cleanup Reading Time: 4 minutes From a Dutch teenager’s question in 2013 to 50 million kilograms of debris removed, Ocean Cleanup proves ingenuity can still tackle one of the ocean’s most overwhelming problems. Our oceans cover 71% of the planet’s surface, plunging down nearly 11,000 meters at their deepest point in the Mariana Trench, deeper than Mount Everest is tall. Below the waves lies home to billions of species spread across coral reefs, mangrove forests, seagrass beds, and hydrothermal vents. The deep-sea bed alone hosts an estimated 500,000 to 10 million species, with scientists believing 91% of ocean species remain unclassified to this day. Despite this astounding biodiversity, humans continue to put large portions of it at risk with persistent detrimental activities. In 2023, the 5 Gyres Institute, set up by Marcus Eriksen and Anna Cummings to carry out in-depth research on plastic pollution, published data revealing that 82-358 trillion plastic particles currently float on the ocean’s surface, equal to between 2.4 and 4.9 million tonnes. However, this figure is only the portion of plastic that floats; the United Nations Regional Information Centre for Western Europe (UNRIC) estimates that in total from rivers, lakes and oceans, between nine and 23 million tonnes of plastic waste reach aquatic ecosystems annually. These are the statistics that led Boyan Slat, at the age of only 18, to ask himself why no real progress was being made to tackle the plastics that had found their way into our world’s seas. In 2013, Slat set up Ocean Cleanup, which has now grown into a globally recognized non-profit organisation that utilises sustainable innovation to systematically clear non-biodegradable waste from oceans. The idea was brought to life when the Dutch innovator designed a system that harnesses the natural movement of waves and currents to push plastic into the curve of a U-shaped inflatable barrier which floats on the ocean’s surface, with both ends steered by a boat. Once the retention zone is full, it is detached from the main inflatable system, emptied into a third boat and replaced, continuing the process. The plastics on board the collection boat are taken back to shore and recycled. At 18, Boyan Slat designed a U-shaped floating barrier that uses natural wave and current movement to concentrate ocean plastic into a collection zone, creating the foundation of what Ocean Cleanup has become today. Photo courtesy of Ocean Cleanup . A perfected process now allows the organization to use an Automated Debris Imaging System (ADIS), which not only keeps track of plastic collected, but also monitors and maps the distribution of plastic debris using embedded AI. This helps to plot where to place their cleanup systems as efficiently as possible. The crew onboard also includes independent observers to monitor interactions with marine life, such as protected turtle species or whales. The key to the design is that ocean animals can easily swim under or around the system without harm. The retention zone has numerous inbuilt safety measures, including acoustic deterrents, escape aids for any animals caught up in the rubbish, and breathing hatches for mammals to ensure they can access a clear patch of ocean surface. In 2025, Ocean Cleanup launched System 03, which is almost three times larger than previous systems and measures up to 2.2km long, hoping to make even more impact on the effects of the climate crisis. The organisation has found that ocean plastics accumulate mainly in five different zones called ocean garbage patches, the biggest of them all being the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. This is bounded by the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, a network of ocean currents, which rotates clockwise around an area of 20 million square kilometres. As the currents churn the plastics piled up in the Patch, they break down further, becoming microplastics which are known to build up in food chains that are reaching humans. Turtles are eating plastic bags mistaking them for jellyfish, albatrosses are feeding resin pellets to young instead of fish eggs, and a phenomenon known as ‘ghost fishing’ is becoming ever more common as marine mammals get tangled in discarded plastic fishing nets. This is why this Patch has become a main target zone for the organisation. However, by weight 70-80% of ocean plastic actually arrives there by rivers, with studies suggesting that just a few major rivers are the worst offenders. This is why Ocean Cleanup tackles the root of the problem as well, working with government leaders, individuals and private companies to set up interceptors at points along some of the most polluted rivers, like the Sandy Gully in Kingston, Jamaica. These interceptors include barriers, barricades, guards and the Interceptor Original: an autonomous, 100% solar powered craft that utilises a conveyor belt to continuously extract debris and distribute it evenly between containers that can store up to 50m 3 of trash combined before needing to be emptied. All of which work together to drastically reduce the trash flow from rivers into the wider sea. In March 2026, Ocean Cleanup reached 50 million kg of debris removed. This organization is living proof that with perseverance and ingenious solutions we can come together to tackle some of our world’s largest problems. But how can you play your part to help reduce plastics in our oceans? So how can you help reduce plastic in our oceans? Every little bit counts. Refuse single-use plastics like straws, and bring reusable bags when you shop. Recycle properly, following your local program’s rules closely. Avoid microbeads in products like face scrubs, usually listed as “polyethylene” or “polypropylene” on ingredient labels. Share what you’ve learned with others. Support organizations fighting plastic pollution. Join a river or beach cleanup, and never flush non-biodegradable items down the toilet. The post The innovative approach of Ocean Cleanup appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Η διατήρηση του Cuatro Ciénegas ξεκινά σε μια κοιλάδα που έχουν οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Cuatro Ciénegas Conservation Restores Mexico’s Ancient Desert Oasis Reading Time: 3 minutes Cuatro Ciénegas conservation efforts in Mexico’s Chihuahuan Desert are reviving ancient pools and returning bison to the land, offering a model for desert restoration worldwide. Cuatro Ciénegas conservation begins in a valley most people have never heard of. Tucked into the Chihuahuan Desert in Coahuila, the basin holds hundreds of crystal-clear pools called pozas that Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas has spent years working to protect. These pools support life found nowhere else on the planet. The valley became a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2006. It spans more than 413,000 hectares, an area larger than Los Angeles. Within that space live over 800 plant species and roughly 360 animal species, many found only here. The pools themselves hold something even stranger. Scientists have traced microbial life in the pozas back nearly 500 million years. Researchers believe these microbes descended from an ancient sea trapped underground when mountains rose around the basin. Some pozas also contain stromatolites, layered rock structures built by microbial colonies. Scientists consider them living relatives of some of Earth’s earliest life forms, similar to formations found in Australia’s Shark Bay. Few places on the planet still host stromatolites forming under natural conditions today. Mexican scientists Valeria Souza and Luis Eguiarte made that discovery, turning a quiet desert valley into a living laboratory. Their work found more bacterial diversity in a single pool than scientists had documented across China’s entire Pearl River. The find helped convince Mexico to take the area’s protection more seriously. Protection came just in time. Decades of irrigation for alfalfa farming, much of it feeding dairy operations, drained the aquifer feeding the pozas. Nearly 90 percent of the valley’s surface water has disappeared since the 1960s. Churince, once the basin’s largest lagoon, dried up completely in 2016. That loss sparked a wave of local action. In 2018, conservationists won a court order forcing officials to close a canal draining two major pools. The ruling marked a turning point for regional water policy. Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas has since built on that momentum, becoming the driving force behind on-the-ground Cuatro Ciénegas conservation. The nonprofit works to protect the valley’s water, restore native habitat, and support ranching methods that use less water. Its programs also train local students in environmental science, turning former skeptics into active partners in the valley’s recovery. That shift in local support matters. Many families once saw conservation as a threat to their livelihoods. Years of education and dialogue changed that view for many residents, who now see healthy pozas as tied to their own future. The clearest sign of progress arrived in December 2025. Forty-four American bison arrived at a reserve called El Santuario in Coahuila, marking a major step in Cuatro Ciénegas conservation efforts. The animals came from a managed herd at Rancho El Uno in Chihuahua’s Janos Biosphere Reserve, overseen by the conservation group Cuenca Los Ojos. American bison graze on restored grassland in Coahuila, part of a new Cuatro Ciénegas conservation effort to bring the keystone species back to northern Mexico. Photo courtesy of Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas . Bison do more than roam grasslands. Their grazing improves soil structure and helps native plants recover. Unlike cattle, bison tolerate drought well, making them a natural fit for a region growing hotter and drier. The project brought together Mexico’s environment ministry, SEMARNAT, along with its national parks commission, CONANP, and several conservation groups. Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas partnered with the N’dee/N’nee/Ndé Indigenous nation to open reserve land for the herd. The Mexican Fund for the Conservation of Nature also supported the effort, reflecting the broad coalition needed to pull off a reintroduction of this scale. Officials involved called the partnership a model for Cuatro Ciénegas conservation going forward. Government agencies, scientists, ranchers, and Indigenous communities rarely align this closely. Their shared success offers a template other desert regions could follow. Cuatro Ciénegas conservation still faces real challenges. Water rights in Mexico remain tangled in overlapping laws, and some irrigation canals draining the basin remain open. Full recovery of dried lagoons like Churince could take years, if it happens at all. Even so, the signs of resilience are hard to ignore. Researchers have found that dormant microbes can survive in dry mud for years, springing back to life once water returns. A desert valley that nearly vanished is showing what patient, collaborative Cuatro Ciénegas conservation can achieve. Scientists study its microbes, ranchers adjust old habits, students learn to protect their backyard, and American bison once again roam land shaped by their ancestors. What happens next in Cuatro Ciénegas may show the rest of the world how to save a dying ecosystem before it is too late. The post Cuatro Ciénegas Conservation Restores Mexico’s Ancient Desert Oasis appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Urban Food Forest Transforms Singapore’s Skyscrapers into Edible Landscapes Reading Time: 3 minutes An urban food forest thrives 51 floors above Singapore’s streets, proving hyperdense cities can grow far more than ornamental greenery. Permaculture educator Andrew Millison traveled to Singapore to answer a deceptively simple question: how much food, greenery, and habitat can a hyperdense urban environment actually produce? What he found reshaped his understanding of what cities can grow. At the top of one Singapore skyscraper sits what is described as the world’s highest rooftop farm, an urban food forest producing roughly a ton of organic food annually on the 51st floor. Bananas, mulberries, star fruit, and water apples grow alongside pumpkin vines. Bees pollinate crops despite the extreme elevation, including kadong , a native fruit with a tart, green-apple flavor whose edible leaves are traditionally used in local salads. A nearby miracle berry temporarily transforms sour flavors into sweet ones, delighting visitors encountering the effect for the first time. Unlike conventional rooftop farms arranged in single horizontal rows of vegetables, this urban food forest layers vertically within a tight footprint. Tree layers rise above shrub layers, herbs fill the understory, and vines climb through the structure, creating a legitimate multi-tiered food production system rather than a novelty garden. The restaurant sourcing from this rooftop describes the space as inseparable from its culinary philosophy, using every part of each harvest to minimize waste while drawing creative inspiration directly from what grows above the kitchen. Beyond this single example, Millison explored how urban food forest principles could scale across Singapore’s built environment. The island nation has almost no farmland and imports nearly all of its food, yet government policy already mandates extensive greenery integration. A landscape replacement policy requires developers to replace any land they build on with equivalent greenery elsewhere on the structure, driving widespread adoption of vertical gardens and rooftop plantings across the city. One striking example of this policy in action covers roughly 200% of its building footprint in combined horizontal and vertical greenery, effectively treating the high-rise as a small mountain, with the ground extending upward through multiple stories. The landscape architect behind the design explained that root space is the central engineering challenge, requiring sufficient soil depth or widened planters, root barriers to prevent structural damage, built-in drainage systems, maintenance walkways, and anchor cables to stabilize mature tree canopies as they grow denser over time. Currently, Singapore maintains roughly 2,000 hectares of green rooftop space, but most of this greenery consists of exotic ornamental plants rather than food-producing species. The country spends approximately one billion dollars annually managing this urban vegetation. Replacing ornamental plantings with productive alternatives, while maintaining the same underlying infrastructure, could transform this investment into a genuine urban food forest network spanning the entire city, rather than a purely decorative one. Singapore’s landscape replacement policy has created roughly 2,000 hectares of green rooftop space citywide, with Edible Garden City working to transform this largely ornamental urban food forest infrastructure into a genuine perennial food production network using resilient native and traditional crops. Photo by Cyrill on Pexels. Edible Garden City, a Singapore-based urban farming social enterprise, is actively developing the plant genetics needed to make this transition possible. At Gardens by the Bay, the organization experiments with diversified, multi-tiered plantings that move away from monoculture rows toward genuine food forest design. This approach reduces pest pressure by diluting concentrated crops across diverse species, minimizes pesticide use, and incorporates flowering plants that attract pollinators while producing edible blooms. Perennial plants form the backbone of this urban food forest model, since street-side and terrace plantings cannot practically be tilled and replanted annually like conventional vegetable plots. Species proven successful at the test site are introduced to industry partners and community gardens, spreading resilient, low-maintenance crops including lemongrass, pandan, cassava, sweet potato, and Brazilian spinach, alongside traditional vegetables once grown by earlier generations before industrial food systems replaced them. Singapore currently allocates only about 1% of its land to farming, yet its extensive rooftop and vertical greening infrastructure suggests far greater capacity remains untapped. The research, plant trials, and structural engineering needed to convert ornamental cityscapes into a genuine urban food forest have already been completed and proven at scale within the city itself, requiring policy rather than new invention for wider implementation. What makes Singapore’s example significant extends beyond any single rooftop or building. The city demonstrates that food production and dense urban living are not inherently incompatible, provided cities are willing to reimagine landscaping budgets, structural design, and plant selection around productivity rather than appearance alone. An urban food forest at this scale offers a template other hyperdense cities worldwide could adapt, transforming skylines already covered in decorative greenery into genuine sources of food, habitat, and community resilience. The post Urban Food Forest Transforms Singapore’s Skyscrapers into Edible Landscapes appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Το Κάλεσμα είναι Πραγματικό

items.description: Ο Emanuel Kuntzelman έχει ιδιαίτερη σχέση με τα δέντρα. Καθισμένος σε μια μηλιά σε ηλικία έξι ετών, αποφάσισε να αφιερώσει τη ζωή του στην υπηρεσία του σύμπαντος. Κάτω από μια βελανιδιά στο κολέγιο, διατύπωσε μια ιδέα για να ενώσει τους ανθρώπους σε έναν κοινό σκοπό. Διαβάζοντας κάτω από μια ιτιά που κλαίει, του ήρθε το όνομα Holomovement για αυτόν τον κοινό σκοπό, ένα κίνημα…
items.descriptionOriginal: Emanuel Kuntzelman has a special relationship with trees. Sitting in an apple tree at the early age of six, he decided to dedicate his life to serving the universe. Under an oak in college, he formulated an idea to unite people in a common purpose. Reading under a weeping willow, the name Holomovement came to him for that common purpose, a movement he later helped realize. People also appeared along the way as if on cue to point him in a direction when he didn’t know which way he was going. “Sometimes the universe makes things so easy for us — if you're on that quest for truth, and you're willing to say it here and there.” Emanuel believes each person has a calling, a purpose, and trees and people are there to help us as long as we keep learning and seeking. In doing so, all can join in the Holomovement “to unite humanity through our collective purpose.”

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Κάθε φθινόπωρο, κάτι συμβαίνει στο σώμα πριν συμβεί στο μυαλό. Η μυρωδιά του καπνού του ξύλου που παρασύρεται μέσα από ένα ραγισμένο παράθυρο, το ιδιαίτερο βάρος του φωτός του Οκτωβρίου που γέρνει στο πάτωμα, και ξαφνικά βρίσκεστε κάπου αλλού εντελώς, πίσω σε μια κουζίνα που δεν έχετε σκεφτεί εδώ και χρόνια ή αισθάνεστε τεταρτημένοι…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall, something happens in the body before it happens in the mind. The smell of wood smoke drifting through a cracked window, the particular weight of October light slanting across the floor, and suddenly you’re somewhere else entirely, back in a kitchen you haven’t thought about in years, or feeling fourteen again for no apparent reason. Then you reach for the show you always watch this time of year, or the book with the cracked spine, and the evening softens. If that pull toward the familiar feels like something you should probably resist, it isn’t. Mental health professionals describe what happens each autumn as a predictable response to something real: the season changing registers in your nervous system as a small form of loss. The nostalgia that follows isn’t a distraction from fall; rather, it’s a part of how you move through it. Seasonal transitions are a form of small loss “Transitions mean something is changing, and change inherently means something is being lost,” says Janna Sayfie , L.M.S.W., co-founder and psychotherapist at Urban Mind Psychotherapy. “These ‘endings,’ however small, register to us as a form of loss. Looking back at something familiar anchors us to a sense of continuity and stability that we try to find when it feels like the ground is shifting beneath us.” That sense of loss takes different shapes for different people. For a lot of adults, the end of summer is the end of a looser way of moving through the week, a rhythm that’s harder to hold onto once September arrives. For parents, back-to-school season carries a weight that’s difficult to articulate, the passage of time made suddenly visible. And even without children in the picture, fall tends to settle in with a certain pressure attached: fresh starts implied, intentions expected, a vague sense that you should be doing more with the season than you are. Matt Sosnowsky , L.C.S.W., founder and psychotherapist at Philadelphia Talk Therapy, compares it to New Year’s, with all the same weight and none of the festivities. Your body recognizes fall before your brain does Part of why autumn nostalgia can feel so sudden and strange is that it often bypasses the thinking mind entirely. Sarah Haugh , L.M.H.C., founder of North Shore Professional Therapy, describes these as somatic memories: body-based recall that surfaces through sensory cues before any conscious recognition has kicked in. “Even before we know what these triggers remind us of, we’re swept away into visceral or nervous system memory,” Haugh says. She explains that this kind of implicit memory, a felt sense rather than a story you can retrieve, is the same part of the memory system that holds experiences from before we had language. Fall is unusually thick with these triggers. Wood smoke through a cracked window. The low angle of October light that somehow reads as different from September even when the temperature hasn’t shifted. Damp leaves, a candle you only bring out once a year, the sound of a school bus on a Tuesday morning. Any of these can pull a decade-old feeling into your chest before you’ve had a chance to ask where it came from. Why reruns feel better than something new Once the nervous system has registered the season as a kind of ending, it tends to steer toward the known. Sayfie puts it plainly: “Our brains tend to favor the predictable over the unpredictable.” We associate the unknown with risk, and when things are shifting, even in the small seasonal way they do every year, the familiar offers something new experiences can’t: you already know how it ends. Revisiting a favorite show or book is one way of meeting that need without quite naming it. The characters feel like company you trust. There’s no uncertainty about whether it will be good. Sosnowsky describes this as a form of safety-seeking, not a failure to engage with what’s ahead, but a way of steadying yourself so that you can. Nostalgia as a tool, not just a feeling Sosnowsky calls nostalgia “an engine for positive emotions,” pointing to research showing that wellbeing draws from three sources: anticipating the future, savoring the present, and looking back at the past. “Taking time to sink into a memory with gratitude and appreciation can help us elevate seminal experiences of joy, connection, and deep meaning,” he says. Nostalgia works that third channel. Don’t think of it as wallowing but as a return to something that still has something to give. Sometimes it carries grief alongside the warmth, which is its own kind of usefulness. A young person packing for college while their mind keeps wandering back to high school. A parent watching a kid start middle school while some part of them is still at kindergarten drop-off. Someone moving through a first round of holidays without a person they love. Looking backward in these moments isn’t getting stuck; it’s how the past gets processed. “Looking back, though sometimes difficult, helps us to integrate our past and make meaning from life,” Sosnowsky says. “In this way, we benefit from the people, places, and experiences that helped shape our lives by recognizing what remains a part of us as we move forward.” So when October settles in, and you find yourself scrolling down to the same playlist, reaching for the same worn-out novel, or clicking on the same show you’ve already seen more times than you can count, that pull isn’t something to override. It may be your nervous system holding onto who you are while the season changes around you. Remind yourself that you can gift yourself that return. At some point, when you’re ready, you can always put something new on. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.title: Η ψηλότερη ανεμογεννήτρια στον κόσμο φτάνει τα 1.197 πόδια στη Γερμανία
items.titleOriginal: World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached full height in Germany. GICON ‘s pilot turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, now stands 365 meters (1,197 feet) tall from base to blade tip, making it Germany’s second-tallest structure after Berlin’s TV tower . Official commissioning is set for November. Higher altitude, stronger winds Higher up, winds are faster and more reliable. That translates to more hours of generation per year, and GICON says its design could produce roughly twice the electricity of a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter. One thing to flag: that’s a claim about cumulative generation over time, not rated power. The turbine’s rated capacity is 3.8 megawatts; future versions are designed to go past seven. The rotor hub sits 300 meters (984 feet) above the ground. Building that high required rethinking construction. A crane capable of reaching 1,197 feet wasn’t realistic, so GICON used a telescoping tower instead. A specialized lifting system raised an inner tower through a surrounding lattice structure, then locked it at full extension. “365 meters – this is an overwhelming moment for our entire team,” said GICON founder and CEO Jochen Großmann. “What was long a challenging idea and then an equally challenging construction project now stands as a globally unique facility in Schipkau.” A second tier for existing wind farms GICON and its funder, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation (SPRIND), aren’t pitching these turbines as replacements for existing wind farms. The plan is to stack them above. A “second tier” of tall turbines with their rotors spinning above those of conventional turbines already in the ground, adding generation without touching any new land. Germany’s existing wind farms could potentially fit up to 4,000 of them, per the companies’ own estimate. That’s a significant amount of added capacity without a single new wind farm permit. The Schipkau turbine is still a pilot, and the yield projections haven’t been proven in operation yet. GICON and SPRIND are in talks with wind energy companies about commercialization, with series production as the goal. Everything depends on what the numbers look like once it’s running. items.description: Ένα παντρεμένο ζευγάρι από την Καλιφόρνια έχει κάνει αποστολή του να φωτογραφίσει και τα 40 είδη άγριων γατών στη Γη — και έχουν μόνο ένα ακόμα μπροστά τους. Οι εκπληκτικές εικόνες χρησιμεύουν για την ευαισθητοποίηση σχετικά με τα ζώα, πολλά από τα οποία είναι ευάλωτα ή απειλούνται με εξαφάνιση. Μέχρι στιγμής, ο Sebastian Kennerknecht και η Rachel Tobias έχουν ταξιδέψει σε 33 χώρες σε πέντε ηπείρους και…
items.descriptionOriginal: A married California couple has made it their mission to photograph all 40 wild cat species on Earth — and they only have one more to go. The stunning images serve to raise awareness about the animals, many of which are vulnerable or endangered. So far, Sebastian Kennerknecht and Rachel Tobias have traveled to 33 countries across five continents and photographed 39 species in the Felidae family, often using camera traps in forests, deserts, and grasslands where the elusive cats roam. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht The San Francisco-based duo has captured images of a cheetah in Tanzania, a tiger in India, and an ocelot in Panama. The only species they have yet to cross off the list is the northern oncilla, found in Central America. It’s a rarely seen animal, and one of smallest wild cats in the Americas. View this post on Instagram Kennerknecht, 41, has been photographing cats since college: He studied ecology at the University of California, Santa Cruz, to understand animals and became particularly interested in bobcats. Tobias, 37, grew up loving wildlife and was always drawn to the ocean and photography. The two met online, and they instantly connected over their love of nature. Fittingly, their first date was searching for bobcats. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht In 2024, Kennerknecht realized he had photos of 30 of the world’s wild cats, so he and Tobias decided to go for the full 40. In addition to photography, the couple run cat expeditions together, taking out small groups to observe the felines in their natural habitat and learn how to photograph them. They’ve raised hundreds of thousands of dollars through their work. One photo of a Borneo Bay cat brought in $120,000 for conservation efforts, and they collected around $70,000 per year for five years to protect lion species in Zambia’s Kafue National Park. They are partnered with Panthera, the world’s leading wild cat conservation organization. Kennerknecht told Talk to the Press that the couple’s work is “99% frustration and 1% joy,” noting that they’ve seen elephants crush their expensive camera traps, insects get into them, and humidity fog up lenses, rendering images unusable. “We set up a studio in the forest,” Tobias explained, adding: “In Malaysia, we set up six traps; we had to sleep in the jungle full of bugs and carry 60 pounds of gear.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Despite the project’s challenges, the couple is dedicated to ethical photography. They don’t use any bait or lures to attract the cats towards the cameras, so they can observe their natural behavior. “It’s much more successful for telling a story about the species,” said Tobias. “Telling a story between the viewer and the animal is really powerful for conservation.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht A large part of their aim is to introduce the world to the 33 small wild cat species that are relatively unknown, so more can be done to protect them. “If you protect small cats, you protect big cats,” she added. The pair also wants to prove humans can coexist with big and small wild cats. “There are lots of human activities that might negatively impact cats without people knowing,” Tobias said. “People want to protect natural spaces and help with coexistence.” View this post on Instagram In Paraguay at the time of this writing, the team has had camera traps set up since April to capture the northern oncilla, with a ground crew frequently checking on them, but the cat has remained elusive. View this post on Instagram “It’s been pretty incredible,” Kennerknecht said, “but measuring local awareness has been tough.” They’ve set up billboards in areas with wild cats, featuring pictures of the local cats with the slogan, “I’m your neighbor.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht As for their favorite species, Kennerknecht said his is a bobcat, as that’s the feline that launched his photographic journey in Santa Cruz. But for Tobias: “There’s nothing more beautiful than a female leopard.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Below are the cats they’ve photographed so far: Lion — Zambia Jaguar — Brazil Tiger — India Snow Leopard — Kyrgyzstan Leopard — Zambia Mainland Clouded Leopard — Malaysia Sunda Clouded Leopard — Malaysia African Golden Cat — Uganda Caracal — Yemen Serval — Tanzania Geoffroy’s Cat — Argentina Southern Oncila — Brazil Andean Mountain Cat- Argentina Pampas Cat- Bolivia Ocelot — Panama Margay — Panama Marbled Cat — Malaysia Borneo Bay Cat — Malaysia Asiatic Golden Cat — Indonesia Bobcat — U.S. Canada Lynx — Canada Eurasian Lynx — Kyrgyzstan Iberian Lynx — Spain Mountain Lion — Chile Cheetah — Tanzania Mainland Leopard Cat — Malaysia Sunda Leopard Cat — Malaysia Flat-Headed Cat — Malaysia Rusty-Spotted Cat — India Fishing Cat — Thailand Pallas’s Cat — Mongolia Jungle Cat — India Sand Cat — Western Sahara Black-footed Cat — South Africa European Wild Cat — Spain Afro-Asiatic Wild Cat — Botswana Chinese Mountain Cat — China Jaguarundi — Location Unconfirmed/South America Güiña — Location Unconfirmed/Chile/Argentina This article was originally written by William Ormes Roder for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.title: Γνωρίστε το πρώτο πουλί στον κόσμο με 3D-εκτυπωμένες προσθέσεις άνω και κάτω ράμφους
items.titleOriginal: Meet the World’s First Bird With 3D-Printed Upper and Lower Beak Prostheses
items.description: Η ζωή είναι λίγο πιο εύκολη τώρα για ένα νότιο κέρας στην Ολλανδία, χάρη στις τρισδιάστατες προθέσεις για το πάνω και το κάτω ράμφος του. Το πουλί στο μέγεθος της γαλοπούλας στον Βασιλικό Ζωολογικό Κήπο ARTIS του Άμστερνταμ υπέστη σοβαρό τραυματισμό που έσπασε και τα δύο τμήματα του λογαριασμού του και του άφησε δύο κολοβώματα, δυσκολεύοντάς του να πάρει φαγητό και να περιποιηθεί τον εαυτό του.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Life is a little easier now for a southern ground hornbill in the Netherlands, thanks to 3D-printed prostheses for his upper and lower beak. The turkey-sized bird at the ARTIS Amsterdam Royal Zoo suffered a severe injury that broke both sections of his bill and left him with two stumps, making it difficult for him to pick up food and groom himself. “He managed reasonably well with them, but he could no longer do everything a hornbill naturally does,” ARTIS veterinarian Martine van Zijll Langhout said in a press release . To improve his well-being, the team perfected custom prostheses that are “virtually identical” to his original beak. “A bird uses its beak all day long, to pick up food and, for example, to preen its plumage. Especially with a young bird that can still live to a very old age, we felt it was important to see if we could improve its quality of life,” van Zijll Langhout added. ARTIS Although several birds have been fitted with artificial beaks, this hornbill is believed to be the first to receive replacements for both the upper and lower beak. Should the beak parts continue to function well for the long-term, the team plans to publish a scientific paper detailing exactly how they created the prostheses, so veterinarians around the world can help similar patients. The process is technically complex, as every bird has a unique beak that perfectly aligns to its skull and other anatomy. If the shape isn’t exactly right for either part of the bill, the animal will struggle to use the prosthesis. To ensure their creation would be a success, van Zijll Langhout and her colleagues performed a CT scan of the bird’s head as well as the broken beak pieces. The prostheses were then 3D-printed from plastic, and orthopedic surgeons meticulously attached them using titanium components. View this post on Instagram One of the biggest risks with a procedure like this is that the bird will reject the new beak, which could result in the animal refusing to eat. The zoo staff planned for that possibility and were prepared to have the prostheses removed if need be — but so far, all is going well: The team reported the bird settled in right away after the beak attachment operation and even appeared to be “smiling” afterward . And the day following the surgery, he began eating independently. “That was an incredibly important moment for us,” said van Zijll Langhout. “He understood that he could use his beak and began to discover for himself what was possible with it.” RELATED: From a Dolphin’s Tail to a Bird’s Beak: 7 Innovative Prosthetics That Have Helped Animals
